WILD WEATHER OUTSIDE; • Wild weather outside where the br.fe ships And fierce horn all quarters tht, four winds blow Wild weather and cold and the great waves swea. With chasms beneath them as black as hell. The waters frolic in Titan play, They dash the decks with an icy spray, The spent sails shiver, the lithe masts_reel. And the sheeted ropes are-as smooth as steel. And oh that the sailor were safe once more Where the sweet wife smiles in the cottage door. The little cottage, it shines afar O'er the lurid seas like the polar star, The mariner tossed in the :ws of death Hurls at the storm a delair, breath; Shouts to 1115 mates through the writhing foam, 'Courage please God, we shall yet win home:" Frozen and haggard and wan and gray, But resolute still; 'tis the sailor's way. And perhaps—at the fancy the s:ern eyes dim— Someboda 's praying to•night for him. Ah me, through t-as drench of the bitter rain, How bright the picture that rises plain I Sure he can see, with her merry look, His little maid crooning her spelling book; The baby crows in the cradle fair; _ The grandam nods in her easy ; While hither and you, with a quiet grace, A woman flits with an earnest face. The kitten purrs and tile kettle sings. And a nameless comfort the picture brlpg3. Rough weather outside, but the winds ot the balm -tin;a4te For ever float o'er that isle if calm. tke Oh friends who read over tea and toast Of the wild night's work on the storm-swept coast, Think, when the vessels are yverdue, Of the perilous voy.ige, the baffled crew, " Of stout hearts battling for love and home 'Mid the cruel blasts end the curdling foam. And breathe a prayer from your happy lips For those who must go "to the sea in ships ; " Ask that the sailor may stand once more Where the sweet wife smiles in the cottage doer. —From Harper's Maiiazine.

Ths greatest Icßalth is contentment wita a tittle. Good temper, lik a summer day, sheds a locightnees over everything,. It is the sweetener of toil and the soother of disquietude. A man is said to 143 absent-miniled wlacm he thinks he has ltft his wa.tch at h,rne ar;d ta},-.3 it out of his pocket to see if he hat time to return hipme to get it. No man is ever oil duty. In all places and at all times he is to he armed, w ttchful, ready for hit work. The Scrip- tares make no provision for "putting off" thc armour of God.—Unitfd Presbyterian. Religion is that nobler half of life without which nr:th:rg stands in a true balance. I-. wants tb.e same kind of practical training as the other side, and will marvellously help and steady that —Dr. Bush-rtell. Who huh a guiater combat than he that la'-aoureth to overcome•himseli ? This ought to be our endeavour, to con• quer ottrselves and d4ly wax Stronger and to make a farther growth in holiness Thomas a Kempis 1.-1 Let rue find iu Thy empoy Peace that dearer is than joy; t bosh 4:.: Out of e,if to love be lei, - • • -• And to Ileaveo ace/located.— Whitt i fir. "The meanest jlt [ever undertook," mused a Gilorado man," was that of apologising to a widow, oa behalf of 3 vigilance committee- wllicti hanged her htubani by mistake. It was hard to find ju.,t the-excve that would satLtv her." Daniel Ryan Kate, Q.l, for some time Recorder of Cork, uttered some gnat lon mots. Walking along the streets one day, he met a friend whose coat was much torn near the breast. Kane at once cried out, " Rtnts are enormons." "Well." replied the wearer of the coat, "Yon cannot siay it is Rent in Arrear." • = A youngster, on casing the old homestead from which _ thr. family had boon renoved for some time, and which the

• lad had often had pointed out to him as the house in which ha and his little br3thers bad been born, on seeingit removed L p-eparatory to the erection of a new one, surveyed in silence 1- tor a few momenta the chanzed scene, and then said, pathetically, "Oh, papa, we weren't born nowhere now, were we?" Nature only tells of 111 rd, pitiless, remorseless law. The fir.' burns, though there be a saintly martyr in the flame. • The tide surges in, though a Christian maiden is bound to a etake in its course. Lean over the precipice, and T n are dashed in pieces. There is no mercy in the electric cloud, in the ocean or the Land. Everywhere you see wisdom and power in creation and providence, but not mercy.— W. M. _

eeeheee Poor sad humanity, eletiet,ZlP i Through all the dust and heat, faarraaae,:, Tarns back wii,h Weeding feet, _ By the weary roll it came, Unto the simple thought By the Great Master taught, And that remaineth still : Not be that repetteth the name, . t ect But he thet deeth the - At an election for Perthehire,Sir John Campbell solicited a Mr. M`Gregor to nee his influence with his son to give his vote for Sir George Murray. Old M•ilregor said it was use- less, as his son bad plAged hirmelf to support the opposite party; at which Sir John gave expression te his displeasure by saying he was " not a true M`Gregor ; there was some bad blood in bins." "I wadna donbt bet there is," replied the' old man," for his mother was a Campbell." The scene was a )lay-field attached to a most respectable academical estahliehment. Boys were busy crieketing, and .engaged in other sports. Eepying one solitary little fellow stretched out on the grate in listless abandonment of all control over his lituhe, "Find the weather too warm for` exertion?" I remarked. "Ne," he said; " but when I bore myself dcing nothing, playtime seems se cinch longer." I have not yet recovered from the stupendous depth of this answer. Samuel Rogers tells one of the best stories of absent- mindedness that we have ever heard. His friend Maltby was its hero, and it was to this effect r—Otre day, while the two ware at the L ravro looking at t'e pictures, a lady en- tered who spoke to the poet. When h- r joined Maltby, who was cernpletely absori)ed, he 'aid, "That was Mrs. Blank; we have not met (pr to loug that she had almost forgotten me, and asked ma if my neree was Rogers." Maltby simply saide" Well, and W 3,4 it ?" Robert Kettle, of Glasgow, was of a jeyons nature. Every cbject seemed to beam upon bias, and the very things which would have irritated others only excited his mirth. Having left some temperance tracts at the home of a friend, he found them, on calling a few days after, serving the pur- pose of curhpapers to one of the young ladies, "Well," said he, " I see you have made use of the tracts ;" but im- rcedietely cenverted confusion into merriment by adding, "Oily ye hie put them on the wrang side o' yer head, twee." Dr. Jasper Main, who lived in the reign of James I. of England, was celebrated as a scholar and a wit. He dis- played through life a strong propensity for innocent rail- lery and practical jokes. Just before he expired, he told his servant, who was sadly addicted to intemperance, that he had bequeathed him " sernethiog that would make him drink." The servant, as soon as his master was dead, impa- tiently opened the legacy, expecting, of. course, to find a heap of treasure: but, alas! his disappointment was great in finding nothing but a "red herring." The Queen, when Princess Victoria, was one day reading the Roman history to her noble nreceptrese, the Duchees of Northumberland. It happened to be the passage where a Roman lady, having visited Cornelia, "the mother of the Gracchi," after the custom of the time, displayed her casket of precious stones, and called upon the Roman matron to produce her jewels in return, when Cornelia brought for- ward her children, exclaiming with maternal pride, "These are my jewels I" The jittle Princess here leid down the book, and, looking up into the face of the Duchess. said, "Jewels! Now, I think they must have been Cornellaus." TIE MAUCH TO MAGDA-LA.—To give in detail all the toils undergone by the troops on their march to Magdala might but weary the reader. They proceeded sometimes by plains, or watered valleys full of immense herds cf cattle, by mountain steeps, on the eminences of which were perched deserted villages, by hills whose sides were clothed with the gigantic tropical cactue bursting into white and pink bins. sums, and dells where grew the honeysuckle, the bramble, and the common dogo-ose ; at times by terrible gullies and stony ravines, where the paths wound along the faces of the hills, " when a false step would have involved a roll of a thousand feet down ;" but in these places tolerably fair roads were cut by the advanced parties of our Royal En- gineers and the Punjaub Pioneers, a fine-looking body of men, attired in loose cotton costumes, with claret-coloured turbans, and who marched with their shovels and pickaxes slung in addition to their arms and accoutrements. Some- times the troops toiled over plains where the luxuriant wild grass and stunted bushes rose high above the girths of tee horses; in other places where a wilderness of stone covered all the land—

_ Crags, knolls, and mounds confusedly hurled, The fragments of an earlier worid. The villages were found to be always surrounded by strong walls, thus evincing the predatory habits of the people; and In one place, amid the vast solitude, the troops, to their sur- prise, passed "a curious castle exactly resembling the old baronial piles one meets with in Scotland and the north of England."—British Battles on Land and Sea. HOW JONIS WHIFFEN BOUGHT HIS HORSE —ln the first stable into which he went he saw a horse which he liked, and which the dealer assured him would suit him ex- actly. Nor did Mr. Whiffen 0-ject to the price, £4O. He must need, however, show off a little of hie knowledge 80 he discovered that the animal's tail was not set on quite as It should be, that he was a little heavy on his hrelegs and the like. "All right, sir," paid the dealer ; " plenty more for you to choose from." Mr. Whiffen and the dealer moved on from stable to Stable, till, in about half an hour's time, they came to a stall, where Mr. Whiffen exclaimul, Ah ! this 1.1 more my sort !" "Capital Sound horse," said the dealer. " Something after the fashion of the one We saw first," said Mr. Whiffen. "Arout the same height, and much the same colour," replie,i the healer, " What do yon want for him ?" asked Mr. lyriitTen. "Fifty.ftumeas," said the dealer. "Make it pounds," said Mr. Whiffen, "and I'll take the horse ;" and the bargain was struck. Now Mr. Whiffen's coachman, when he came to fetch the horse away, happened to hear from one of the tabl...boys that the horse was not only something after the fasnon of the one which Mr. Whiffen had seen fl-st, tut that it was the very same animal. It had simply been shifted from the first stable to the last, and had been taught in the mealtime, dealers very well know how to teach a horse, to hold up Its tail and to look lively on it 9 hrs, ad for these quickly acquired accomplishments Mr. Whiffen bad in his innocence gladly paid an extra ten pounds.—Lein?re Hoar.

NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &c, The Glasgow Tramway Company have sold upwards of 50 horses to the Government, and will probably send 100 or so more, for war purposes. Two large stacks of new hay belonging to Mr. John Gre- gory, of Cotton, Salop, were last week set on fire with matches by hia son, aged six yens ; only a small quantity was saved. The value of hay is £470. A large transectian in cattle has taken place in the Pan Handle couraty in Texas. Mr. J. M. Day has sold to the Demilion Cattle Company the whole of his cattle stock, numbering upwards af 20,000 head, together with his ranche privileges, the price paid being stated at about £90,000 ster- ling. Heavy draught horses have become a necessity in the cities of the United States, or at least horses of a heavier stamp are being inquired for in all the large towns. it is foand that big horses fetch relatively mach higher prices than small Ones, and Uncle Sam has set himself to work to breed the eort of horse which sells best. The Earl of Dalhousie, K.T., paid a visit to Lord Tolle- macho last week, and accompanied hie Lordship in a drive over the Helminghana estate, for the purpose of seeing the farms, and also of making himself acquainted witia .the working of the cottage system, which his prevailed now for many years with such thoroagh success on this estate. A well-known maker of Cheddar cheese, Mr. Harding, of Merkshary, Somerset, England, gives the folloeing receipt for making a perfect rennet: —Mix a brine of strong salt and water sufficient to float an egg well; boil half an hour and let it stand till cold. To two gallons add six " veels" (dried stomachs of young calves). One lemon sliced, and one ounce of ealtpetre. It will be lit for use in a month, and will keep any length of time. The ram n sales of the leading breeders of Oxfordshire Dewne have concluded with satienactory result& The aver- age at Mr. Brassey's sale was £l3 6s. 9d.; at Mr. Charles Howard's, within is. of £l5; at Mr. Milton Dreee'e, 58.; at Mr. John Treedwell'e .56 shearling rams averaged £26 17s. His average last year was between £l7 and £lB, and this year's average is stated to be the highest ever made at any public sale of rams of the Oxfordshire breed. Dr. Sturtevant, of the New York Experimental Szatien, hee, from a series of experiments conducted by him, arrived at an interesting conclusion in reference to the preparing of 'teed for the potato crop. He says that be hate !eland that single eyes cut deeply are superior for seed in every reepee. either to plecee of potatoes or even to whole potatoes; and remarks that the deeper the cut, the better and earlier the crop. He believes that this discovery may result not only in an enermons saving of seed, but also in al incre:se in the produce of the crop. CHEMICAL COMPOSITION OF RICE, MAIZE, AND BAILKY. —Rice contains much more etareh, but also in proportion lese shaman and ash, than barley and maize. The comp- sition of different sorts of dry rice does not vary much, but the proportion of moisture in the raw grain is from 5 to 15 oer cent. Rico contains ahout 20 per cent. more starch than berley, and about 10 to 12 per cent, more than maize. Hut, on the other hand, barley and maize are ricaer in alba- minnaerometter and ash. The extractive matter, soluble in cold water, is ranch greater in barley and maize than Li rice. It is from 8 7 per cent. in barley, and in maize from 3 per cent., whereas rice only contains 21, and it is cern- pesed in each case of dextrine, sugar, the soluele portion of the ash, and a little albumenous matter (soluble albumen). The quantity of cellulose is considerable in nom decerticated rice; on the contrary, it is very small in decorticated rice En rice the inorganic matter is chiefly fnund in the husk, and as this has besides a great value as a food for the yeast, it remains to be seen whether the non-decurtie ated rice would not be preferable for brewers' purposes. Maize con- tain.; comparatively the larger proportion of fatty matter, hut ae this produces a bad result in brewing, different means have been proposed to rid maize of the fatty matter which it contains.—Biertrauer. A train of ten improved stock cars, containing 158 head of cattle, arrived in New York on the night of May 28. The train left Chicago on the 26th, and ran to Buffalo on Slow time. From Buffalo to New "York a speed of from 30 to 45 nellee was maintained. This is said to be the quickest trip ever made by a cattle train, and the condition of the 6IOCk „pn their arrival proved the excellence of the treatment they lad received on their long journev. The weight of the cattle when loaded in Chicago was 226,098 pounds, anieser- age of 1,430 pomade a head. They arrived in New Yo-k at midnight, and early the neet morning their aggregate weight was found to be 222,370 pounds, an average of 1,410 pounds each, howing a shrinkage of only 20 pounds a head. The ustrtl shrinkage for this journey is from 70 to 100 pounds. The cattle were watered at stations along the road,. and at the same time supplied with hay to be eaten while the train was running. The improved cars are each 40 feat long, inside measurement, or 10 feet longer than the ordinary cattle car. Etch car contains sixteen stalls, eight of which face to one side and eight to the other. These stalls are 4- feet in width, 83. feet in length, and 7,-1 feet high, allowing ample Tooth for the largest steer to lie nown and rise at will from his comfortable dried sand bed of an inch and a halt's thickness. They are separated by gates, which are cushioned, with spring fastenings, against which the animal can lean without being bruised by the motion of the train. Fur ahour one--iath of the width of the car the gates are permanent, and extend from the floor to the ceiling, but for the re- mainder of their length fold upward into the rigid section, 'thus making a free passage for the cattle to pass out'of or into the care. The gates are dropped down one at. a tine, as each animal is walked into its stall, while the ear is being loaded. The heads of the animals are between the stationary sections. so that "hooking" or quarrelling about feed ie effsctually prevented. In front of the beasts, along the sides of the car, are continuous troughs for feed and water. The fond, which may be cat feed or dry hay, is eteily intro- duced front the outside by raising a hinged board that is up- held by a honk while the feed is being placed, and after- wards -dropped and fastened by another hook on the outside to ptevent the feed from being thrown out. The water is received through an aperture in the top of the car, and is convt:yed directly to the troughs through pipes. The train wee provided with automatic brakes.

M. D. Tomasie, has discovered that when one metal is

ittbatituted for another in a solution of salts, the quentity of heat disengaged is the same for all metals, whatever may be the nature of the acid or halogen wily in the compound. From this law M. Tomasle has deduced several important considerations, which have led Lim to constuct a table, by the help of which the combining heat of 11 the soluble salts mAy be predieted. There aPpeare to be a special fatality attendirg scientific men thie summer. The accidental death in Algeria of a eistinguished young botenist, M. Auguste Roux, is an- neueeed. M. Roux had undertaken long excursions in South Algeria and Tanis, collecting materials for a work on the fiera of North Africa. He was an excellent swimmer; hut his been drowned whi!e taking a sea-bath. He was only 25, The Municipal Council of Paris has decided to mime a estrest in that city after Crsvaux. the unfortunate explorer. We 1-am n from the New York Xation that Prof. Jesnss D, Butler, of Wisconsin, by actual count, in Schmidt'e " Seeks- ps-re Lexicon," found that 364 words begienir g with A oc- curred only once, and 310 beginning with M, 9r needs, one-fifth of our entire stock of M's. He accordingly esti- tra'es the whole number at 5,000 and upwards. A small proportion are compounds. In nine nearly consecutive lines relating to Qleen Mab (" Romeo and Jnliet," 1., iv.) there are nine of three once-used words, including grasshoppers, film, and benefice. Even variety, in "Nor custom state his infinite variety," occurs nowhere else in Shakspere's plays. Amongst the papers read at the July meeting of the Asiatic Society of Bengal was one on the habits and iu- stiocni of birds and other animals, by Mr. John Cockburn. The author described the injuries inflicted on a cobra by a which included the dm:3 ttrguocot ;Oen (oHf beropthestfuasngast:iaspnudnfictatatteuds )grounds for believing the destruction of the fangs to be a deliberate act of reason, and not accidental. An instance of the crested serpent eagle destroying the maxillary bones of a snake was given, and the development of the specially protected tare of Circaltas Gelicvs G. 2W. speculated upon. CONTROLLING DREARIS.—A French investigator, M. Del au - nay, finds from experiments upon himself that the character of his dreaming may be controlled by stimulating various por- tions of the brain by means of heat. By covering his fore- head with a layer of wadding he gets sane, intelligent dreams. He has also experimented on modes of lying, which favour the flow of blood to particular parts, increasing their nutrition and functior al activity. He has observed that the dreams he has while lying on his back are sensorial, variegated, luxu- rious. Those experienced when on the right side are mobile, fall of exaggeration, absurd, and refer to old bitters; but those produced when on the left side are intelligent and reasonable, and relate to recent matters; in tbeSe dreams Dna often speaks. These observations may be correct BO far as M. Delauray is concerned; but most people who venture i to lie on their back, especially after eating, are apt to find their dreams any thing but luxurious. A very curious and interesting entomological note has been communicated to the French National Horticultural Society by M. Maurice Girard. It appears that the unfor- tunate vine has become a prey to a new enemy, the 11.y10b103 abietis of Linnmus, which Is well-known to attack conifers, but which has not hitherto been charged with destroe log the vine. The incredulity which was felt when the discovery was made led to a very close examination which resulted in its confirmation. In the vineyards attacked there is a pine- wood which apparently had been the point of departure for the invasion of the vines. Strange to say, not one of the !meets was found in the pine-wood, and the vines in its im- mediate vicinity were not the most damaged. It would ap- pear from this that the insect, having accidentallv been induced to feed upon the vine, found it to its taste and therefore forsook its natural food-plant. That which Ireland, was to English adventurers in the sixteenth and -seventeenth centuries, India was in the eighteenth. Between the two classes, howevei, there was a wide difference. The Irish-, unlike the natives of India, saw the.soil of their country appropriated by landlords of another ,race; bat iany of the English adventurers, at great cost, effected vast improvements in the country. The natives of India were fleeced unmeroffully by Englishmen, whose chief object was to get as much wealth out of the country in the 'shortest possible trine, and then take it away with them. : I have not yet dealt with any landlords of the Nabob class, and I thlrefore now propose to take the house whose founder was immeasurztb'y superior to most 21i:10-Indian nabobs.. - Tnree earls bc..ar the name of Herbert—Pembroke, Carnal.- von. and Pow's. Of the first I have already spoken; of the last I now propose to speak: Strictly speaking, the Earl isf •Powis 'is, not a Herbert, bu; a Clive; but in the femaie line lie iS descended from the Herberts' and inherits a Consider- able pbrtion-of the-estates once held by a branch of this great Norman-Welsh house. He owns in Shrdpihlre 25,086 acres. _ Montgomery 33,545 „ .

- . Total • I (30,531 „ t with a rent-roll of £62.925. The union of the two hsuses of Herbert and,Clive can hardly be desctibed as an alliance of new men anctold acros, foithe 'Clives are certainly as old a family as the Herberts, and held lads in the Marches of Wales long before the Herberts were known in the district. But to the Clives,:at the beginning of the last century, there must have appeared an immense distance between themselves and the owners .of that stately pile in Montgomeryshire keown to the Welsh as Castel' Coch, or the Red Castle, and to the English as Powis Castle' -For though some of the Clives had sat -in Parliament Parliament es county members, the father of Robert Clive had but an estate of £5OO a year, followed the profession'of a solicitor, was in embarrassed circumstances, and was glad to accept an Indian writsrship for his eldest son at a time when the East India Company was nothing more than a society of traders. I have no space to describe, even in the most cursory manner, the brilliant and rapid career of Robert Give ,in India. In 1744 he obtained a writership, in 1747 he tein- porarily exchanged the pen for the sword, and achieved his first successes. Soon after he was apnointeJ to the lucrative office of Commissary-General. In 1751 he again distin- guished himself as a military leader, and at the Age of 27 he returned to England with such large gains in the shape I of prize-money th it he was-able to extricate his father from pecuniary embarrassment, and to excite the wonder of the Metropolis by his extravagant mode of living. In two years he returned to India. lam more concerned with his gains than with his career as a soldier and administrator. Having set up in the room of Sujah Dowlah, a wretched tyrant, one of that Prince's officers, Meer Jaffier, as Nabob of Calcutta, he received enormous gifts from the man whom he had placed in power. At one time Meer littler presented him with £210,000, and afterwards with the quit-rent for lifetof the lands held by the East India Company nsar Calcutta, amounting to not fir short of £30,000 per annum. By the time Clive had reached the age of 34, he had an annual in- come of upwards of ;£40,000, and there is every reason-to believe that he might have made yet larger gains if head so c'dosen. Meer Jaffier, at his death, bequeathed to Clive a legacy of £70,000, which the legatee generously devoted: to the reief of Indian soldiers. While it_ is impossible to acquit Clive of the charge of heatingvinians by their own weapons, among which forgery was included, tt must be remerhbered that his enormous gains were net wrung, like the gains of many of his strcces- sors, directly from the sufferings of the wretched nativics. He played for high stakes With high players. The wealth he obtained was from princes, not from ryota, and it was Oot the fruit of personal extortion. In his later years, too, the efforts of Clive were strained to the utmost to restrain the rapacity of those who had been dazzled and demoralised by his own astonishing career. Fiercely assailed as Clive was after his final return to England; it is now generally recog- nised that the worst charges against him were unjust, and that the final judgment .of Parliament will also be the final jadgment of history. It was but natural that Clive, in the midst of his suc- cesses, shonld determine to become a great landowner. In his native ,county. Shropshire, the Walcots, of Walcot Hall, had been settled for many generations. Clive availed him- self of an opportunity to purchase the Walcot estate, which have since remained in the possession of his descendants, Walcot Hall being one of the seats of the Earl of Powis. But he wanted a residence nearer London. Sir John Vanbrugh, the architect for wl,loin was composed the well- known epitaph— -

Lie heavy on him, Earth, for he Eras laid full many a load on thee, purchased some land at Esher, in Surrey, whereon he built himself a house. In 1715 it was sold to Pelham, Duke of Newcastle and Earl of Clare, by whom the house was greatly enlarged and beautified. The Duke added to the property p4rtly by purchase and partly by enclosing a heath, and after his second title the place was called Claremont. Kent, a celebrated landscape gardener, was employed in laying out the grounds of— Esher's peaceful grove, Where Kent and Nature strive for Pelham's love. At the death of the Duke, Clive purchased the property and rebuilt the house at a cost of £lOO,OOO. The neigh- bouring peasantry used to say that the great, wicked lord had built the walls so thick in order to keep out the Devil, who wou'd one day carry him away. At Give's death the place was sold; and, after passing through several hands, it was purchased by the Government as a residence for the amiable Princess Charlotte, who there died in chi'dbed. • Of late the mansion has been the residence of the Orleans family. To return to the Clives, Robert Clive received a peerage, and at his death was succeeded by his eldest son, who married the sister and heiress of the last Earl of Powis of the Herbert creation.

I find it more difficult to obtain information in regard to Welsh property than in regard to English, but I have little doubt thw the Hei buts owed their property in Montgomery- shire to the favour of the Crown. During the reigns of the Norman and Plantagenet kings, the Marches or borders of Wales were the scene of constant struggles between the Welsh and the Barons. At length Mortimer, Earl of March, the favourite of the Queen of Edward 11, became the most powerful baron in that district, seating himself at Wigmore, in Herefordshire. He came to a ignominious end, but his descendants obtained the restoration of their lands. A Mor- timer heiress at last brought them by marriage to the Royal Family, and for some time they were in the possession of the Crown. The great stronghold on the English side was Montgomery Castle, which appears to have been given into the custody of Sir Richard Herbert by Edward IV. By what process this castle, and the great estates in Montgii. meryshire, ultimately came into the absolute possession of the Herberts I am unable to say, but it is not at all probable that they acquired either by purchase: Powis Castle itself, ! by the way, was purchased by the Herberts of the Greys in the reign of Elizabeth. The Richard Herbert just mentioned was brother of William Herbert, Earl of Pembroke, and, like him, was a staunch adherent of the Yorkist cause during the Wars of the Roses. Richard Herbert, during a Welsh war laid siege to Harlech Castle, which made a stout defence. It is said that the popular Welsh tune, "The March of the Men Of Harlech," was composed in.commemoration of theevent; so, the English words now wedded to the tune are sadly out of place. There is another story in referenceto this siege which I would fain believe to be true. Dafydd ap Ivan ap Einion only surrendered the castle on condition that his life should be spared; nevertheless Edward IV. would have exe- cuted his vanquished foe had not Sir Richard Herbert de- manded of the King that either he should restore the brave WelAman to the castle, and send some one else to take it, or else take his own life instead of his prisoner's. Sir Richard, like his brothel, was afterwards beheaded by the victorious Lancastrians. One of his younger sons re-obtained posses- sion of Montgomery Castle, and in the reign of Henry VIII. was Steward of the Marches of North Wales and East Wales. His son, as already noted, increased his estates by purchase. Of the grandsons of the latter the fifth was George Herbert, the poet; the eldest became Lord Herbert of Cherbury. Cherbury, by the way, is a little town on the Shropshire side of the border, two or three miles from Montgomery, and has

THE PRISON LIFE OF MICHAEL DAVITT.
ET THE AUTHOR OF "SKETCHES OF CONVICT LIFB," we. CHAPTER VL—DAVITT'S RELEASE FROM DARTMOOR: SENT TO PRISON AGAIN: CONVICT LIFE A 1( POET- LAND.

When a convict is about to be released on ticket-of-leave, he is not left in ignorance of the subject. He can calculate by means of "mark register card" exactly to a day how loughe inuetserve before he is entitled to his license;- and three months before that day he asks the governor's permis- sion to "grow his hair." Leave to that effect hairing been obtained, he counts the days, the hours even, that must elapse ere the three months expires, and he can depart, with as much freedom as his ticket-of-leave will give him. But there is still a great deal of mystery observed by the officials as to his actuafrelease. For several days prior to his discharge he is kept on the tenter hooksof expectation. Every mbru- ing when the men leave chapel, he lisfens attentivey. in hopeskif, hearing the, principal Warder call Out his -ifrison number,'-and, on his answering, to receive a summons to the cells. &range as it may seem, every convict before being 'released on license has to pass the last 21 hours of his im- prisonment in the punishment cells. It is hard to say what is the exact motive of the authorities in such a curious pro- cedure, but the fact Ternains. If the convict is in one of the public world; prisOni—Chatham, Portland, "Dartmoor, Park- hurst, or Woking—he is sent to Millbank to. be discharged, and is compelled to travel in the convict dress handcuffed, and accompanied by a convict warder' in uniform, the authorities appare, tly being determinei to keep up. the prisoner's degradatiou to the last Minute prior to his dia- charge. - -

Up to the time of his actual release, Mr. David had not the least idea at the Government's intentions, ,He had served nearly seven years and a half, and probably rooked forward to obtaining a ticket of leave in another four years. Butoen the morning of the 19 December, 1877, he was taken .from hie ordinary, cell to the punishment cells, donbtless- -until informed of his prospective release—wondering Which -of the thousand-and-ono prison offences he had committed. But the usual precedere of signing the prisou hooka having been gone through he was taken_from Dartmoor to Nilthank, and the next day set at liberty .on a special license. Filled- with a sense of the wrongs he had suffered ftt Dartmoor, Mr. -Devitt 'gave evidence before the Penal Servitude Commission, referriog especially to the crUelties practised by warders and other superior officere on the un- fortunate beings tinder their charge. • From the minutes of that evidence the writer has obtained some of the facts given in thepresent narrative. Mr. Devitt then stated, as one instance of the exceptionally harsh treatment to which helves subjected, that he had been coefined in the penal class [punishment:l .cells for fifteen months, for, greater 'security. - During his long imprisonment, Mr. Devitt probably thought deeply of: the wrongs of his couutry, for on his liberation he entered heart and soul into the projects of the Irish agitator. Becoming mere and more reckless in his diatribes against the Government, and in faystutaf resistance, he was again arrested on the 19th November, 1879, when be had been at liberty a year and eleven months. But there was no intention to treat him as an ordinary convict sent back to serve out the remainder of his license. It was Merely in order to keep- him in safe custody- that he 'Was sent to rortland, that prison being considered the most healthy for a- convict estu4lerlng from a chest complaint, as Devitt weel at. e tlift time of his re-arrest. The routine of prison life -it Portland was far different .to whetit had beeneatDartutioot. At the latter prison Devitt, as I have shown in„prevjous .chapters, was subjected to all kinds of petty indignities and annoyance.. He had to work . hard, and was half-starved. Except that be was a prisoner, experietbe,eeof Portland were very different. His diet , was good, he was located in one of the new and greatly improved .cells' very much larger and better ventilated than, those to which he had been accustomed at Dartmoor, and found no fault when Visited by his frieeds—an amelioration -of his impriioninentnot allowed at Dartmoor—with. the way in wlich fie was-treated. He was allowed to work in a little garden in the infirmary grounds, the same piece of garden which a convict almost as remarkable as Devitt himself— Roupell, the banker, and ex-member for Lam'oeth—culti- vated-during his stay at Portland. Of Davitt's experience at Portland very little has trauspira, but a few anecdotes of other remarkable convicts who have been located there will doubtless be read with interest. • A convict who has published some of his experiences thus describes Roupell : —"I foiled him a tolerably intelligent man, but not perticulart so. I think I shall be doing him no injustice when I say that most of his reading was done after his con- viction.' The little knowledge he possessed was very super- flcial, and he impressed me with-the idea that it could have been nothing but ready morreyf-and--beer which deluded the electors .of Lambeth into supposing him a statesman. Win., Roupell told one that after finishing his 'separates he had been sent to -Portsmouth,- and had- there been compelled to work in the i"chain-cable gang in the dockyard. Fine wotk for a gentleman,' he remarked, 'polishing Cliaies.' I asked him if he was in good health, and he said Oh, yes ; but I am not going to do that sort of thing.' . But he had to do it, for a governor who was not open to outside influences was then in authority at. Portsmouth, and Roupell's friends could produce no. impression upon him •, Roupell was treated • with-humanity and impartial justice, but with no favour. William Roupell, hoeing that Captain Harvey was not to be I tampered with, pulled another s:ring. Ihroueli some influenca brought to bear upon the directors he was trans- ferred to Portland, and his future path was strewn with roses. He was soon.installed as head nurse in the infirmary. He bad - had the good hirtune to- be convicted before the passing of the Act of 1864, so that he Was entitled to a'very different diet to that served out to:the rest of the prisoners, and better diet, in fact, than can be regularly obtained by : the best and most honest of, English anecbanics. Roupell, however, was not satisfied with that. • By some .neans or ether he got-on the blind side of governor and doctors, and, there was no luxury ordered to any sick Man which was not the Command of Roupell. I taste/ neither fish nor poultry, game nor fruit for nearly six years, but I saw him get such luxuries every day, and he never lacked port mine, stout, or brandy. In the nice piece of garden in the infimary grounds, in which be whiled away his idle hours, he built ; himself a summer house and a grotto, 'and had a pleasant. time tending his flowers." .

This is probably a fair picture of the life led by Davitt at Portland. His friends were allowed to visit him, be had no task of work, his diet was good, and his health greatly im- proved. When the Government determined in Ike beginning of May last to try a concilietory policy in Ireland, Devitt was again released, and his constitution seenis to have been so much braced by his sojourn at Portland that he has since been able to work harder than ever in the cause to which be has app trently,devoted his life. Before the present narrative is brought to a conclusion, a brief description of convict life at Portland will not be out of place. Life at Portland Convict Prisomis somewhat different to other convict prisons, in consequence of its situation. It is built on the isthmus of Portland, at a considerable height above the level of the sea, and is exposed to winter gales, rendering it extremely cold and inclement. For this reason none but the strongest men are sent to Portland by the authorities of Pentonville, Millbank, and Wormwoed Scrubs; and it is therefore, only natural that more rigid discipline is regarded there to control the convicts, Desperate aeeaulte upon officers, attempted escapes, and suicides, are at Port- land more frequent than at other convict Kisons. From the report of the directors of convict prisons for 1880, it seems there were then 1,565 convicts in the prison on the last day of March ; no other convict prison contains so many. The work at Portland is very heavy, and perhaps accounts for the desperate attempts to escape. A successful escape is rare; it is seldom that a convict can elude capture until lie has discarded everything that would connect him with a convict prison. It has been done, in cases where the escape has been assisted by the warders, and the convict has been enabled immediately on emerging from the prison to exchange his prison suit for other clothing. Convicts show the greatest coolness; ingenuity, and daring in their attempts at escape; but the odds are terribly against them. Every labourer in the neighbourhood of a convict prison is perfectly aware, that £5 reward is given for the capture of an escaped. convict, and this incentive has led to the re-capture of many a con- vict, who, so far as the authorities were concerned, might have got clear away. Attempted escapes are very severely punished—three dozen lashes, six months' cross irons, three months' remission taken off, and probably 28 days' bread and water diet. knowing that it is next to impossible to (*ape, the desperate convict,goaded to recklessness by re- peated punishments, commits suicide. One of these cases at Portland was a very sad one. A young man, not much more than a youth, of former respectability, and of some education and intelligence, was the occupant of a cell upon the top landing of the hall. lie had been suffering for several weeks from diarrbcea, and had been more than on one occision subjected to punishment for an act which it was quite impossible for him to avoid. On this Sun- day morning he repeated the so-called offence under neces- sity, and his warder notified him that on Monday morning he should report him to the governor. The poor young fellow had nearly completed his sentence; he had but a few weeks to serve; his anxious and heart-broken 'mother was making preparations to welcome home her prodigal son ; he was counting the hours which stood between him and free- dom ; his prison spoon had served him for a wooden calendar, and he had just scored if with childish glee "the daily notch." To be taken before the governor on ,the following day was probably to be condemned to another week of imprisonment. The threat was too horrible to the poor youth ; Ile was in exceedingly delicate health—consump-

tion had wasted his frame; he had told a fellow-convict that the highest hope of his life was that he might be restored to freedom in order to die in his mother's arms. Another week The thought was tuo dreadful for a mind weakened by a combination of disease, dissipation, and remorse. " Re could be patient no longer under "hope deferred." He made a spring (Nei the balustrade, and in a second his body lay on the flags below; the leap was as from the top of a four-storey house, and it was fatal. He was carried to the, infirmary, and when the prison bell ,had tolled for vespers he had gone to his everlasting reet. Was not the tyrannical warder morally responsible for the,youth's miser- able death?

In another remarkable case of suicide •at Portland the victim—a victim of the tyranny and oppression of a brutal and heartless warder—had seen better days. What his station in life had been originally was not,known, for the man never wrote or received letters. He had been sentenced to seven years' penal servitude for a series of frauds with worthless cheques.. He was exceedingly reticent, and had very little to say to hiafallow convicts, except such as -had been in good' or respectable positions outside. But even then he never by any chance alluded to his life prior to his colligation. This we's 'just the sort •of man tber`tiarders liked to torment; and-hiving once got him punished, he was thereafter often in "choky." He became more moody than ever, lint nobody ever suspected him of an intention to com- mit suicide. Repeated sentences of bread and water diet seemed to affect him very little, so the governor tried "penal class." Prisoners sentenced to penal class are located in a special part of the prison and the discipline is so strict that it is no wonder most Of the suicides take place there. Nothing strange' in the manner Of the poor fellow was ob- served when he was placed in his cell at noon. At four o'clock he asked for a library book, and selected one out of four whiah were named to him. At 4-45 p.m:.hts supper Was served. to him, and five-minutes afthwards he was dis- covered suspended by a piece of his shirt to -the perforated iron shield over his cell window. Ho was instantly mit down, both medical officers sent for, but it was too late— life was found to be extinct. The usual formal inquest was held on the body, when the prison officials were of course exonorated from any blame ;• a verdict of felo-cle-se was returned by the- jury, and he was buried at midnight. On his prison slate were found written ILe following lines:—

At last oh glorious hour! IM free, - I taste the joys of liberty. For years I've longed to see this day, And now those years have r..died away, Yet •,'m not happy. Vomething Seems To cloud the sun sad bide its beams.. 'Tis not that friends are cold. Oh! no: Their hearts with warm affedions glow. Why then should I so heartsick feel, 0.• thoughts se gloomy o'er me steal? Alas! 'Tis that I ra)w shall be An outcast from society;. Once I could look the world Rh' Ist:a— -/Tow hangs my head in deep digrace. Unsullied once was myfaii• fame, But now I dare not own my name. Bbciety then upon me smiled, But now 'twill shun me, au:10'0, Until, like Cain, I cry in mute despair, "My punishment is nwe than I can bear."

Those who read these lines and the story of their author will doubtless agree that it was a thousand pities that such a man should be hounded to a suicide's grave by. the brutality •of prison warders. Portland being a prison to which a large proportion of men with long sentences are sent, it is neces- sary to maintain strict, discipline. But the constant petty annoyances to which many unfeeling wretches among the warders subject the unhappy beings under their charge have too often resulted in deepair and suicide, and many a poor fellow who, had he live- to regain his liberty, might have. become once more a respectabc; and respected member of society, now fills a nameless grave in the little churchyard/ on the bleak cliffs of Portland.

Itsuttertow IN Tan OUTPUT OF IRON.—Following the meeting' of the Middlesborough ironmasters on Tuesday, the Scotch Ironmasters' Association met on Wednesday, in Glasgow, to consider whether they should also continue the agreement of reducing-the furnaces by 121- per cent. As one of the members has not received tke consent of his directors, the meeting was adjourned for a week, but the feeling,expressed was favograble to continuing the restric- tion. The Glasgow iron market waited the result with interest.

FARMING AND. TRE CORN TRADE.—The Mai* lane Express says—" More unsettled weather has• somewhat Checked harvest operations, but the rainfall has not been of a nature to do any damage, excepting were thunderstorms have been very violent. A very 'large proportion of the samples of grain which have hitherto been placed outhe market required more time, and the result of this 'hasty pro- ceeding has been general disappointment at the prices realised, which have ranged chiefly- between 403 and 47s for new crop samples more or less wanting in condition, Quite -independent of this particular feature of deliveries ad valorem rates have been declining throughout the country. Flotir, although offered in small quantities, is gradually losing value, sales being almost ltnpoesibleLexcept at some reduc- tion. Spring grain and pulse of,the'new crop has not yet been delivered in suflicient.quantities„to establish the bases of value, but there appears th joe.A fair inquiry for new 'mai t- barley. 'Vide for wheat off stands in London dull and past week, and to effect sales a reductioa from Monday% rates, *mounting fiom Is to 2e per quarter, would level:Alen neceaaary. In Liverpool values also de- cline 4. t •Maize,. barley; r oats, bean, and peas in London have nominally niaintamed,rates, but all have been cheaper to sell.

Tent LAND kSITIRI3 IRON AND COAL TRADES.—MANdIIES- TER, WFDNESDAY.—Both blast furnaces and forges in this district are still kept well employed. The condition of the market may be described as steady at late vales, with very little doing. For delivery equal to Manchester, Lancashire pig iron is still quoted at 465., less 21 for forgo and foundry qualities, and district brands remain at 478 Gd for forge up to 50a for foundry Derbyshire, less per cent. For finished iron there is a moderate demand, chiefly for shipment, and prices are firm on the bases of £3 7s Gd to £6 103 for local and North Staffordshire bars delivered equal to Manchester or Liverpool. The conditon of the engineering trades is without material change. Tool makers are still receiving a fair number of new orders. Afthough the coal trade is still ! very dull, there- has been, if anything, rather more busim.ss stirring. Housefire coals are moving off somewhat more freely, and for shipment there is a fairly good demand. , So far as fuel for iron making and manufacturing purposes are concerned there is no material change to notice. Supplies continue plentiful with pits on short time, and very low prices have still to be taken to do business. At the pit-. mouth the average prices remain at about 8s to 83 61 for best coals, 6s to 6s 6d for seconds, 43 91 to 5a 61 for common round coals for steam and forge purposes, 4s alto 4s Gd for hurgy, 336,1 to 3s 9d for good slack, and 3s to 3s 33 for in- ferior sorts. For shipment, Lancashire steam co il can still be bought at Gs 61 to 78 per ton, and good seconds bons e coal at 8s 3.1 to 8a 6tl per ton deliverett, either at the high level, Liverpool or at the Garsfam docks. Coke continues in fairly good demand at late rates, best qualities fetching us to 12s, amid coMmon sorts about 8s per ton at the pit month.

Tarn LABOUR MARKEL—The labour market has, if any- thing, somewhat improved during the last week, and hi several colliery districts there is more activity than at date of last reports. There is also a marked improvement in the pig-iron and steel trades of North Lancashire. At Barrow-in-Furness several more furnaces are being blown in, and at all the leaeting ports irori shipbuilding and marine engineering continue very brisk. Holidays over, the staple trades of Birmingham are again better employed, and at Wolverhampton there is also a fair amount of business. Navvies are still in active demand on several important contracts, and harvest is in full progress in many districts. In Sunderland the strike of bottlernakers is as yet unsettled, but the other trades of the town are well employed. At Hull shipping has been very active, whilst at Cardiff there ' has been a dispute which is now settled. In the textile trades no important changes have taken place, though at Oldham proposals have been made for short-time working. At Huddersfield the leading manufacturers are well em- ployed, and there is every prospect of employment being plentiful during the coming winter. At Leeds machinery is, as a rule, running full time. Metropolitan industries are on the whole well employed, though few new important building contracts are announced. The reports from the Kentish hop gardens .continue unfavourable, and very little foreign labour will be required. Emigration to the United States has again slightly Men, aud most of the strikes in that country have ended without gain to the operative-3. The order for infantry recruits for the Cape of Good Hope has been officially countermanded. Prospects of immigrants in New Zealand areKtnore encouraging.—Labour Yews.

BiIIGHT COLOURS AND DRESS.—The Arabs and other Orientals dress in very picturesque attire—white or striped raiment, with gorgeously tinctured turbans, and scarfs for the waist, silk fabrics from the Damascus looms, chosen with that wonderfully correct taste which Easterns possess in the arrangement of colours, so as to harmonise with each other and with the dark skin of the wearers Even in playthings for their children they show great artistic judgment in har- monising colours—one of these was an orange, into the sur- face of which they had cat a mosaic pattern, leaving the orange rind as a ground, and filling in all the triangles and other hollows with various brilliant colours, than, which (comparing small things with great) nothing could be found more harmonious in the mosaics of Italy. of Damascus, or on the walls of the Alhambra itself. Blue appears to be the most favourite of all colours in the lower grades of society. A licensed beggar in Scotland, celled a " becirs- man" or " gaberlunzie," was so privileged on receiving a blue gown- Pliny informs us that blue was the colour in which the Gauls clothed their slaves; and blue coats for many ages were the liveries of servants, apprentices, and even of younger brothers, as now of the Blue Coat Boys, and of other Blue Schools in the countrv. Women used to do Penance in blue gowns.—Cassell's Household Guide.
