div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDA Y, AUGUST 26, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDA Y, AUGUST 26, 1882.

A destructive fire broke out on Tuesday on the premises of Messrs. Wilkinson and Simpson, wholesale druggists and oil Rierehan te, Newgate-street, Manchester. The damage is estimated at about £12,000. CONFESSION OF MURDER.—An Ipswich correspondent states that, acting on information received from Stranraer, Wietownshire, the Ipswich police on Wednesday made inquiries at the tramps' lodging houses in the town for a man (whose name has not transpired) who had written from Ipswich to the Scotch police, confessing to the murder of Mr. Milligan in Glenluce Wigtownshire. The report of the ioyal Commissioners appointed to inquire into the Medical Acts was 'issued on Tuesday. It proposes that there shall be one medical council, and that in cacti of the three divisions of the kingdom there shall be a divisional board, and that the right of admitting to the medical register and the general control over divisional boards shall vest in the medical council. SEQUEL TO A CRICKET MATCH.—In the Chichester County Court, on Wednesday, Charles Howard, of the Sussex county eleven, sued 'Mr. W. R. Gilbert, the well- known Gloucestershire player, to recover £lO for services rendered as professional cricketer. The defendant engaged with some Chichester gentlemen to bring a united 11 to Chi- chesVr to oppose the Australian team on payment of £l2O. The match was played last June' but the defendant, inetead of bringing eleven, only brought eight, and plaintiff was requested to fill one of the vacancies. He did so, and cl limed £lO for his services, but the defendant refused to exceed £s.—Verdict for a. HADDINGTON BURGHS ELECTION—The result of the palling for the election of a candidate to represent the Haddington Burghs in the room of Sir David Viredderburn, resigned, was announced at Haddington about ten minutes to one on Wednesday afternoon, as follows :—Mr. Alexander Craig Seller (Liberal), 833 ; Mr. Walter Scott Seton-Karr (Conservative), 544 ; majority for the Liberal, 239. The result was received •with cheers. Mr. Sellar addressed a meeting of electors, and Mr. Karr addressed his committee, each gentleman thanking his friends for the manner in which they had fought the contest. A DOMESTIC TRAGEDY AT TOTTENHAM.—A murder and snicideltook place on WednesJay, at Tottenham. Mrs. Clarke, aged 35, wife of a packing-case maker, of Carribria-villa, Birbeck-road, had for some time been depressed, owing to the weak constitution of the youngest child, aged three months. On Wednesday she received vaccination orders for the child, and it appears to have caused her some trouble. About noon she locked her four other children in a room, and took the youngest to an adjoining room, where she removed some boards, and she was found lying with her child on her face in a water cistern beneath the floor. Medi- cal assistance was summoned, but mother and child were quite dead. ATTEMPTED MURDER THROUGH JEA.LOUSY.— Birming- ham, on Monday, Alfred Ellis, tinker, was committed for trial for attempting to murder his paramour, Sarah Nicholls, and subsequently cutting his own throat. The prisoner was jealous of the roman's intimacy with a militia- man, for stabbing whom he was locked up three weeks ago. The militiaman refused to press the charge, but when the prisoner was released he got drunk for a week, and while in- toxicated murderously attacked Nicholls with a table knife. She was found lying unconscious in a pool of blood with three dangerous wounds in the head, one of the stabs hav- ing cut a piece of bone out of the skull. The prisoner was arrested while attempting his own life, and both were con- veyed to the hospital. BOATING FATALITY ON THE THAMES.— A. shocking acci- dent has occurred off Dundee Wharf, Wapping, by which four persons lost their lives. A sailing skiff was returning from a day's excursion up the Thames on Tuesday night, and had obtained a tow from a sailing barge, which, when it arrived off Dundee Wharf, Wapping, encountered a steam tug having two eel schuyts in tow. The sailing barge tacked in order to avoid them, and at the same time it heavy gust of wind caught the skiff towing behind and sent her across the stem of the nearest eel vessel, which cut her in two, throwing all the occupants into the water. Mr. Stan- ley, pilot of the eel boats, saved two out of the six occu- pants of the skiff, a man named Hunt and his daughter; bet Mrs. Hunt and a Mrs. Siggers and her two grown up daughters were drowned. A LIVERPOOL SOLICIICOR KILLED ON SNOIVDOW.—MT. Thomas George Disenore, solicitor, of Liverpool, was killed on Sunday by a fall down a precipice on Snowdon. The unfortunate gentleman was a member of the firm of Thornely and Dismore, Water-street,, Liverpool, and his father is a well-known jeweller and goldsmith in that city. On Saturday Mr. Dismore, who had recently returned from a Swiss tour, started for a trip in Wales, accompanied by Mr. Norton, a Liverpool solicitor, and on Sunday morning they attempted an ascent of Snowdon on the Llanberis side. Although an expert mountaineer, and having whilst in Switzerland made an ascent of the Matterhorn in safety, the deceased gentleman missed his footing and fell, sustaining fatal injuries. Mr. Dismore was treasurer of the Liverpool Junior Reform Club. •

PRITA.TE PARCELS FOR THE EAST.—Permisssion to send private parcels free of charge to officers and others belong- •ine. to the fleet or the army in the East will be granted only to their relatives or to the recognised army and navyagents. All applications must be made to the Director of Transports, Admiralty, London (with the word "parcel "legibly written in the left-hand corner), by whom an order will be issued to the applicant, which must be sent with the parcel, free of charge, to the Royal Victoria Yard, Deptford, where a parcel office has been established. Parcels nmet he securely packed I and legibly addressed. They must not contain letters, pro- visions, or dangerous articles, and must not exceed three I cubic. feet in measurement or 561 in weight. They will in I no case be forwarded by mail steamers, but only by Govern- I ment store ships and transports as opportunities offer. Ap- plications must contain full particulars, and parcels not in accordance with the regulations will be rejected at the par- I cel office. Forms of application can be obtained at the Transport Department, Admiralty, or at the Royal Victoria Yard, Deptford. TRH HOP HAnynsr.—Reports from the hop-growing districts are, generally speaking, less favourable, the weather during the past week having been wet' and altogether un- kindly. In Kent the plantations have made little if any progress, and complaints come from all parts of the ravages of mauld, which in many instances has attacked the lion flowers. Thus a farther source of trouble has been cast upon the growers, who are now resorting to tbe use of the sulphurator, with a view to check the further spread of the disease. While, however, some of the hitherto more pro- mising grounds have gone back, there is a general report of improvement in what had been considered as absolutely hopeless gardens. This is notably the case in East Kent, where plants that had turned black from blight have sud- denly begun to develop in a surprising manner, and now look like growing a fair sprinkling of hops. Picking will commence in the Faversham district on Monday in next week, but will not be general for a week or ten days later. The best hops will be grown in that district and in the Isle of Thanet. The gardens in the last-named district are, in- deed, most luxuriant, and promise-immense returns to the growers. The Mid-Kent and Sussex grounds are not going on any better than they were a week ago, but politics that have 'suffered the least will be ready for gathering at the middle of next week. THE LEIGH SMITH EXPEDITION.—The captain of the Eiraz Mr. Lofll7, arrived in Dundee late on Sunday night. He Says that the hut they built at Cape Flora had a sail for a covering. It was 39ft. long and 12a. wide, with walls 3ft. thick. They attempted to blow up the decks of the Eira with gun cotton, in order to get out some of the pro- visions, but the fuse would not light. On October 21 the sun disappeared, and they did not see it again until March 23 this year. Fortunately the whole of the crew remained well, with the exception of the first and second mate, the former suffering with a sore arm, and the latter with a cancer on the lip: There was no trace of scurvy. In the course of the winter they experienced many severe gales of wind with much drifting snow. So much did the snow drift that their but was completely buried out of sight. Not- withstanding that it was covered with snow, -with all the crew living and cooking in it, the thermometer was at zero for a considerable time, while outside the spirits of wine froze in the bulb at 45 degrees below Zero. None of the men were in the least disturbed by their situation, and each did all he could to amuse his comrades.

EXECUTION AT LIVERPOOL. William Turner, 45 years of age, a collier, was executed on Monday morning at Kirk- dale Prison, Liverpool, for the murder of his wife at Skel- masciale, near Orrnskirk, on the 23rd June. The crime was one of unrelieved brutality, the prisoner h wing gone home, put on a pair of heavy clogs, and, announcing his intention to kill her, proceeded to kick the unfortunate woman to death. He was found guilty after a brief trial before Mr. Justice North, and sentenced to death. The circumstances of the case were of so simple and at the same time so brutal a nature that not a vestige of public sympathy or even in- terest was aroused in the prisoner's case. He was un- visited whilst in gaol, and no effort was made to secure a commutation of his sentence. The execution rook place at eight o'clock on Monday morning, Marwood being the hangman. No reporters were admitted to the execution itself, but representatives of the press were present at the inquest a couple of hours afterwards. The Governor of the gaol, Major Leggett, stated, in reply to inquiries, that Mar- wood had given the convict a drop of no less than Oft. 3in., and that death was instantaneous. The convict paid great attention to the ministrations of the Protestant chaplain and of a Scripture reader. He walked to the scaffold with greater firmness than had been exhibited at any. execution within the recollection of the warders of the gaol. A NEW METHOD or COAL—GETTING.—On Monday, a series of interesting experiments took place in the workings of the Wharncliffe Silkstone Colliery, near Sheffield, the object being to test the new method of winning coal by the use of compressed lime instead of blasting pawder. These collieries, which are amongst the largest in South Yorkshire, employing over six hundred hands, were opened in 1854, arm have been remarkably free from explosions, though eras is met with in the workings. The experiments, which were witnessed by the officials of this and other collieries, took place in the Parkgate seam. A hole about three inches in diameter and four feet deep was drilled through the solid , coal, and cleaned out. A perforated iron tube was then inserted, and the lime cartridge, three inches long, put in. When the lime had been rammed home and the hole made up, a force pump was used to inject water into the bottom of the tube around the cartridge. Simultaneously with the injection of the water the rending process began, and in 30 minutes about 10 tons of coal came down, almost in an un- broken mass, one piece being 9 feet long. Of the whole of the fall not more than 6 per cent. of the coal was "small," a much smaller percentage than under the old system. A second trial was made in another part of the pit, and the result was exceedingly satisfactory to the colliery officials. It is anticipated that compressed lime will eventually super- sede the use of blasting powder, and thus revolutio.nise the system of winning coal.
Mr. Justice North on Thursday made an order changing the venue of the Freethinker trial to Middlesex. .

Two men, named James Longman and Thomas Burke, were bathing off 6trad.bally, Ireland, on Thursday mornirg, when the former got out of his depth. Burke went to his assistance but failed to rescue him, and both were drowned. . _ _

An unconfirmed report was published on Thursday even- ing in Belfast that Mr. Gladstone intended making 4t week's tour in the north of Ireland with Mrs. Gladstone and his son Herbert during the Parliamentary interval. A special Lloyd's telegram from Muros (North of Spain) stated that the steamer Rotterdam, of London, 790 tons register, homiwarcl bound from the Spanish coast.to South- ampton with a valuable cargo, has gone ashore at Cape Torinnana. and will probably be a total loss. No lives lost. Assistance has b?en sent from Cadiz.

During Wednesday night same scoundrel entered a field in the occupation of William Earp, Dunstable Farm, Wol- verhampton, and cut off about five inches of the fleshy part of a heifer's tail, which the miscreant left hanging en a fence near to Earp's house. A platelayer named Jeffcote, in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company, met with a frightful death on Thursday. He was engaged at his work near Shilton Station, and observing a luggage train approaching he stepped on to the opposite line, and was immediately knocked down by the Holyhead express. His body was literally cut to pieces. The division lists in the Oxford local examinations,issued on Thursday, show that the total number examined was 2,137, namely 711 seniors and 1,426 juniors. Of these 461 seniors and 822 juniors passed. The first place in the seniors was won by W. S. Mundahl, Grove Park School, Wrexham, and the first in the juniors is J. F. Young, from Bishop Gore's Grammar School, Swansea. A petition for liquidation was filed at Bradford on Thurs- day on behalf of Matthew and Alphonso Wright, worsted spinners and stuff manufacturers, of Prospect Mills, Wibsey, and Peel Place, Bradford, the former of whom is also •a partner in the firm of Knowles' Wright, and Knowles, c•al- liery proprietors, of Brampton Colliery, Chesterfield. The liabilities are estimated at £170,000.

An eXplosion of gas causing the death of two colliers occurred on Wednesday evening, at the Holly Wood Pit, Silverdale, North Stafford. Two men named Lovatt and Wilkinson were engaged in the air roads of the pit when an explosion took place, killing them instantly, and injuring several other men. It is believed the explosion occurred through the deceased men smokier. During the severe gale on Monet3y the barque Arethusa, from Liverpool for Quebec, was driven ashore near Black- pool. The crew were rescued from their perilous position by the Blackpool lifeboat. The same gallant service was rendered by the lifeboat men at Po-trush, on the Irish coast, to the crews of two vessels wrecked by the gale. A " conference of the Chinese merchants in England," including "delegates from Manchester, Liverpool, Leeds, and Birmingham as well as Chinese from Cilifornia, New York, and Bombay," has been held in London, and it is stated that resolutions were passed recommending Chinese emigration to Cyprus and England, and condemning the opium traffic as the curse of China. By a fire which broke out early on Tuesday morning in the Protector Lamp and Lighting Company's Mill at Wore- ley, property of the value of about £lO,OOO was destroyed. For some time the cottages occupied by the workers in the mill were in great danger. Owing to the destruction of the factory 40 or 50 of the occupants of the cottages have been deprived of employment. On Thursday the Bolton operative cotton spinners issued a circular to their employers soliciting a holiday on Wed- nesday the Gth September, to afford them an opportunity of taking part in or witnessing the trades' procession at Preston Guild. If the favour be granted, they promise it khan not be taken as establishing a precedent for increasing the number of holidays at present recognised. On Thursday there commenced at Lytham one of the most important sales of horses in the Nertb of England, in connection with the Blackpool, Lytham, and Kirkham Agricultural Society. There were 333 horses catalogued; the animals offered being for saddle and harness purposes. Buyers were present from London, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Manchester, Liverpool, and all parts of the country. Reports published on Thursday state that the bay crop is one-fourth above the average. Turnips are everywhere a full crop. Potatoes show considerable evidence of disease, which will increase if the weather is wet. All kinds of , grain are better in quantity and quality, the increase being estimated at four millions sterling. The Scotch harvest, including turnips, is five millions better than last year. A gang of Cheshire poachers, who had invaded Flint- shire, have been neatly trapped by the Elintshire constabu- lary. Hearing that the poachers would arrive at Hope Junction to go by the early train, two officers rode there from the next station, and, jumping out, collared the gang. fight ensued on the platform,%ut eventually all the poachers bolted, leaving two large bags full of game with the officers, who possess the men's names. Dr. Lyon Playfair (says Life), who has sailed for the United States to visit his third wife's kindred, intends to make a special investigation into the manner in which the business of Congress is, and has been conducted. When he returns he will take a prominent part in the coming debates on the new rules, and his success or failure will determine ,the questions of his peerage and the India governorship. A few days ago Dr. ritley, of Brigts,, was called in to the house of John Kennington, a bird staler, at Brigg, Lincoln- shire, and found the father, three sons, and one daughter suffering from the effects of poison. They were all in a critical state, but prompt remedies saved their lives. On Thursday the dotor expressed an opinion that they would not recover. On Inquiry it has been found that the family ate some Irish geese which had been suffocated in transit, and were supposed to be putrefied. At the Bradford West Riding Police Court, on Thursday, John M'Clelland, manager of the Keighley branch of the Bradford Old Bank, and Edwin Holmes, grocer, were charged with forgery. It seems from the opening of the case, that Holmes gave a guarantee for £l,OOO in 1877, which was pur- ported to have been signed by a Mr. J. D. Myers, of Keighley, and M'Clelland as testator. Subsequently another security was given for an extra £5OO, and again supposed to be signed by Myers. Six weeks ago Holmes filed his petition, and when Myers was called upon for security he repudiated his signature, and the forgery was discovered. Prisoners were remanded.

At Wolverhampton, on Thursday, Edward Connelly, an Irishman, was committed for trial on a charge of fraud and robbery. The prisoner came to the Tanot Hotel, Wolver- hampton, and making the excuse that he had lost his lug- gage, was allowed to remain three or four days. He ran up a bill amounting to £2 155., and went away forgetting to pay the account, and t thing with him a pair of boots and a gold watch belonging to the proprietress, which he pledged. A large ;lumber of pawntickets were found on him when arrested. Inquiries by the police elicited the fact that the prisoner had been twice previously arrested for similar robberies at BugbYand Northampton. A fire which broke out on Wednesday morning in the Owersyllt Colliery, North Wales, was still. burning on Thursday, and seemed to be spreading. The lining of the shaft had become affected, and several yards had already fallen in. Streams of water were being continually poured upon the flames, butfwith little effect. All the work was §topped, and the damage must be great. The colliery belongs to Mr. Thomas Clayton, and last Thursday fire destroyed the stables, granaries, and machinery on another part of his estate, damage being done to the extent of £5,000, which is not covered by insurance. Sir Stafford Northcote, whilst holiday making on the South coast, was " interviewed " on Thursday by a deputa- tion of Weymouth Conservatives, who presented him with an address. The right hon, gentleman, in reply, disclaimed any political intention in his visit. He spoke briefly of the past session and the coming autumn meetingof Parliament, remarking that the evil of obstruction was too deeply rooted to be destroyed by an alteration of rules. The concluding portion of his address warned "their friends in the coun- try " to be ready for the conflict, which might come at a time least expected by themselves. RIII.WAY ACCIDENT.—The other morning a Great Western train from Birmingham, which was entering the Wolverhampton Station, left the metals, owing to a dis- arrangement of the points. Some of the carriages were overthrown, and a number of passengers sustained injuries of a more of less severe character. The driver, George Gil,hs, jumped from the engine on perceiving that it had left the line, but was run over and killed, whilst the stoker, who remained at his post and endeavoured to stop the train, esclped unhurt. Much damage was caused to rolling stock and the station fittings. An inquiry will be held into the affair. •

Sir Stafford Northcote opened the oratory of the recess by a speech at Bournemouth, on Monday, in which he ex- pressed great misgivings as to the soothing effect of Mr. Gladstone's Irish legislation, but admitted that as it should be judged by its results, it was too soon to express any opinion upon it. He took up a somewhat similar tone in regard to Egypt, but maintained that a wiser and more dis- creet policy some months ago would have prevented the , present war. Lord Salisbury has already explained that, aecording to the Tory idea, the wiser and more discreet policy would have been to have brought a large body of Indian troops to Cyprus early this year, and the most probable result of such an action would, Mr. Gladstone says, have been,a general European war. CONROY'S MALT COFFEE.—The patentees of Conroy's malt coffee have at length been accorded justice, which hat been been too long withheld. In the course of Nlonday the entire quantity of coffee in stock seizd on the let of March, amounting to nearly three tons in weight, was res,ored by direction of the Government, and thus some atonement, at least, has been made for what was at the time generally denounced as an arbitrary proceeding. This restitution has taken place in terms of the third section of an Act passed in the session just closed—to the effect that the duties under the Tariff Act, 1876, on vegetable matter, applicable to the use of chicory or ceffee, shall cease and determine. The patentees ha.ve,•therefore, been enabled not only to restart their valuable machinery at 34, Fleet-street, Liverpool, but to employ all the hands whose services were so suddenly rtispensed with in March. There was some exeitement and much lusty cheering on Monday in Fleet-street, when. the recommencement of work was made known. The seizure, it may be remembered, was made by the Board of Inland Revenue, who are permanent officials, and without the sanction or authority of the Government. There can he no doubt that the Government had been misled by the officials of Somerset House, otherwise the Premier would not have entered into some statements in regard to coffee in his budget speech. The difficulty, however, was solved by the repre- sentations made by Messrs. Evans, Sons, and Co., with the result now stated.

!The Egyptian gunners at Aboukir will long tell how the great fleet came swiftly and silently into the hay at ten on Saturday evening, how they were threatened with bombard- ment in the dead of night, and how when mornlng dawned every trace of ths expedition had disappeared, learing only the ordinary naval force to watch the forts. The great fleet had sailed away to Port Said, and many of those who had asked for passes to :see the bombardment must have been surprised to fiud themselves entering the Suez Canal."

div.head: CAMPAIGN IN EGYPT.
div.p: THE CAMPAIGN IN EGYPT.
THE SEIZURE OF THE SUEZ CANAL.

Witft the celerity that always distinguishes Sir Garnet Wolseley's movements, he has suddenly changed the scene of most important military operations from Alexandria to the Suez Canal. Acting in purpuance of an admirably- phoned mancenvre, and no doubt with instructions front the Commander-in-Chief, Adntiral Hoskins, who commands the squadron at Port Said, made alli•angements on Saturday for seizing simultaneously on two or three points of the Canal. Commander Edwards occupied the Canal with gun- boats, and took possession of Kantara, while Fairfax occu- pied Port Said and Fitzroy Ismailia. In Port Said the Egyptian troops laid down their arms without an attempt at resistance, but Fitzroy had to shell the enemy out of Nefiche, three miles from Ismailia, where they were supposed .to have taken up a strong position. Three hundred and forty marines were immediately sent off to reinforce him and make his hold of Ismailia secure. At noon on Sunday Admiral Hoskins telegraphed to the Admiralty that all these duties had been promptly executed, with only one casualty on our side, Commander Kane being slightly wounded. Thus Ismailia and Kantara, very important as basis of opera- tions for our land forces, were secured without any attempt at resistance. Sir Beauchamp Seymour and Sir Garnet Wolseley were in sight of Port Said before Admiral Hoskins had despatched hi, telegram. Having secured Port Said, Kantara, and Ismailia, the hold of the northern half of the Canal may be considered secure, and Sir Garnet Wolseley's communications as far as Ismailia are thus both easy and safe.

With regard to the southern portion of the Canal, the position is almost equally satisfactory. Major-General Macpherson, the Commander of the Indian contingent, ac- companied by his staff, arrived at Suez on Monday morn- ing, and later in the day the arrival of the 7th Bengal Infantry was announced. The Indian contingent thus began to arrive two days earlier than was expected, and as the whole force left Bombay almost at the same time, the full contingent may be expected at Suet within a few days. Meanwhile Suez is held by a small force, and on Sunday Captain Hastings with a force of seamen and marines and 200 Highlanders went up the Canal to Chalouf, the first statioa from Suez, and after a smart engagement with 600 rebels, who were entrenched behind the station, succeeded in capturing the position at the point-of the bayonet. Unfor- tunately, two Highlanders were drowned and two other rn,-,n were wounded in this gallant exploit, but the loss on the other side was about 100 killed and 40 taken prisoners. The bank of the fresh water cmal at Chalouf, which supplies Suez with water, had hem cut by the enemy, but was at once repaired and guarded. The capture of Chalouf sec:lres possession of the canal between Suez and the Bitter Lakes, through which it passes to Serapeum, only a few miles to the south of Ismailia, and consequently gives the British practical possession of the whole waterway between Suez and Port Said.

Arabi's reply to Sir Garnet Wolseley's movement upon his rear is said to be a retirement upon Damanhour, about forty miles south-east of Alexandria, the first large station on the Cairo line to the south of Alexandria, and the point at which a line branches off to Rosetta. He is also said to have an entrenched camp at Tanta, about forty miles south- east of Damanhour, and the junction at which the Damietta line joins the main line to Cairo. The point at which the Ismailia line joins the Tanta-Cairo Railway is about twenty- Aye miles south of Tanta, and as this is probably the first important interior position, after passitig Zagazig, which Sir Garnet Wolseley will endeavour to seize, Arabi's object in going to either Damanhour or Tanta is not very obvious. At neither place' would he be able to prevent a British advance upon Cairo. Zagazig, at which there is said to be a considerable rebel force, is about forty-five or fifty miles due west of Ismailia, and Benha—the junction with the Cairo line—about twenty miles further west and thirty miles north of Cairo. If, therefore, Arabi should not retire further south than Tanta, and the British forces should push on to Benba, the British Army would lie almost exactly midway between Arabi's camp and Cairo, and about seventy miles distant from Ismailia. Arabi is not likely to leave the way to Cairo thus open if be can do otherwise. He will no doubt endeavour to hold Damanhour and Tanta, because these are the junctions respectively for Rosetta and Damietta; but if he thus guards two junctions which command lilacs upon which no enemy is approaching, he is all the more likely to make a desperate effort to defend the position which is the key to the Egyptian capital and all Southern Egypt. Trains have been seen moving up to Arabi's camp at Ital.'. Dowar, with a view, it is supposed, of withdrawing troops from that stronghold. THE FIGHTING AT CHALOUF. Describing the fighting at Chalouf, a correspondent says: —I have returned from Chalouf, 14 miles up the Canal, where I witnessed the conclusion of a fight in which 250 men, including the 72nd Highlanders, with the blue-jackets and marines from the gunboats Seagull and Mosquito, bril- liantly defeated a force of twice their number. The fighting lasted from eleven till nearly five. The firing of the High- landers was remarkable for coolness and steadiness. The Getting guns in the tops of the gunboats worked with admirable precision, doing much execution amont the enemy, who had advanced to 100 yards of the Canal B ink. The enemy had broken the bank, thus admitting the fresh water canal into the maritime, bat this is already dammed up by the men from the gunboats. The fresh-water lock is also secured by the Highlanders. A considerable number of prisoners were brought in, and also a field gun. Two men of the Highlanders were drowned in crossing the fresh-water canal. The success is all the more brilliant on account of the extremely difficult nature of the country, consisting of low ridges and water courses. Lieutenant Lang, of the Highlanders, gallantly crossed the fresh-water canal in face of a het fire, and brought back a boat, thus enabling the company of Highlanders and marines to cross and take the enemy on the right flank. The loss on our side is only one wounded. The casualties of the enemy were very great, including the commander killed. The enemy fought bravely. THE VOYAGE FROM ALEXANDRIA.

The correspondent .of the Times, who was on board the Calabria, sends the following account of the voyage from Alexandria :—" It was announced by the authorities that the secret expedition would proceed to Aboukir, and it was generally assumed that it was intended to reduce the forts there, still insolently holding out against the Khedive ; but, although the ships arrived at four o'clock this afternoon, they merely gathered in formidable array before the naked and desolate shore, anchored there, and four hours after- wards, as soon as it was dark, slipped quietly away, whither I may not yet say. It was an inspiring and beautiful spectacle, as we steamed out of the harbour this morning. The sun shone, if anything, too brightly. When I joined the Calabria at seven o'clock there was not a breath of air, and the Arabs, always present on the quay, who, I am sure, cannot go to bed, gazed languidly on the brawny Life Guardsmen as they pulled and pushed at horses and baggage. Twenty-six stately vessels of the first-class, including such ironclads as the Inflexible, Temeraire, and Agincourt followed one another out of the port of the ruined city and • disappeared eastwards. Oar ship, the Calabria, carried three parties of the House, hold Cavalry, with their horses, destined to cut up Arabi's irregular cavalry on the march to Cairo. All along the decks peered the heads of restless chargers silently sweating in their narrow stalls. The sufferin4 of the poor brutes on the. lower decks must have been terrible, but no relief was possible. We started without certain know- ledge of our destination. Lieutenant Thompson, R.N., was acting under sealed orders not to be opened until he bad anclered of Aboukir ; and when they were opened they were found to order us to proceed again eastwards at eight o'clock. A Greek clique was warned out of the way, as she was about to sail across our bows, by 'a loud whistle, and immediately afterwards we cast anchor. The sunset was worthy of the pencil of Turner or the pen of Ruskin. The orb by which men work and battle sank with surprising quickness into the shimmering waves, and left the moon gleaming pale and trembling in a faint purple sky, changing by delicate gra- dations of grey and flaming chrome into a crimson flush upon the water. Then the ship lights shone out, red, white, and green, for miles and miles about us on every head, and while.niessengers were galloping fast to bring Arabi to the rescue of the forts, the ships were quietly got under way again, and filed off into the night." THE OCCUPATION OF PORT SAID.

Telegraphing from Port Said on Sunday, the correspon- dent of the Dzily News gives the following, description of the occupation :—'This morning at half-past three Port Said was occupied by 500 bluejackets and marines, with three Gatling guns, and the Governor, Ismail Pasha Mundy, who has been for five weeks a refugee on board the Peninsular steamers, was reinstated in authority. No resis- tance was offered. The military, numbering -200, allowed themselves to be quietly disarmed, and are now doing duty with the police in the Arab town, which is perfectly tranquil. The Governor addressed the troops, telling them that those who were for the Khedive could remain and would not be interfered with, while those for Arabi had better go and find him. The spokesman said they had eaten the Khedive's bread and wished to serve him. Two officers, well known Arabists, were arrested and sent on board ship. Mohammed Aboulata, commander of troops, a fanatic of the worst class and a very dangerous man, who had been acting as vice-governor for some time past, succeeded it is stated, in making his escape to Fort Guemil, with 120 soldiers. He had been feigning sickness for some days This morning I accompanied Major Talloch, chief of the intelligence department, all over the town, and when just at t dawn we went to make a call on the Commander we found the bird had flown. OurabPs Governor left for Ismailia three days ago upon the pretext of fetching his family, and has not since been seen. The occupation of Port Said quietly and without bloodshed is,! am assured- by Major Tulloch, mainly duo to the preparations made by M‘Culloch and Clarke, two clerks in the employ of the Egyptian Govern- ment, wllo have been untiring in their energy for several weeks past to achieve the result just affected. Every European in the place, irrespective of nationality, except those employed at the Suez Canal Company, hails the British occupation with unfeigned delight. The Canal people are vety angry.

THE GREAT "MYSTIFICA.TTON." As to the bombarding theory, a correspondent telegraphs: —"As to our great mystification of the Aboukir bombard- ment there lfas been considerable laughter at the gallant officers and energetic correspondents who believed Sir Gar- net's bombarding theory, and lay rolling about off Aboukir in small crafts to witness the great event. The German, Rus- sian, and Italian war vessels also honoured us with their attention, and were close at hand ready to profit by English experience in gunnery. It was the greatest mystification of the age, and we may hope that Arabi was also puzzled by it.

div.head: INTERVIEW WITH M. DE LESSEPS.
div.p: INTERVIEW WITH M. DE LESSEPS.

The Standirq publiehes the following account of an interview with M. do Lezeeps:-7ictor de Lessens haviug arrived here, I called upon him, and asked explanations as to the general rAtitude of the Canal Chtnpany.! M. de Leeseps said that the ErgHA papers are full of false and absurd reports in reference to his father. He never threat- ened to destroy the. Canal if the English lender?, and has I held actually no communicatiten with Arabi save despatch- ing telegrams, at the request of the Greek Consul, to inter- cede for Europeans. Every each reqnnt was granted by Arabi. On this point M. de Lesseps gave me repeated assurances. He is perfectly satisfied that Arabi will not interfere with the Canal if the English do not make it a base of operations ; but if they do so, he will certainly use to the utmost of his power his right of self-defence. rn order to preserve the Canal, therefore, in the interest of all the world, M. de Lesseps vehemently protests against England's operations therein. He would do the same, neither more nor less, if it were France instead of England that was fighting Arabi. What an outcry, he said. would England raise if the Canal were blocked in consequence of the military pro- ceedings of another nation. I pointed out the danger wh:sh threatened the Sweet Water Canal from the presence of Arabi's troops at Ismailia and other parts as necessitating an advance on Cairo and the duty of restoring order in Egypt. In answer to this M. de Lesseps insisted that Arabi would not injure the Canal if the English moved by other routes open to them. As to the question of sustain'ng the hedive's authority, he declined to enter upon it, simply declaring that he was no 'politician. The whole argument, in fact, rests upon the point that M. de Lesseps places implicit con- fidence in Arabi 's good intentions to all the Powers except England, while with England, with its grave and compl- cated responsibilities, he could not feel the same confi- dence. This is the sum of a long and passionate harangue. I transcribe the arguments without comment. That the , landing of English troops will excite Arabi to do his best to injure the Canal, may he accepted as certain. Whether he will have any power to do so is altogether another matter. For any interruption of the Sweet Water Canal we are already prepared.

div.head: PROCLAMATION BY SIR GARNET WOLSELEY.
div.p: PROCLAMATION BY SIR GARNET WOLSELEY.

The following proclamation of Sir Garnet Wolseley was promulmated on Saturday —" The General in comtnancl of the British forces wishes to make known that the object of Her Majesty's Government in sending troops to this country is to re-establish the authority of the Khedive. The artily is therefore only fighting against those in arms against his Highness. All peaceful inhabitants will be treated with kindness and no violence will be offered to them, their religion, their mosques, on their families. Their property will be_ respected. Any supplies which may he required will be paid for, and the inhabitants are invited to bring them. The General in command will be glad to receive visits from the chiefs who are willing to assist in repressing the rebellion against the Khedive, the lawful rnler of Egypt, appointed by the Sultan.—(Signed) " WOLSELF.Y.”

div.head: DECREE OF THE KEIEDIVE.
div.p: DECREE OF THE KEIEDIVE.

The Khedive has si4ned the decree charging Cherif Pasha with the formation of a new Ministry. The text is as follows :—"ln proposing that you should, in present circum- stances, undertake the formation of a new Cabinet, I address I myself to your patriotism and devotion, upon which I know I can always rely. I give entire adhesion to the ideas which you have expressed to me. All hearts and minds must unite in one sentiment, that of the re-establishment of the moral and material prosperity of the country. I also think that in a troubled time like the present the direct action of the sovereiz,n authority on the populations and in the con- duct of public business, should become more sensible and more manifest, and shall, therefore, use my right to assemble the Council of Ministers under my own presidency, to examine together important international and external ques- tions. As supreme chief of the Egyptian land and naval forces, I also intend to render this command effective, with- out, however, restricting the powers which the Minister of War holds from me. I know you share my opinion upon every one of these points, and firmly hope that your Ministry will contribute to make the country ester upon a new era of progress and prosperity. (Signed) TEWFIK."

div.head: MISCFLLA.NEOUS.
div.p: MISCFLLA.NEOUS.

The Assembly of Notables, it is stated, has decreed a com- pulsory loan of 80,000,000 piastres. A telegram from Tripoli states that the Arab tribe of Ouled Solimia is preparing to assist Arabi. Confirmation has been received of the rumoured arrest, at Ismailia, of Mahmoud Fehmi Pasha, formerly Egyptian Minister of Public Works.

We learn from Constantinople that telegraphic communi- cation between that city and Cairo has been cut by the British military authorities in Egypt. Another decree has ben issued by the Khedive enjoining obedience to Sir Garnet Wolseley, who has the Viceroy's authority for re-establishing order in Egypt. The Catalonia, which went aground in the Suez Canal, has been safely floated again, and the Canal is now clear. Merchant vessels are entering freely, and the company has resumed the ordinary working of the traffic. - The Condor, which'went to Aboukir, on Tuesday morn- ing and returned in the evening, reports that the forts appeared almost deserted. At Mex, on Monday night, 40 or 50 Arabs pillaged two villages and carried off three watch- men.

A special correspondent at Ismailia telegraphs that on Monday afternoon our troops engaged the enemy at Sera- peum, and drove them back. Our losses were two killed and four or five wounded. The enemy lost about 100 men and four guns. A correspondent at Alexandria states that the Austrian gunboat Nautilus, while on her way there from Port Said oa Monday, supposing that the forts were occupied by the Bri- tish troops, sent a boat ashore, the crew of which wero at once made prisoners by Arabi's troops. Admiral Hewett, prior to his taking possession of Suez, landed a secret party of four or five men with instructions to blow up a portion of the railway lines with dynamite, and so prevent the removal of the stock to Cairo. The surprise party were, however, unsuccessful, as the lines were care- fully guarded by soldiers. Sir Garnet Wolseley immediately after landing at Ismailia visited M. de Lesseps and explained to him that we must use the Canal for the present, but that everything would he over in three or four days. M. de Lessens, after hearing Sir Garnet Wolseley's friendly explanations, expressed himself fully satisfied, and tet,eretted that there had been any mis- understanding. Sir Garnet Wolseley and the other officers of the staff have provided themselves with a new pattern bedstead, which weighs only 1.71 b.; and folds up to go inside the camp bag which every officer is allowed to take. An officer's kit con- sists of this bag, a bullock-trunk of limited dimensions, and a metal canteen, which, besides serving as a camp kettle, contains all the culinary utensils requisite for three persons.

On Tuesday afternoon 600 men of the Black Watch made a reconnaissance from Ramieh in the direction of Kafr Dowar, in order to draw out the enemy's forces. The 40- pounders on the Waterworks Hill opened fire at the same time. The Egyptian guns did not reply until three rounds had been fired. There was no infantry firing. Heavy gang are being brought into position by our troops about 150 yards beyond the present Ratnleh lines. Late telegrams from Alexandria show that Arabi is still maintaining a considerable force in front of the British lines. A report was spread on Wednesday that the Arabs were in full retreat, but Sir E. liamley found that it was unfounded. From Familia we learn that the success at Chalouf has had a great effect on the Arabs in that quarter. Deserters, some of them otlicfrs, have given themselves up to our posts, and they state that thousands of men are only kept in Arabi's service bY intimidation. Several reports agree in stating that Arabi has concentrated a considerable forq at Tel .el-Kebir. On TuesdAy night fires were observed in the neighbourhood of Aboukir and Kafrdowar, giving rise to the belief that the Arabs were retreating and burning the villages through which they passed.

div.head: LATER PARTICULARS. REPORTED AfCRIVAL OF SIR GARNET AT TR L-EL-KRBIR.
div.p: LATER PARTICULARS. REPORTED AfCRIVAL OF SIR GARNET AT TR L-EL-KRBIR.

The military movement foreshadowed on Thursday has been vigorously begun, and at night it was reported that the British were already in possession of the fortified place called Tel-el-Ketir. Doubt, however, is entertained as to the authenticity of this news, which comes by way of Alexandria, it being thought impossible that Sir Garnet Wolseley's forces can have advanced so .rapidly as to capture Tel-el-Kebir at an early hour on Thursday after- noon. This, however, is the point Sir Garnet must first aim at, and the report, though it may be premature, is in other respects probable. Swift- ness and decision of movement are prime fac- tors in the tactics of the present campaign. The speed with which Sir Garnet Wolseley has thrown his forces forward, after suddenly descending upon Ismailia, not only shows the immense importance he attaches to time, but also his appreciation of the effect of dash upon the enemy. It is scarcely a week since the transports carrying Sir Garnet's forces sailed with sealed orders from Alexan- dria. On Sunday the whole Canal was seized," and an advance force installed at the railway junction at Nefisheh, two miles from Ismailia. On Monday, Sir Garnet Wolselev himself arrived at Ismailia, and two days afterwards the fleet of transports had disembarked nearly the whole of the' troops. Next morning—five days after -leaving Alexandria —the Guards, Hussars mounted Infantry, and Marine Artillery, made an early start for the interior. Whether Tel-el-Kebir, which is t4)irty miles distant, and was held by 15,000 regular Egyptian troops, with 80 auns, was captured on Thursday or not, this is an eyloit which sheds lustre upon the general in command and upon the whole adminis- trative department of the army, and shows the immense value of the Suez Canal as a base of military operations. THE MILITARY CONVENTION WITH TURKEY. Turkey ie again beginning to show signs of accepting the inevitable, and it would not be surprising if in a few days a Military Convention were to be agreed upon. Some slight concessions, more in appearance than in reality, have been ',frayed by. the British, such as that instead of the Turkish forces beißg under British command, they should be under Turkish command subject to a previous agreement with the English commander. On the main points of the proposed Convention, however, there is no modification. The number of Turks is to be strictly limited, their place of debarkation

detloNl, and the period of their stay in Egypt clearly limited. After The delay inevitable in negotiations with the Porte, the Britith terms, including the proclamation of Arabi as a rebel, willsETO doubt be accepted.

ARABI'S REPORTED WIIIIDRAWAL. It is still believed at Alexandria that Arabi has with- drawn a considerable force from his lines at Karr- Dowar, but no trustworthy information on the subject has been rec,_•ived. Shots were exchanged by the artillery at Ramie)) and Knfr Dowar on Thursday, but witlyout any material result. An unpleasant incident at Ramlel) Is the rettmi of a number of plundering Bedouins to the resithnces there, and a good deal, of consequent pillage. It is scarcely reassuring to be told that these marauders passed the British lines znperceived. SIR GARNE r NT E LEY'S ADVANCE.

A telegram from Ismailia on Thursday, at 10 am., s rys —The advance sf the heavy cavalry and the marine artillery comrnocced this morning. A correspondent telegraphed from Ismailia on Wednesday, at 9-3 l p.m. :—Sir Garnet Wolseley intends pushing for- ward into the inter'Por at once. A tramway is being rapidly laid between the sta'zion and the quay. VISIT TO TME GAMMON AT IiEFICHE.

A late edition of the Daily Chronicle contains a telegram from its Ismailia correspondent, who has just returned from a visit to our advance post at Nefiche. The garrison from the 84th and 40!.h regiments and Marines is laagered between the canal and the railway. The effects of the Orion's bona- balarnent were terrific. The equipments thrown away show that the enemy was admirably provided. The panic was utterly hysterical, the Orion being invisible. Our men stand heat admirably. TfIE FRESH WATER CANAL CUT. GI eat activity is being shown in perfecting the communi- cation between the quays at Ismailia and the railway at Netilheh by means of a tramway. A few days ago it was stated that enough railway carriages had been secured to form a train, but there was no engine; now, however, it is reported that there is one engine upon the line. This is an important acquisition, and will much facilitate the move- ment of troops and war material to the interior. The Fresh Water Canal has been cut, and the supply of Nrater at Ismailia and Suez is consequently affected, but efforts will be made to repair the damage without delay. At Port Said sqme apprehension of an attack has been entertained, but none has yet taken place.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

Mr. Finigan, the member for Ennis, who has already an- nounced his intention of applying for the Chiltern Hun- dreds, owing to i.P.-hea:th, was seized on Sunday night with paralysis. It let het:gilt he has broken a blood vessel. "Poor-law Guardians and Town Commissioners through- out the country, undeterred by the sentence of Mr. Gray, M.P., are passing resorutions condemning the arbitrary and tyrannical' conduct of Judge Lawson in passing that sentence. The Lord-Lieutenant has declined to hold any inquiry into the conduct of the jury in the Ennis murder ease, but ' intimates his intention of examining the affidavits with a view of ascertaining whether sufficient grounds exist for in- terfering with the due course of the law. A murderous outrage was perpetrated in Parliament-street, Dublin, on Monday afternoon. Just after the Lord Lieutenant had passed through to the Castle, a man smashed the window of Mr. Trulock's gunshop and ran away with a revolver. He was chased to Essex Bridge by an assist int, upon whom the man turned and delineratelv stabbed him in two places, in- flicting serious wounds. The ruffian was at once appre- hended.

Tbe Special Commission in Dublin was on Wednescliy adjourned to the 27th September on a statement that wit- news important to the proper defence of the young man Walsh, charged with the murder of Constable Cavanagh, could not be produced at present, notably the prisoner's mother, who was said to be prostrated by grief at the fate of the son already sentenced to death. In adjourning; the Court Mr. Justice Lawson paid a high compliment to the manner in which the juries had discharged their duty. _

TIDE TRISH SECRETARY ON THE STATE OF THIS COUNTRY. —Mr. Trevelyan, replying to an address of welcome, presented by the Mayor and Corporation of Belfast, on Wed- nesday, on the occasion of his visit, said it would be idle to deny the existence of personal danger in the task of govern- ing Ireland, but the remedy for that state of things lay in one course, which though Slow he believed to be sure. The fixed policy of the Irish Goveinment was to distinguish between what is criminal and what is political, and acrainst outrages of all kinds they were determined to wage an undenying and unrelenting war. EXECUTION AT CORK.—Thomas Hynes, a farmer, was on Tuesday hanged at the County Gaol, Cork, for the murder of his wife on the 25th Mardi last. The condemned man for some time after conviction seemed resigned to his fate, but on Monday night unexpectedly attacked a warder, and would probably have injured him if he had not been pre- vented by other warders. He subsequently became calmer, and on Tuesday morning, without resistance, allowed him- self to be led to the scaffold. Reporters were not admitted to witness the execution, which was carried out by two local men.

The Chief Secretary for Ireland, Mr. G. 0. Trevelyan, M.P., was on Saturday presented with an address by the Londonderry Corporation, who accorded to the right hon. gentleman a hearty welcome. In his reply Mr. Trevelyan thanked the Corporation for their address, and ascribed much of their estimation of himself to the fact that he was brought up at the feet of Lord Macaulay, who had done much to commemorate the ancient glory of their city. On that neutral ground he (Mr. Trevelyan) thought it justifi- able to say that tht Government of Ireland were beginning to feel a sense of hope, and almost of confidence, to which three months ago they were strangers, and he recognised the consideration shown by the "three Irish parties" in Parlia- ment towards himself, which had made more easy a dubious and difficult task.

Mr. Sexton, M.P., has received from the Under Secretary, Dublin Castle, the following letter, dated Saturday :—" Sir, —I am directed by the Lord Lieutenant to request you will be good enough to transmit the affidavits or statutory decla- rations respecting the conduct of the jury in the case of the Queen v. Hynes, which were referred to in the debate in the House of Commons on the 17th inst., in order that they may be submitted to His Excellency for his consideration." Mr. Sexton, accordingly forwarded on Monday to the Lord Lieutenant six affidavits made by the housekeeper, waiters, and porters at tDe Imperial lietel, in addition to the five quoted in the House of Commons, concerning the conduct of the jury in the Hynes case, urging that there should be a public and sworn inquiry. THE SERIOTJS CHARGE AGAINST AN IRISH JIIRY.—MI E. C. Hamilton, of the Bengal staff corps (half-pay), who was one of the jurors in the Hynes case at Dublin, has pub- -I:shecl a letter containing very explicit denials of the charges so curiously brought against hird and his colleagues by the editor of the seditious organ United Irelani. Mr. Hamilton gives a narrative of facts which show that the blame for the separation of the jury rests entirely. with the sub-Sheriff. He denies that any of the jurors misoonducted themselves, and explains several of Mr. O'Brien's "facts" in a manner which removes all the gloss which that indi- vidual had put on them. The whole story is a very cprious one. Mr. Hamilton says that the jury were taken againt their wills to the Imperial Hotel, and as chance, of course, would have it, the ex-suspect was accommodated on the same "landing," where he was conveniently placed to see 1 and hear the alarming and discreditable sights and sounds which, as he says, ditturbed his repose. He would probably have borne with the annoyance in silence if the jury next morning had acquitted Hynes. REPORTED RELIGIOUS MANIFESTATIONS AT ATHLONE.— The Athlone correspondent of the Press Association telegraphs that an extraordinary sensation has been caused Nin that place by the recital of the following circumstances : —On Sunday evening, while' a large congregaticn were at worship in the Franciscan Church, and just as the priest, ' the Ttev. Father McDermott, had concluded his sermon, a brilliant light shone from the roof immediately above the figure of the Virgin Marv. Showers of stars descended on the head of the figure, the eyes opened and rolled from side to side, the hands moved, and the figure assumed the atti- tude of blessing the congregation, after which it resumed its former appearance. Those who SIM the sight moved from their seats in different parts of the church, and pushed to the altar. A scene of the greatest excitement ensued. The religious services were suspended, but the church remained crowded until a late hour at night. Even then the church was with difficulty cleared. On Monday morning the thoroughfares near the church had become impassable. Much credence is attached to the accounts of the "wonder," as numbers of persons who witnessed it all give the same version of what took place.

• ---- . THE LETTERFRACK MURDER. On Tuesday, at the Dublin Special Commission, Patrick Walsh was tried a second time for the murder of Martin Lyden,, at Letterfrack, county Gilway. On Friday last the jury then enga:.ted on the else disagreed, but the Crown counsel were so convinced of the desirability of a final verdict ttat they again arraigned the prisoner. To the ordinary observer the evidence, both direct and circumstan- tial, was of the clearest possible character, and apparently it has convinced Via second jury, in spite of elaborate attempts to prove an alibi, that the prisoner was one of the gang of midnight assassins who broke into Lyden's house, dragged him and his father from bed, and deliberately shot them to death. Mr. Justice Lawson passed sentence of death upon the prisoner, remarking,that the evidene2 was unanswerable and the crime "most barbarous and brutal." APPALLING TRAGEDY: A FAMILY

- _ BUTCHERED. A massacre in county Galway, on the shores of Lough Mask, on Friday last, is the most appalling occ,urrence with- • out exception, perhaps, which has yet occurred in connec- tion with agrarian crime in Ireland. Five people have been butchered, and the only remaining member of the family who was in the house at the time, a young lad of eleven years, is in a precarious state. John Joyce, the head of the murdered family, was a small farmer holding, in the par- lance Of the district, .£3 worth of land from Col. Clements, who succeeded to ,a portion of the estate of the late Lord Leitram. His tenement consisted of a hovel with a patch of ground, in which be grew potatoes and cabbage, with the right of grazing on a stretch of mountain. The locality, which is known as "time Joyce country," is wild beyond description,and far removed from any of the centres of town, or even village life. The Joyces, consisting of the father and husband, agA about forty-five years; Bridget Joyce, his wife, aged forty years, Peggy Joyce, his -mother, aged eighty-five years; Peggy Joyce, his daughter, aged nineteen years; Michael, his son, aged seventeen years; and Patrick, another son, aged twelve years, went to bed between nine aEd ten o'clock on Thursday night. The house

consists of two apartments, or rather one from which a portion has been partly built off. There are no windows iii the building. Only one aperture in the wall affords it light. Built with stones the cabin is a horribx hovel, in li:liCh it would seem impossible for human beings to exist. There was nothing in the shape of ferniture. A few pieces of wood served every household purpose front table to bed, the latter being covered with a little straw and old clothes. The bed occupied by Joyce art his wife was placed its an alcove, built as it were in the wall. of the entrance room, while the grandmother, the two bore, ,arol. daughter, slept toeether in the semi-detached portion, v Inch is fess than six feet bread, and double that apace in length. The bed an old pillow-. here was composed of a few planks with Nothing further seems k , noon of the family, till about six o'clock sin named Collins, celled to alh mornmg, when a neighbour, b. in tirea cards for spinning wool, the only industry practised tdae peasantry of the country. He found the door ey hing naked nee' lifeles'sne arrd discevered Joyce e floor. It is the custom for the men thole% the Connaught to people living sleep naked. Fae at once alarmelf'') round about, and returning with them fopueoreN lying dead in the bed out of which the haeband bed .eperruwzife, and the crandmother and daughter dead in the oh' The two boys were :ivine. Further examination disclosed that the father bad received a terrible blow on the back of the head, Which wasamashed in, and bad been shot twice in the back just under the right shonldcr. Mrs. Joyce's head ' was fearfully fractured, as was that of the other two dead persons. The weapons used must have been heavy wooden or iron bars, for the bones of the entire head in each case were shattered into fragments, being held together merely by the scalp. The boy Michael had been shot in two places in the body, but survived until three o'clock in the afternoon. He wee conscious most of the time, and died in intense agony. His brother Patrick was not shot, but had been beaten with ferocious violence on the head. Both were able to state that the house had been entered about one o'clock in the morning by three or four men, who fired skots, two of which were aimed at Michael. To the people who first came to-the house in the morning the two boys said they could not identify any of the parties. They repeated this to the police' who en hearing of the tragedy arrived at the scene about ten o'clock, but it has since tianspired that Michael before dying made a deposi- tion implicating persons since arrested. Patrick also sub- seqaently, on getting a little stronger, was able to give a clearer narrative of what had taisma place, and to mention names, which for the present, the police refuse to give. The appearance of the house was more that of a slaughter- house than the habitation of human beings. All the bodies lay as they had just been placed on a little pi:o of straw on the floor. The father lay just as be had died, partly on his side, with his arms crossed. It was said that two dogs were found gnawing in bod the body of the aged grandmother. Mr. A. Newton Brady, RM., and Mr. Gardner, as well as several sub-inspectors of police, arrived at the place in the course of Friday afternoon. Medical skill had, of course, been summoned for the relief of the wounded boys, and Drs. In.ghain and Hegartv arrived shortly before Michael died. Dr. Robert M'Donell, the eminent surgeon of Dublin, who was staying—en a visit with sir Richard M'Causland, at Cuppaberm, some miles off, hearing of the occurrence, came across with Captain M'Ceusland, J.P., in his opinion, the ' surviving boy has some chance of recovery. The latter was on SaturdaY tenderly wad carefully placed on a stretcher and carried by four men a long and weary journey across the mountains to the shores of Lough Mask, whence, by the boat and car, the unhappy lad was removed to Conn, where he remains under medicel treatment. On Friday evening Mr. Brady, RM., offered a large sum of money to any of the women of the district—hundreds of whom clustered together on the face of the mountain within a few score yards of the house—who would come and tend the boy, but not one responded to the call of humanity. Another son of the family, named Martin, was, fortunately, out at service, and only heard of the occurrence on Satur- day. Considerable difference of opinion exists as to the motive of the murderers, but the most reliable seems to be that Joyce was suspected of giving information to the police relative to a murder: Others say he was accused of paying his rent. No rents, except in one or two cases, hare been paid for three years to Colonel Clements in the Joyce country, where be has between 300 and 400 tenants. A large number of persons have been apprehended, and it is said that seven men placed with several others ha'• been identified by young Joyce, the only sure:Tor. Witnesses are now under police protectian, who were actual witnesses of the crime. The names of these witnesses are withheld by the authorities, but it seems that on the night of the murders, a respectable farmer, living in Cappana- creecha, was awakened shortly before midnight by the bark- ing of a dog, and on getting up saw six men approaching his house. He immediately slipped out into an adjoining potato field, where he lay concealed. They passed his house, but feeling convinced that some bad work was contemplated, and fearing that an attack was meditated upon his brother's residence some distance further on, he followed them up. They passed on, however, and he alarmed his brother, who, with his son, accompanied him in following the suspected party. After 'walking some distance the men entered a house, and after a little time came out with four others, this place being evidently a rendezvous. The ten men then walked towards Maasmtrassna, ?still followed by their pursuers, whose proxitnity they never once seemed to snspect. On reaching Joyce's house the ten men entered, and within a few minutes the three watchers, who lay concealed among some bushes in the garden, heard a revolver shot, succeeded by blows with bludgeons and cries of agony. Overwhelmed with fear the three men fled. All the parties engaged in the massacre had, hoseaver, been long and intimately known to them, and their identification of the prisoners is complete. The Coroner's inqnest relative to the massacre was held on Wednesday. The police only tendered evidence of the cause of death, and the verdict returned was one of wilful murder agiinst some persons unknown. That the authori- ties, however, have in their possession evidence of the utmost importance is beyond doubt. Ten men are under remand, and it is alleged that four men who chanced to wit- ness some of the incidents of the terrible tragedy are pre- pared to give the most convincing testimony of the guilt of the prisoners. ANOTHER FIENDISH MURDER. John Leahy, a farmer residing at Scarteen, within a few miles of Killarney, was on Sunday night murdered by a " Moonlight " party, and the facts that have come to .light place the crime among the most heartless and atrocious of these perpetrated in the name of the lend agitation. Leahy was an aged man, and bad a large and respectable family. He was formerly employed as a driver or rent warner on the estate of Lord Kenmare, but 'bad given up that position in order to turn his attention to the cultivation of the several farms which he and members of his faintly possessed. It does not appear that in the discharge of his duties as rent warner he became an object of popular enmity or dislike ; on the contrary, those who knew him describe him as a goad-natured sort of man, never inclined to harshness or un- fair dealing. The special facilities which his connection with the Kenmare Estate Office afforded him of acquiring farms exposed him to the charge of lanci-orabbing, which jealous neighbours were not slow to level against him. Leahy, the victim of the present clime, was in Killarney on Sunday, and returned home at eight o'clock. There were in the house his son John, his daughter Honore, and his wife, together with the three male servants. His son shortly afterwards left the house to visit his brother-in-law, Daniel Daly, who resided a mile away. The household went to bad, leaving the door unlocked till the return of the young man. -The husband and wife were sleeping oa the ground floor in a ioom off the kitchen, and the daughter and servants up- stairs. Mrs. Leahy, while awake, awaiting the return of her son, heard a person enter the kitchen and in a per- emptory manner order her husband to get out of bed. In a few mements men entered the room and dragged Leahy out of bed. Mrs. Leahy estimates the numb-r of marauders at between twelve and fifteen. They wets fully armed, but undisguised. One man, who appeared to be the leader, ordered her husband to be placed on his knees in tl • kitchen, and, addressing his followers called on "No. 1 "to fire. Despite the frantic' efforts of his wife, who placed herself between the doomed man and the assassins, the order was obeyed. and Leahy WAS badly wounded. The captain then called on ",'O. 10" to advance, and another shot WAS tired. "No. 14, was then summoned and this was the last shot fired, though a bayonet-thrust waik made at the prostrate old man. Miss Leahy, leaning over the stair- case, asked the wretches to desist, hut the person in com- mand only replied with a brutal threat against her own life. When the assassins had finished their work they searched for young Leahy. Fortunately he had not returned from his brother-in-law's hheise, and they took their departure. The servant men who were witnesses of the shocking out rage never interfered to prevent the violence, and when Mrs. Leahy requested them to go to Daniel Daly's house for her son they refused, and she herself went away in the dark scross the fields and brought assistance. When the medical man and the priest arrived Leahy was dead. On Monday morning Captain Pluiskett visited the place, and five young men, principally farmers' sons, were arrested.
