div.p: he
i
Il

Prevention of Crime Ad confers,—that is t-4 say, if the peaceably-disposed people of Irelaai,' d are to be allowed to pursue the even tenour of their ways without molestation, and if the tot:entry is to be rid of some of the brutal ruffians which infest it. The amounts of the massacre at Maamtrasna surpass in their horror anything which have preceded them, though they have been committed in a district now notorious for crime. The smite of the awful tragedy is in the very heart of what is known as the Joyce eountry, one of the most inaccessible parts of Conne- mara, of which we have reeently read too mach, and that not the most creditable in Irish affairs. Here at the base of a small mountain—from the summit of which can be distinguished the scenes of several other murders, including that of Lord Mount- morres—a poor farmer named Joyce, with his wife, his mother, and three children, have been so but- chered that only one of them—a son about twelve years of age—at present survives, and it is doubtful whether he will ever recover the effects of the cruel treatment to which he was subjected. Judging from the facts which have come to light, the murders must have been committed by some bloodthirsty gang belonging to the neighbourhood. Happily, several witnesses are now under protection who can identify the murderers. They say :they actually saw, the men—about ten or a dozen in number—enter Joyce's dwelling on their murderous errand, and heard the shots fired, the blows dealt, and the screams of the inmates ; but because they were unarmed and fewer in number than the bloodthirsty party they were afraid to interfere. What the motive for the crime was it is hard to tell, but like many others it is believed to be agrarian in its origin. The generally accepted belief appears to be that Joyce had at some time or other given information about the murder of Lord Ardilaun's-bailiffs, who it may be reme,mbered were some time in December last killed in the act of serving writs, and their bodies thrown into Lough Mask near to where the Joyees live. When the Lough was firstdragged the bodies were not found; bat the second search proved :successful, and it is thought that Joyce, or some one of his family, gave the information:which led to this second search. Be that as it may, it is no reason why Joyce should be deprived of his life, but in Ireland in these times it is dangerous to do anything which savours of upholding law and order, 'and Joyce and his family have had to pay the penalty with their lives. In this instance, ne respect whatever has been shown to any person in the dwelling; and the intention would seem to have been to extirpate all the inmates. The crffending party was not singled out for attack, but all were treated alike. Each was either shot or blu.dgeotted to death,r,till ,the: dwelling must have presented the appearance of a slaughter-house, and when the bodies were discovered bathed in blood they had been partly; eaten by doge. It passes belief that for no grosser offenee than that of being supposed ito have given information as to a certain murder, the lives of five more individuals should be taken; still enoh is the case. The murders in Phcenix Park aroused the indignation of the law- abiding portion of the Irish people, but that tragedy, I horrible as it was, pales into insignificance before such a crime of savagery as that reported from Connemarra ; yet te us it is rather significant that it has not called forth the denunciations from Irish members which were so plentiful when Lord 'Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke were. alaugh.. tered. Scarcely had the first rumour of Olio massacre been circulated than there came Ole intelli- gence that another murder, differing: only in degree, had been committed in Killarney. The victim was a farmer named John Leahy. His house was entered on Monday morning .by nine or ten ":Moonlighters," who dragged Leahy from his bed, and killed him in the presence of his wife. Subsequently the gang made a search for the deceased's son, who only escaped his father's fate by being absent from the house on a. visit to his brother-in-law. It is astounding to read that the servant men were witnesses of this shocking crime, yet they dire not interfere to prevent the vio- lence; and when requested by the wife to fetch the assistance of her son they refused. The consequence was that sho had herself to walk across the Belds in the dark for help, leaving her husband prostrate on the floor; but before she returned he had breathed his last. So far as can be ascertained his only offence was that he had been a rent warner for Lord Ken- , mare, and while acting in that capacity he had sun- seeded it acquiring several farms, which he cultivated. There is no evidence that he had injured anyone; on the contrary, he seems to have earned a reputation for fair dealing; but to satisfy personal enmity he, too, uuoffending man, is foully murdered. These 1 and other such crimes cry aloud for the most condign punishment, and it is to be hoped that it will be swift and sure in 'following the guilty actors. I Remedial and repressive legislation alike appear to to be inadequate to appease the thirst so popular in some districts for bloodshed. This has its root and branch in the secret societies with which the country is honeycombed; and, though the Executive have not hitherto found it necessary to put into execution the exceptional powers with which Parliament has invested it, no time should be lost in doing so, if, as is believed, they will have a deterring influence upon evil doers. We cannot but hail with satisfaction the declaration of the Irish Chief-Secretary that the fixed policy of the Government is to draw a deep line be- tween what is criminal and what is political, a line which, unfortunately, has nat been sufficiently marked in the past. With political writings and speeches said re.olutious at public meetings, Mr. Trevelyan added, the Government does not care to concern themselves, but against crime and outrage they have proclaimed, and will continue to wage, an undying and unrelent- ing war. In this policy the Government deserve the support of the people of Ireland themselves; and we feel confident that has only to be made sufficiently plain in order that the support maybe ungrudgingly conceded. The recent special commission, which closed on Wednesday, and which has more than justi- fied its institution, has done much in maintaining the cause of law and order, but the Irish people them- selves can do much more if they only so will it.

div.head: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES,
div.p: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES,

The incident I related last week with regard to the revivifying influence of the atmosphere of Widnes, is totally eclipsed by the following story, for which I am indebted to the kindness of a correspondent :—" All things seem to start into newness of life in America—the region is so healthy. Apropos they tell a story in Kansas of an old resident in Deer Creek, Ile hal lived se long, we are told, that life was a burden—to his heirs probably—and yet the country was so healthy he could not die. Weary of existence, he moved back to Illinois, and there he succeeded in giving up the ghost, having stipulated that he should be brought back to be buried on his Kansas farm. Bat such was the life-giving properties of this soil that, when laid in it, anima- tion returned to his limbs, his heart resumed its pulsations, and the incorrigible centenarian walked forth in recovered health, to the disgust of his heirs and the confusion of those who had doubts about Kansas."

IHow long, I wonder, has the nuisance which comes from the direction of the Spinal to be suffered to exist? For weeks, nay months, have the inhabitants of that neighbour- hood, and beyond it, top, been breathing air polluted with a gas, before which the fumes across the river become of-little consequence. The medical officer has stated that it may not improbably cause an epidemic of gastric fever ; while the Commissioners have received a memorial, signed by a number of influential town's people, which bears test.i- monv to the fact that the inhabitants are fleeing from it, like Pharoah fled from the plagues of Egypt. And yet in spite of this testimony the air, as I write, is redolent with the nauseating and sickening stench. Why is it tolera- ted? The nuisance can be prevented, why is not? The Board .of Commissioners does not appear to wish to use the powers it possesses stringently, but a nuisance dangerous to health, as this is. should not be permitted to continue a day longer than is absolutely necesasary for remedial measures to be adopted. But at present no attempts seem to be made to stop it, and great indignation is expressed thereat in more than one quarter. If the Commissioners do not speedily take up the question with a full determination to deal with it is a thorough mauuer, the Local Government Board will

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, AUGUST 26, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, AUGUST 26, 1882.
perhaps have something to say on the subject. Such an occurrence, I hear, is not unlikely.

• Militiamen, as a rule, are not universally regarded as models of sanctity and propriety of behaviour. They often seem to think that when they don their uniform they also acquire certain rights and privileges to make use of the per- sons and property of those among whom they are as if they were—instead of being valiant defenders as they are expected to be—a sort of hostile garrison, and entitled to conduct themselves as such. At times, in fact, they are too like Falstaff's famous company of irregulars, to be very pleasant neighbours. Acting in this spirit, however, some- times brings them into positions which, a chivalrous warrior, ought not to be in. At St. Helens, for instance, during this past syeek, one of these modern knights found himself indicted at the police-court on a charge of having despoiled a widow of her hen, and, what is more regrettable, was found guilty of the same. Animated, however, by more proper feelings, this, I hope not representative militia- man, offered, if the magistrates would look lightly over the offence, to volunteer into foreign service, and thus expatri- ate himself for his country's good, and the benefit of St. Helens in particular. It is almost a pity that a proper sense of justice on the part of the magistrates woul I not allow them to accede to this request, as it is not difficult to be- lieve that if the delinquent was not always found to the fore in battle, he would, at least have been a most valuable auxiliary to a foraging party. The establishment of a parcels pest by the Government has already— ere yet it has come into actual operation— begun to bear good fruits, and this is to be found in the material reduction about to be made by the great railway companies in their charges for the conveyance of parcels over' their lines. The London and North-Western, the Midland, and the Great Western companies announce a new scale of charges for parcels carried by passenger trains, and this scale is to come into operation so early as the first of next month. A parcel of 11b. will, under the revised scale, be carried up to SO miles for 4d.. and up to and over 400 miles for 21. more. Heavier parcels will, of course, be charged at proportionate rates ; while parcels containing articles of a fragile character, or bulky in comparison with their weight, are to be charged a certain percentage higher. The announcement of the Midland Company—probably the most enterprising of the three—adds that the charges include free delivery within the usual limits in London and all the principal towns, and to places distant not more than half-a-mile from country stations. Of course, these terms are not by any means so advantageous as those offered by the Post-Office, still they are a decided improvement on the present rates, but the thought suggests itself that if the railway companies would direct their attention to the charges for goods rather than that for parcels by passenger trains they would be more likely to earn the thanks of the public, and a greater profit for their shareholders than they do at present. We shall be better served by the Post-Office in the way of parcels than by the companies; the latter on the other hand have a wide margin for making concessions for goods.

• The Haddington burghs election passed of very auietly. Very little importance need be attached to it, but the result is satisfactory as showing that Liberalism has by no means ost its power among the electors. The vacancy was caused by the resignation of Sir. D. Wedderburn, who had represented the constituency since 1879, wheh he was returned by a majority of 198 over the Cooservative candidate, Mr. J. H. Hay Macdonald: At the general electiohin 1880, Sir David was again returned, his majority being 412 over Captain J. F. Houston. The number of voters who polled on that occasion was 1,623; whereas on Wednesday the total of voters who exercised the privilege was only 1,392. Of these 833 voted for Mr. Craig &liar, 6e Liberal candidate, and 544 for Mr. Seton Karr (Conser- vative), the majority for the former being 289. In 1880 the Conservative candidate polled 607 votes, so that the figures now recorded shows a diminution in the Conservative strength of 63, a diminution which to me is extremely gratifying. I doubt not that were other constituencies polled it would be found there is a similar decrease.

Everybody is now on the qui vice for the next move in the Egyptian campaign, By a very clever stroke the Com- mander-in-Chief at the beginning of the preent week changed the edene of his operations from Alexandria to. the Suet Canal, all the chief points on which—Kantara, Port 3nld, Ismailia, &c.—are now in possession et the British forces. The occupation of the Canal was of course resented by M. de Lesseps, who strongly protested against the action of Sir Garnet; but the latter is as skilful in diplomacy as he is in war, and when he had an opportunity of speaking with M. de Lesseps he was very soon talked over and made to understand that England had no nefarious schemes in view. The traffic was suspended only for a brief period ; now it has been resumed and working freely. The result of the gallant general's move is that the rebels are completely hemmed in on all sides b, and before these lines have seen the light it is not improbable that the enemy will have sustained a severe defeat. During the week there have been a few skirmishes, the enemy usually coming oft second best • but the deciding battle has yet to be fought, and this is likely to take place not at Kafrdowr' but at Tel-el-Kebir. There is, indeed, every prospect of Sir Garnet's anticipations beiug realised, that is the completion of the campaign before September 15th. FLACCUS.

A WIFE BEATER IN CUSTODY AT WIDNES. Joseph Stanley, a man who has been convicted of wife beating, was charged at the Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, be- fore Mr. John Brock, with assaulting his wife. On Tues- day evening, when the prisoner went home, a "wordy war" took place. He then struck his wife in the mouth with such violence that she lost a great quantity of blood. The prisoner was remanded until Wednesday, on the application of Inspector Barnett. RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS' ELECTION. ROBBERY FROM A LODGING-HOUSE AT RUNCORN.— Annie Jenks, a disorderly character, was brought up, on remand, at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, to answer a charge of stealing a shawl, a skirt, and a hankerchief, the property of Mary Macdonald. On Tuesday night the pro- secutrix slept in the same room as the prisoner, at Mrs. McGarra's lodging-house, Mersey-street, and early next morning she was told the prisoner had taken the articles named from her bed, and she arose and informed the police. P.C. Thompson afterwards apprehended the prisoner on the bridge, and she had the articles in her possession.—Prisoner -pleaded guilty, and was committed to gaol for a month's hard labour. •

How TEE CROCKERY GOES: A "BACK ". SCENE AT RVECORN.—At the Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. James Reynolds, Miss Mary and Miss Sarah Nickson, sisters, were summoned, the former for making use of language calculated to provoke a breach of tide peace, and the latter with assaulting Mrs. Elizabeth, the wife of Mr. William Frodsham, painter, Lord-street, Ruecorn. On the other hand Mrs. Frodsham was charged with using language to Miss Mary calculated to provoke a breach of the peace, and with unlawfully and wilfully damaging the property of Mr. Wilaam Nickson by breaking three panes of glass. Mr. Burton represented ?tin Nickson and others, and Mr. Tnurnham (Robert Davies and Co., Warrington) appeared for Mrs. Frodsham. It was alleged that on Thursday, the 10th inst., the defendaets in the first case made use of abusive language, and charged Mrs. Fred- sham with being drunk, and that she was struck by a stone sent by Miss 'Sarah Nickson. In her hand she held a jug and a plate, and she was so " startled " at this occurrence, that she was "obliged to let these articles go," and the jug unfortunately broke tbree panes of glass in the bedroom window. Dr. Williams stated Mrs. Frodsham was subject to hysterics, and she herself stated there was no ground for the charge of drunkenness, as she was a total abstainer. For the defence a number of witnesses were called, who proved that on one occasion Mrs. Frodsham threw five jugsfull of water into the kitchen of Mrs. Frodsham, and that on the day in question, without the least provocation, jugs, mugs, plates, and saucers went flying from her hand into Mr. Nickson's yard, and at the bedroom window. It was denied that the Nicksons sent anything in return, or made use of language other than telling Mrs. Frodsham to go in the house and mind her own business. After the occurrence, a witness named Mrs. Ormson stated there was a crowd congregated about the back door of the house of Mrs. Frodsham, who was lying on her back on the ground in the back yard, murmuring" poor chucky ! poor chucky 1" Without hear- ing all the evidence for the defence. the Bench dismissed the charges against the Nicksons, and said they were satisfied Mrs. Frodsham had made use of very obscene and abusive language. She would be bound over to keep the peace for six months in her husband's recognizances of £lO, pay a fine of 2s. ed. for wilfully damaging the window, and costs, amounting in all to £3 12s. How A WESTON PUBLICAN GOT ROBBED.—Yesterday at Runcern Police Court, before Mr. W. Bankes, Joseph William Chorley alias John Trighton, a young man, was brought up in custody charged with havin g on Wednesday, stolen a bag containing £lB, the property of John Capper, landlord of the Prospect Inn, Weston. The prosecutor: said he was also a pig dealer. On Wednesday he went to War- rington to sell some pigs. He saw the prisoner on "Pig Hill," Warrington, and treated him to several glasses of beer. He (witness) went to the railway station to leave for Runcorn about nina o'clock, and he then had the bag, which contained about £2l, in his possession. The prisoner accompanied him to the station, and asked him to pay his fare to Runcorn, but he (witness) refused. He then entered the railway carriage, but he was "fresh in drink," and did not know whether the prisoner id%) got in the same carriage. He, however, went to sleep, and when he awoke he found he was at Edge Hill station. There was then no one in the compartment but himself. He returned to Runcorn by the first available train, and when he arrived home at Weston he discovered he had been robbed of his hag of money. P.S. Walley said from information received, he apprehended the prisoner in Runcorn on Thursday afternoon. He was very drunk. He (witness) searched the prisoner, and found upon him the purse (produced) containing £9 3s. He also learned that the prisoner had purchased a snit of clothes, boots, shirt, Lc., and a number of articles for other people in Run- corn. He had charged the prisoner with the robbery that morning, and he admitted it was Cipper's money. "Yes," he replied, "it was his money. He left it under the seat in the railway carriage."—Mr. Superintendent Williamson, on this evidence, applied for a remand to allow him to make enquiries as to his previous character. On the previous night he gave his name as Crighton and Pickford, and now this morning he gave his name as Chorley.—Prisoner said he took the money, but there was not so much as stated by the prosecutor.—Prisoner was remanded.--Williaru Riley, a sweep, was then put up on a charge of drunkenness and disorderly behaviour on the previous day.—lnspector Hollingworth said the prisoner was creating a disturbance in Mersey-street, at three o'clock, by sendieg paving stones and tubs about. He requested him to go away a dozen times before he attempted to take him into custody, when he became still more violent, and it was with difficulty he brought him to the police office.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson said he might state in extenuation that the prisoner had not been previously before the court, and pro- bably would not have been then, but the prisoner Chorley having more money that he knew well what to do with, made Mr. Sweep very drunk, and a good many others in the same street—The Bench fined him 55., and costs ss. Bd.

RUNCORN COUNTY Comm—There was very *little business at the Runcorn County Court on Tuesday, the Judge, Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, only being occupied hear- ing cases about 40 minutes. The list contained 43 original plaints, 1 adjourned plaint, and 10 original judgment sum- monses; but there were no cases of public interest, ASSAULT ON A CUM]) AT RUNCORN.—A.t Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. James Reynolds, an elderly woman namcd Jane Hardcastle, living in Cambridge-street, was charged with unlawfully assaulting John Wesley Boyle, a child two years of age —Mr. Lake, who appeared for the complainant, said this. assault was not one of those trivial cases, which, he thought, were often excusable where a " box on the ears" was ad- ministered for some little behaviour; but it was of such a nature that the eyesight of the iiittle one might have been permanently injured. The parents of the child live in Robert-street, ne4r where lived the defendant, who had for some-time made herself very unpleasant to her neighbours, and especially to Mrs. Boyle. On the 4th instant, some " words " took place between the defendant and Mrs. Boyle, who shortly afterwards passed the ashpit of the defendant's house. The defendant opened a small door, and made use of some disgusting language, at the same time taking a handful of the filth from the ashpit and sending it in the face of the child. A quantity of the stuff went into its eyes. Whatever quarrel there might be between grown-up people to gratify any spite or ill-will by throwing dirtat the child was mean in the extreme, and he thought deserved severe censure from the Bench—Evidence was given in support of the charge, and Mr. Hitchen, who appeared for the defence, replied.—The defendant was fined 10s. and costs.

A "PROFESSIONAL" AT RUNCORN: ALLEGED RonnErtv.—At the Runcorn Police-court, on Monday, John Walsh, described as a " professional," was brought up in custody, charged with stealing £1 11s., the property of Jane Pickering.--Superintendent Williamson said the prosecutrix was the wife of a shopkeeper in Bridge-street. On Saturday evening the prisoner and another man went into the shop and asked Mrs. Pickering what she had to drink. She told him ginger beer, and ultimately sold to him a bottle of beer of some description. While he was drinking it the other man engaged Mrs. Pickering, and pretended to be anxious about finding the abode of some family of the name of Winter. with whom he stated he was acquainted. Apparently to refresh her memory, the prisoner's companion placed his band upon her shoulder, and asked her if she did not recol- lect that they had a child burned about 18 months ago. Mrs. Pickering expressed her ignorance of the occurrence. At that moment she felt a hand in her pocket, and, turning round, Flaw the prisoner nitll her puree, which she had only a few minutes ago placed in her pocket, in his band. She accused him of stealing it. He dropped it on the floor, and be and his companion made off. Subs,quently the prisoner was apprehended. He gave an address, which on enquiry proved to ba false, ai.d Mr. Williamson asked for a remand in order that enquiries could be made.—The prisoner was remanded until Wednesday.

In making the presentation the president expressed his pleasure at performing the duty which devolved upon him, and said the club was unani- mous in their feeling towards Mr. Foulkes. Mr. Porah read the following address, which will be printed on vellum land framed: "We, the Committe and members of the !Runcorn Workingmen's Club and Institute, have requested Iyour attendance tnis evening for the purpose of presenting you with a tea service in recognition of the many valuable ;services you hare rendered to this institution for the past ; ten years. We all wish that you may remain with us for a longer period, if it be our good fortune to keep the club ; open, which we earnestly trust will be the case. We think I the present a very appropriate occasion for making this pee- sentation, following so closely as it does your recent mar- riage. With this gift the most cordial feeling of respect I from all members are tendered, and they earnestly trust your future career may be happy and prospereus."—Mr. Bennett land Mr. Wm. Howard having addressed a few observations ,to those present, Mr. Foulkes thanked the committee and members for their kind expressions. PROPOSED IMPROVEMENT rTO WIDNES PARISH CHURCH. I —For the purpose of considering and furthering a scheme for removing the front wall of the graveyard of Widnes Parish Church, re-erecting it at an increased height, and surmounting it with a handsome iron railing, a meeting was held in the school-room, Waterloo-road, Widnes, on Monday evening. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams (vicar) presided, land amongst those present were the Rev. W. H. gg W H Du an I Messrs. W. Tracey. senr., Crawford, T. Balmer, Kilcross, Dwerryhonse, W. Tracey, jaw., Crabtree, and Chadwick.— Mr. W. Tracey, senr., in addressing the meeting, said the graves in the churchyard were open to constant trespass and Ide.ecration, for there were hundreds of persons who used lit as a highway, simply to says them from walking round ;Walker's corner, from Church-street to Waterloo-road. The sexton frequently complained of the difficulty be expe- rienced in keeping the children from entering the yard and stealing the flowers from the graves. There were many I other reasons which should induce them to take this matter in hand at once, and he moved a resolution to the effect that ;the churchwardens he called upon to take immediate steps for raising the wall of the churchyard provided they could see their way to obtain the necessary funds to do so. so as Ito effectually prevent the trespassing and desecration of the ! graves, which now existed.—Mr. Balmer observed that in i 1878, when he was a warden, the churchwardens having the sum of £l2O in hand from a bazaar, determined to raise the , wall as far as the money would go, and they erected the south and west sides, but the wall was unfinished to that day. The cost of erecting the front portion of the wall was estimated at £I2O, and the two sides at £25 each, making a total cost of £1.70.—1n answer to Mr. Thomas Atherton, Mr. Balmer said it would be necessary to lay new founda- I tions.—Mr. Crabtree seconded the proposal of Mr. Tracey, and it was carried unanimously. A committee for the pur- pose of collecting subscriptions, &c., consisting of the Church , Council. was formed, and many persons present offered their ! aid in that work. It is to be hoped the improvement, which is a much needed one, will be successfully completed. I TARPORLEY AGRICULTURAL SHOW: PUBLIC MEETING AT • Roxamer.—On Tuesday afternoon a town's meeting was held in the Commissioners' Board Room, Runcorn, to con- , - sider the proposal of the Tarporley Agricultural Society. , There were present Dr. Steele, Messrs. Taylor, Hitchen, Lake, 0. Leak, Williams, W. Handley, H. Jackson, J. Toft, W. Brookes, Steward (Chester), and Cooke (Clayley Hall). —Dr. Steele was voted to the chair, and said he bad sent out about 200 notices, but he regretted to find that there was so few present, and hardly thought it worth while en- tertaining the matter further. He mentioned that he had received letters from Mr. Lello and Mr. Meadowcroft stating they were unable to attend ; and Mr. Charles Wigg had kindly promised a subscription.—Mr. Handley said he bad spoken to several persons about the proposal, and be thought a feeling was being raised in favour of the show being held in Runcorn, but with such a poor attendance it seemed undesirable to proceed further.—The Chairman asked if the Tarporley Agricultural .Society would come to the town on their own responsibility.—Mr. Steward said there did not seem to be any disposition to assist them at all.— The Chairman then asked if the society would come if with- out giving a guarantee two or three gentlemen offered to obtain subscriptions.—Mr. Steward was hardly in a position to take the responsibility of saying the society would come, but if the chairman or any other gentleman would take the matter up, he thought there was yet time to get the show at Runcorn. Otherwise the committee would have to look out for another place.—Mr. Cooke stated there had been no guarantee in previous years. It seemed strange to him the people of Run- corn did not take more interest in the question.—Ultimately Mr. Leak moved that the following committee, with power to add, be appointed to consider the means of arranging for , the show and receive subscriptions :—Messrs. S. B. Chad- wick, Steele, Lloyd, Wigg, Leak, Hitchen, Taylor, NV. Handley, Lelae, T. Handley, J. Williams, Fairhurst, T. Nor- man Steward, R. Gorst, J. C. Jackson, W. Hankinson, P. A SALVATIONIST'S REWABD.—A young and neatly. dressed woman named Jane Ward appeared at the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, to prefer a charge of assault against a man named John Lawton.—On Monday night the complainant attended the "Hallelujah tea meeting" of the Salvation Army, and the proceedings which afterwards took place. It was in consequence ten o'clock when she arrived home, where the defendant lodged'. The defendant told her that was a fine Utile to come home, and that she must go back to the Army. He then seized her by the throat, "held her against the machine," and struck her three times.—The defendant appeared to treat the matter very lightly, and was laughing during the time the witness was gi-ving her evidenee.—Mr. Heald, one of the magistrates, said the defen- dant's conduct was cowardly, and instead of laughing he ought to be ashamed of himself. He would be fined 10i. and costs, Ta. tid. LiNcm AND YOBESMIP.E RAILWAY.—At the half-yearly meeting of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Rail- ' way Company, on Wednesday, the chairman (Mr. T Barnes) stated that the increased traffic during the past half year, amounting to £77,552, had enabled the directors to pay an increased dividend of It half per cent, though the Blackburn disaster had cost the company £22,000. The receipts from first and second class passengers had decreased, while there had been an enormous increase of third-class passengers. With regard to the Post-office parcels post, Mr. Barnes said the railway companies had heartily co-operated with the Postmaster General; and though in the first instance the project would result in a reduction of the shareholders' dividends, they trusted that in the long run there wsuld be no loss at all. Amongst other works which will require Parliamentary sanction the directors have adopted a plan for improving the Company's station in Tithebarn-street, Liverpool. A HOT TEMPERED HUSBAND: SCANDALOUS ASSAULT ON WITE AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday, at Widnes Police Court, Thomas Flannigan was brought up in custody to answer a charge /of assaulting his wife, Mary, who ap- peared to give evidente and was very rcspectably dressed. It seems that on Sunday the prisoner, with more or less violence, requested his wife to leave the house, "and his temper would cool." This most extraordinary request not being at once complied with, he rained blow after blow upon the face and head of his wife with his fist, and savagely kicked her in the side of the body and hip. A witness was called, who stated she heard the prisoner threaten to " rip " his wife open with a knife, and split her head open with a hat chet he held in his hands, and acted altogether in a most excited and brutal manner, whilst another alleged she heard the blows given by the defendant across the street. He repeatedly illused and turned his wife out of the house. Defendant, who gave himself a little the airs of a martyr, was told by the Chairrcan (Mr. Heald) that he had behaved in a most scandalous and a most disgraceful manner. He was fined 403. and coals, or, in default, one month's hard

WOMEN'd O.IJARRELS.—On Wednesday at the Widnes I Petty Sessions, Ann Ghaghan was charged with threatening to assault Mary Smith on the 15th inst., and Elizabeth Ghagban was charged with having on the same day assaulted Mary Smith. After hearing the evidence, the I3ench dismissed the case against Ann, and fined Elizabeth 53. and costs 103. 61—Mary Ann Stokes, a married woman, was summoned on a charge of assaulting Maria Osborne on the 12th inst.; aud a young woman named Elizabeth Tobin was brought up to answer a similar charge. Tobin pleaded guilty. It appeared the complainant was 'making her way acress Widnes Old Marsh on the night of the day in ques- tion, when the dcfendant Tobin, who was sitting on a rail near the house of the defendant Stokes, invited her to pull her ulster off and she would show her bow to fight. She followed her challenge u? bytstriking complainant on the face with her fist, levellir'e, her to the ground. Whilst in this position, it was alleged, the defendant Stokes kicked her on the forehead, and Tobin severely bit her finger, and , extracted a gold earring from her ear. Several witnesses I were called, who stated Stokes no part in the assault, but the Bench tined her ss. and Gs. costs, and 'robin was ordered , to pay a penalty of 101. and Ss. GI. costs, or go to gaol for 14 days. AN INCIDENT IN THE Liz OF i WIDNES BAILIFF. —An elderly man, named John Ball, a contractor living in Lavinia-terrace, was summoned to appear at Widnes Police Court on Wednesday, on a charge of assaulting a bailiff named Frederick Wilson.-Mr. Beasley appeared to prosecute. —On the 17th inst, Mr. Whiteside, the income tax col- lector, and the cmplainant, went to take possession of the defendant's house, for a debt of £1 133.4(1. for income tax, which had been frequently applied for. The defendant was not in, and Wilson went into the parlour while Mr. Whiteside went away. Shortly afterwards, the defendant was brought home in a cab. He was in a drunken and excited state, and seized the complainant by the coat, shook him violently, and in the struggle they both fell to the ground. Cam- plainant had his knee upon the chest of the defendant, and managed to get himself loose, but not before his coat had been badly torn. He made his way from the house as quickly as possible, and information was subsequently given to the police. Afterwards Mr. Whiteside and complainant went back to defendant's house, and finding it locked up, forced the door.—Witnesses were called for the defence, who- stated complainant tripped down the defendant, and that complainant tore his coat with an open drawer.—The Bench tined the defendant Si. and £1 Is. costs, or in default, 21 days' imprisonment. THE BONA-FIDE TRAVELLER'S QUESTION AT FARE- WORTH.—Thomas Sherwood, a young man, was summoned at Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. W. N. Heald and Mr. John Brock, that he, on Sunday, the 13th inst., by falsely representing himself to be a traveller, was supplied with a pint of beer at the Central Inn, Farnworth, during the period which licensed premises were directed to be closed. From the evidence of the landlord, Wm. Twist, and his wife, it. appeared that on the afternoon of the day in question, the defendant,who was accompanied by another young man' called at the Central Inn. He informed the landlady that they bad come from Prescet, and in conse- quence were admitted into the house and served with beer. Whilst there the defendant broke a pup's leg. Mr. Twist afterwards learned the defendant lived in Farnworth.—De- -1 fendant stated to the Bench that he walked to Rainhill on Saturday night with a young man named John Eccleston. He stayed there all night, and returned to Farnworth on Sunday afternoon, and he thought he was entitled to a drink. —Eccleston confirmed this statement.—Mrs. Twist said on Monday night the defendant went to the beerhonse to ask hew the pup was‘and be told her he had slept in Farnworth on Saturday night. On Sunday when her husband threatened to fetch the policeman, the defendant hinted it would be "worse for him and worse for them."—Mr. Heald remarked that defendant bad made himself liable to a fine of £5. -He would be fined 203. and costa, or in default a month. ALLEGED EXTENSIVE WAREHOUSE ROBBERY HE BOYS IT WIDNES.—Mr. W. N. Heald, J.P., and Mr. J. Brock, J.P, were engaged, at the Widnes Police Court on Wednesday, in investigating a charge of breaking and entering the ware- house of Mr. J. W. Wareing, oil and grease manufacturer, Pleasant-street, Widnes. The prisoners were boys, raggedly dressed, whose ages varied from 10 to 14 years and were named Edward Dugan, Patrick Quinn, and Thomas Lee. Mr. John Worth, of Joseph-street, in the employ of the prosecutor, locked the door of the warehouse and office on Saturday afternoon the 12th inst., and saw that all the win- dows, atc., were fully secured; although a pane of glass was broken in one window-frame in the warehouse; through which the "catch" might easily be moved. At six o'clock on the Monday morning following be Arent to the works, and on unlocking the door on the grease shed he observed that its contents had been disturbed from their ordinary position. He then inspected the office, and from marks upon the pay office window, he saw that the catch had been "slid back:" Mr. Alfred W. Wareing, the manager, who resides on Pex Hill, Widnes, was informed of the circumstance, and examined the office. The search revealed that there had been abtracted a canvas bag, containing us. 54., a pack of cards, a hundred cigars, a quantity of black lead pencils, and about three shillinga worth of postage stamps. The aggregate value of the articles was about £2 ss. Certain investigations by the police led to the apprehension of the prisoners by P.C. Pitt, who charged them with robbery. Each made a statement, admitting participation in the robbery to a certain extent, and Quinn described how he had concealed the cigars in tne gram on the railway side. The pack of cards was found in the house of Quinn's parents. The Bench committed the prisoners for trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions.
Mr. J. Parr, of Hatton Hall, Warrington, was cma of the judges for cattle at the Crewe agricultural show, ma Saturday.

The other morning the Clerk of the Peace for Lan- cashire received information that swine fever had broken Grit at Widoes, near Liverpool. The directors of the Lanca,hire and CheaEire Telephonic Exchange Company, Limited, announcel they will recommend a dividend at the rate of 5 pn per annum to be paid to the shareholders.

• DELAYING A Tnux.—A. carpet cutter namefi John Gleave, of 10, Hawthorn Grove, Manchester, was on Mon- day at the:Warringtrm Police Court, charged with obstruct ing Joseph Cann and G. W. Phillips, ticket collectors, at the Central station, on Saturday night, whilst acting in the execution of their duty.— Prisoner was found asleep in the 11-50 p.m. train from Liverpool, and although he had a ticket in his possession he declined to give it tip. Prisoner was so -obstinate that he delayed the train four minutes. He was ordered to pay 20.3. and costs or go to prison for a month.

THII LONDON IND NORTH-WESTIRN RAILWAY.—At the half-yearly meeting of the London and North-Western Railway Company, held on Saturday at Easton Station, the Chairman Mr. Richard Moon, wart enabled to make a very proud and, to the travelling public, very sitisfactory boast He said "We have not had a sit.gle passenger killed on our railway for the past two years and a half, and for the lazt three years and a half only one—an old lady, NI ho was killei by a beam breaking loose in one of the carriages. And yet every year we carry between fifty and sixty million pas- sengeri."

RIDING ON THE CHESHIRE LINES RAILWAY WITHOLIP TICRET.—George Sowerbutts, a musician, living at 45, Bond- street, Manchester, was charged at the Wariington Police Court on Monday with riding in a third-class carriage en the Cheshire Lines Railway, from Liverpool to 'Warrington, on Saturday, without having previously paid his fare is 61, with intent to defraud the company.—Prisoner was four.l asleep in the jl-50 p.m. train from Liverpool by a ticket calector named Shepherd. He was awakened and asked for his ticket. when be presented a Liverpool and Llandudno steamboat ticket. Prisoner was taken out of the carriage and again asked for his ticket or the payment of his fare, when he said he had given his ticket up, and refused to pay. He was fined 63. including costs.

THROwING HOT ASIIO ON J. MAN AT WARRINGTON. —At the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday, before Aldermen Burgess and Chandlev, a man named John Hind- ley, 17, Albert-street, who is occasionally employed at Bewsey Forge as a labourer, was charged with violently assaulting a peddler named Charles Barnes, by throwing a quantity of hot ashes upon him.—Prosecutor went to attend to a furnacs, and the prisoner, without the slightest provo- cation, threw a spade full of .burning cinders upon the back of Barnes, who emerged from the furnace hole shouting for help.—Prosecutor stated that if he had not had his flannel vest on he would have been burnt to death. A young man named William Kincale knocked tin burning cinders off big back.—The prisoner stated that Barnes threw some coal at him, and that he had no intention of throwing the cinders to hurt the prosecutor.—The Bench, however, thought that it was a most violent assault, and they were quite satisfied that it was maliciously done.—The prisoner was sent ta. gaol for a month, without the option of a fine.

E/POSING BID MEAT FOll SALE. —Richard Holeroft was summoned before the magistrates, at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, on a charge of exposing a quantity of liver on a stall in the market which was unfit for human food; and Peter Kenwright was charged with hav- ing the pieces of liver in his possession, he being in charge of the stall -Mr. Whittle (deputy town clerk) appeared to prose- cute, and Mr. Moore represented the defendants.—lnspector Norman was passing through the market hall on the 12th inst., when he saw Kenwright in charge of a stall. On the stall were exposed 15 pieces of liver, which, in his opinion, were unfit for the thd food of man. Kenwright, on being in- terrogated, stated " that the liver was all right, and as sour.l as a bell of brass, and there me not a butcher in Warring- ton who would say it was bad." He also stated that it belonged to Richard Holcroft. The pieces of liver were then taken to the Town Hall to be examined by Dr. Joseph, who pronounced them to be unfit for the food of man. Mr. Robinson, veterinary surgeon, also stated that the liver was diseased. He said in cross-examination that it was very common to find the liver of an apparently healthy animal more or less in an unwholesome condition. Proof was not forthcoming to show that the premises were occupied by Richard Hofcroft, and be was accordingly discharged,. Kenwright was filled 45 and costs. Ann Withingshaw was brought up on remand at the Warring- Police Court, on Monday, charged with stealing from the shop of Mr. John Burgess, Bridge Foot on the lath inst., one box of tea, value £2; from the shop of Win. Fairhurst, Bridge Foot, on the same day, one sack of Indian meal, value ss. 4d.; from the shop of Sergeant Brayshaw, Bridge-street, on May 17th, one lady's black chip hat, vsluo is.; and from the shop of William Bamford, grocer, Bridge-street, on August 16zh, Vbs. beef, value ss. 61., the property of Thomas Faulkner. The prisoner pfeaded guilty to the whole of the charges. Sne was also charged with stealing one nickel silver pint tankard, value 7s. 6d., from the Lion Hotel Company ; one spirit glass, value 4d., from the Ram's Head, Horsemarket-street ; one cheese, weighing 29 lbs., value 16s. 11d., from the shop of Mrs..Eckersley, Bridge-street, on the lath inst.; and with stealing, at divers times, the following goods, the properties of some persons unknown i—One sealskin jacket, 31 yards blue repo, one pair stays, 52i yards tweed cloth, 50 yards Scotch nlaid, one silk jacket, 161 yards brown dress winsey, one girl's frock, one blacA bonnet, and five straw and tuscan hats. As the prisoner pleaded guilty, no evidence was given, and she was sent to prison for nine months. The Bench thought the conduct of Robert Smith, Mr. Burgess's assistant, very smart in locking up the shop and tracking the prisoner, apt hoped his master would think of it.
