OPENING OF THE PARK ON SUNDAY MORNING. , Sir,—Will you kindly allow me to tell "Attains" that my remarks on the onening, of the Park on Sunday morning, were simply intended to show that some additional strength, which means additional expense, would be required to keep some people in order? Whether the Park is opened on Sun- day morning or not is no business of mine. If "Attains" wishes to advocate the opening, let him personally take, or else sand his request, in writing,with his name and address, to the proper quarter. Surely, he does not expect a public 0 body, appointed to conduct our interest, to pay attention to the plea of any anonymous writer. •rAttalus " has not seen - any misbehaviour on Sunday afternoons (I wish all visitors would say the same); for this reason, he says, "I therefore decline to accept all that Mr. Green says about the annoy- ance t) which respectable people are subjected." This ti means he believes Ido not tell the truth. If "Attains" iil persorally see me I plidge myseif not to divulge his name, and if I do not prove to him I have not over-rated my com- plaint he is at liberty to tell your readers that I have not told the truth. I also tell him if he will look in the file of Th,e Examiner, printed, I think, about two or three years ago, he may find among the " notes " ( r " j,.ttings" a corn- .'e plaint,iu vary strong language, about the insolence of V some youths who visit the Park on Sunday afternoons. If I remember right the signature is "Attains." Vex or please, r whom it may, it is my daty, as well as that of , other servants, to put down, if possible, any , act of misbehaviour towards ieTectable visitors

whether those visitors be rich or poor. One gentleman' a little time ago, gave in charge a youth, whom he heard use insulting language to females, for which offence he was heavily fined by the magistrates. This act of the visitor has done much towards lessening the evil. Whenever there is an abatement of this evil the general public soon notice it. Last Sunday was exceptionally good. though not clear from some offenc s against the bye-laws. I. wou'd recomnrnd the fifth and three following bye-laws to the notice of visitors ; to many visitors we are indebted for their endeavour to promote order. If discretion had the , best of me, I ought to pass over the remarks of " Attains " respecting the vegetable matter on the lake, through the manner he writes on this subject; but I wish to tell him if he had made enquiry in the proper quarter be would have found the committee 'Dad complained about the pond, and were making arrangements for appliances to clear it before he wrote in the paper.' I also could have convinced him that the stench did not corns from the water as be suppcsed, bat was destroyed long before the pond was cleansed. When Le ~e;,s any neglect by me, let it be weeds, turning up the grcund, or any other grievance to him, let him honourably and openly bring such neglect before the committee before he rushes in the Pre:s If we could attend all work which he wants doing this little park would be as clean and neat as those of other towns.—Yours respectfully. Warrington, August, 1882. EDW4RD GBEEN.

COLLIERS ON STRIKE ENJOYING THEMSELVES. Sir,—We, the miners at Messrs Evans' collieries, can en- joy ourselves in this strike far better than we could in any previous strike that has yet taken place. Here is an illustra- tion: A party of us commenced to talk about some amuse- ment, until it arrived on a practical shape, and we agreed to pay the small sum of 23. each, Other donors came in so numerously, that we were prepared with a potatoe pie for the whole 26 who paid the 21., the pie having been cooked by the men's wives. And, Mr. Edetor, we have had a splendid dinner. If every family in England had such a dinner, we should not read of so maley cises of starvation as we do. The best of all is, we have a balance of 10s. 63. in hand to- wards a tea for the same parties, which will take place on the premises of Mr. Fisher, clogger. And, Mr. Editor, there were no intoxicants about it. We had a special entertain- ment afterwards, which consisted of a short address from the chairman, who, alluding to the present strike, brought a striking illustration as to how well Englishmen could accomplish the work they had in hand witb modesty and sobriety when the men went to work in a determined man- ner. Whatever at body of Enalishmen take in band, with a determination, they can succeed. We appointed a committee to work out the tea for Wednesday next. I forgot to inform you that the meeting commenced by singing a well known hymn, "Come let us join our cheerful songs." There was another beautiful hymn "When I survey the wenderous crose," after which was a splendid recitation "The Tay 13ridge disaster." Another beautiful hymn "Before Jehovah's awful throne "followed, and then a member gave a melody called "Stand like the brave." This was followed by a temporance melody "Teetotal car." Another temperance melody. entitled "Joe Perkins," was followed by the melody "The negro slave. A melody, "Gipsy warning" was then given. A short address was given by another member, who exerted all to attend some Sunday school, and try to bless others while being blessed. So, Mr. Editor, this concluded our fist day's pleasure, which far outweighs either going to sea-b ithing towns or drinking saloons, for in the first place it is making their money last out well, and in the next we can show to the world that the colliers are not the" drunken colliere " that used to be.—l am, yours, eze., Haydoek, 24th August, 1882. A MINER.
THE CLERGY WIDOWS' & ORPHANS' INSTITUTIONS AT WARRINGTON.
V .

A GOOD SUGGESTION. The following letter from Dr. J. W. Watkins, ef Newton- le-Willows, appears in the Dvcrpoo( Diocesan Garctto for this month : I intended, had there been a good opportunity, at the annual meeting of the subacrieera to these Institutions, held at Warrington, to suggest a plan of augmentir'ee their sadly deficient Income.' I would propose to do this by an Annual Musical Festival, to be held in rotation in Chester, Manchester. and Liverpool. This is a time-honoured practice' seeing the one hundred and fifty-ninth meeting for the Three Choirs' Festival will be begun at Hereford five .weeks te-day. And let me, as far as I can, disarm the hostile criticism of that ;arose numeer of persons, of tender religious susceptibilities, who instinctively object to the holding of these festivals in our cathedrals, by stating that I would not have any musical per- formances—sacred or secular—for which direct payment would be exacted held in our cathedrals. Some persons may say this plan weuld divsst the festival altogether of its religious tone. Quite the contrary; I would rigidly guard the sanctity of our cathedrale, by separating the religious from, by comparison, the more secular part of the work. The key-note to the week's work—charitable and musical— should he given on the Sunday in the cathedral, where the ' •cause of the Institutions might be advocated by an eloquent preacher, and the musical portion of the services by the ,cornbined choirs might illustrate the glorious wealth of Church music bequeathed to us by Palestrina, Bach, Handel, Cherubini, and Mendelssohn. Again, on the first morning of the Festival a religious service, with a special sermon, might be given in the cathedral; and I wou:d also plead to - dedicate one evening, instead of to a patchwork concert, to a Popular religious service, when the " Te Deem," the "Old Hundredth," and the "Evening Hymn" might be poured forth from thousands of throats in grand unison, and thereby convince the congregated crowds that religious music, un- sullied by reminiscences of tlie opera or the clap-trap of the low music halls, can address itself to the hearts of the multi- tude. These services would, of course, be under the sole control of the Dean and Chapter in the city in which the Festival took place. By this plan I should expect to enlist the sympathies of the Deans aid Chapters of the several cathedrals; because they would be spired the disturbance of the solemn serenity of their daily services, and the pain of seeing their cathedral dismantled, disfigured, I had almost said desecrated, for three or four weeks in pre- paration for, and putting to rights after, the Festival. I should atepeel to the wide support of those people who object to be excluded from a church except on payment, and, I think also, to that smaller class who are shocked by the thought even of performers or people turning their backs upon tile Holy Table. The oratorios, and other musical works, and concerts would be given in public halls. lam emboldened to make this proposition by my conviction of the extraordi- nary local facilities and means we possess for giving musical performances to large au4iences. Where, out of London and Birmingham, are there more commodious halls than the Philharmonic and St. George's Hall, in Liverpool, or the Free Trade Hall, and perhaps where, in Manchester ? We are in the heart of a very wide. district containing thousands of chorus singers, professional and amateur; and in each of the three cities there are most eminent musicians, practised in the organisation and conducting of orchestras and choirs, whose eervic,s would be a guarantee of the suc- cessful rendering of the best works of our greatest composers. To carry out this plan there should be -no difficulty in finding two hundred gentlemen in the three dioceses to form a guarantee fund, by each subscribing £5. The general expenses of these festivals should he much less than those of the festivals of the three choirs. If Royalty can condescend to try and convert every clergy- man into a collector for a pet scheme that, whilst it may dis- cover and foster "the tit, though few," humble musical geniuses, will I fear, retard if not suppress the development of National musical education, with how much greater force will the cause of the widow and orphan plead with the clergy to carry on this work. Besides, I should expect every sub- scribing member to these inslitutions to canvass for their support by these special means. Thus, if the work of which I have given but a feeble-outline could be carried out in the fullest extent it is capable of, might the members of the Church in the three Dioceses mate in a very • ' trinity of bene- ficence, arid the bishops, clergy, and laity conspire and combine in a glorious work of charity—an act of "pure religion and undefiled, via., to help the fath.rless and widows in their af2iction.

div.head: STRIKE IN THE COAL TRADE.
div.p: THE STRIKE IN THE COAL TRADE.

The strike of the miners and dav-wagemen employed by the firm of Messrs. Richard Evans 4.i Co., of the Haydock, Ashton, and Golborne Col!cries still continues, though there is no new feature to report in connection therewith. As we stated last Saturday, a loge number of men are obtaining work elesewhere, whilst the remainder are being maintained on the fends of the Miners' Society, and the subscriptions which are being received from other districts. Both the roasters and the men still show a determined front and neither hay- made any offer of a consession one way or another.\ So:far as present appearances are concerned, the strike may still last for a great length of timP. Everything in the distect is remarkably qu!er, and the patience, forti- tude, and peaceable behaviour of the men cannot but be commended.

div.head: LICENSING SESSIONS.
div.p: LICENSING SESSIONS.
WARRINGTON'.

The annual sessions for the granting and renewing of licenses were held at the Borough Police Court, on Tues- day. The presiding magistrates were Alderman Davies and Councillors Monks and Broadbent. In his annual report Mr. Hunt (the chief constable) said the numbers of licensed victuallers and beerhouse keepers were the same as last year, but the off licenses had decreased by two, the numbers being now :—Licensed victuallers 87, beerhouse keepers 48, and off license holders 86. The transfers have been :—Licensed victuallers 15, beerhouss-keepers 5, and off license holders 12. Proceedings had been taken against six licensed victuallers. Convictions were recorded in four cases, and two were dismissed. Two beerhousa keepers had been summoned, both of whom were convicted. Three shopkeepers having off licenses had been proceeded against, and a conviction obtained in each case. The following is a table showing the number of persons proceeded against for drunkenness during the past ten years :
rers7ng chargPd with drunkennes.
Year. Convicted. 1)i ,missed. Total. Male Female ,Male Female 1873

There was one application for a license to sell liquors, to be consumed on or off the-premises ; four to sell beer for consumption off the premises; and one application for transfer of beer license off the premises, the whole of which were to be considered by the licensing committee on Tues- day, September sth. Mr. Monks asked if there was any card playing and gambling that was known to the police, and which could be fairly charged against any individual publican present. Mr. Hunt: There has been noboey summoned or brought up during the year for any such offence; but I have heard at times of card-playing and domino-playing going on in public-houses and beer-houses. There are one or two per- sons in the court who conveyed a report to me that a game of cards was played in a public-house in Warrington last Friday afternoon for £25, and we are doing all we can to work up the report. I have a list of the names of the per- sons who took part in it; but the great difficulty will be in obtaining sufficient information to justify us bringing the case into the court. It is a most disgraceful affair, from the fact that they are men te1.,0 ought to have known better, and that it was perpetrated in a house where there is a good widow who has not been long in the business. A Manchester man and a Birmingham man, from information I have received, played for £25 aside, and men came down to the police station who had lost £3 or £4 with betting on the transaction. I have not heard of any other case during the past year. Thomas Clare, landlord of the Packet House, Bridge-foot, applied for the renewal of his license.—Mr. Hunt said that Mr. Clare was brought before the magistrates in February last for permitting drunkenness on his licensed premises. and the case was dismissed. He had been a license holder in Warrington since August sth, 1878. This was not the only time he 'had been reported by the police, but the other instnnces were not such as to justify the police summoning him before the magistrates.—Alderman Davies observed that it seemed from Mr. Hunt's report he had been reported since the case against him was heard last February, and he would have to be very careful of the way in which he conducted his business. He (the chairman) advised Mr. Clare to keep up the respectability of his trade.—Mr. Clare: It is a corner ' house, and you cannot keep their mouths shut.—Alderman Davies: Not quite, when they are drinking. (Laughter.) Mr. Hunt said that Joseph Dykes, of the Crow, Bridge- , street, was brought before the magistrates on the 17th March, 1882, for permitting drunkenness, and fined in the ' costs, but he had heard no complaint against him since.— Alderman Davies: Hay* you anything to say ?—Mr. Dykes: Only that the parties said to be drunk were not drunk.— The license was granted. I Mr. James Weave, Barley Mow, applied for a. renewal of his license.—The Chief Constable said that Mr. Gleave had held the license since August 6th, 1877. He was reported by the police for haying persons in his house daring pro- hibited hours ; but on enquiry he felt it his duty to withdraw the charge against .him. He bad no further complaint against him.—The application was granted. . Mr. John G. Stevenson, Mid-stone, Sankey-street, applied for the renewal of his license.—Mr. Hunt stated that the applicant bad held the license since January 3rd, 1831. He was summoned before the magistrates for having persons in his house during prohibited hours, and was fined 20s. and costs on February 24th, 1882. 'He had heard no complaints against him since that tirne.—The license Was granted. Alfred Woodhead, of the Higher Angel, applied for the renewal of his license.—Mr. Hunt said Mr. Woodhead had held a license since 18th of August, last year. He had had no complaint against him except the case tried a few days ago, when he was fined 265. and costs, the highest penalty that could be inflicted, for supplying a young girl with drink.—Alderman Davies said the persons whose names were set forth in the list the magistratea believed to be honest respectable people legally connected with a legal trade ; but if people who got into the trade rnisconducted themselves as the applicant had done, they brought disgrace upon the trade. They all admitted ttat there were certain difficulties in conducting the trade ; at the same time the 1 applicant was very much to blame indeed in selling liquor to children of ten-der age. The Bench had some hei-,itation as to whether they should grant the license that day; in the interest of the trade they felt it was a disgrace to the publi- cans that .any of their fellows should be brought before the ' Bench charged Aith misconducting their houses. They, however, would grant the license.—Mr. Woodhead said that he would be more careful in future. He was quite ignorant 1 that he was breaking the law in serving the gill with drink, because she was perfectly sober when she left his house. Mrs. Kershaw applied for a renewal of her license.—Mr. Hunt said Mrs. Kershaw was the landlady of the Hop Pole public-house, Hoesemarket-street, and had not been sum- moned before the Bench during the last year; but a case occurred on the 17th March about which he received a letter I from a tradesman in Warrington who had a number of. apdrenticee working for him. These apprentices left their work about half-past twelve o'clock, and when they returned at two o'clock five of them were more or less drunk, and one of them very much so. After he received the note he despatched P.S. James and another officer to make enquir- ies, and the result was that they found five young women. aged from 14 to 19, drunk, more or less, on private premises' It was ascertaieei that the girl 14 years old bad taken her boots from off her feet an 4 given them to an elder shopmate to pledge. The five girls then went to the public-lionse, and in the space of 40 minutes were supplied with five quarts of ale. The landlady was engaged at the back part of the premises preparing a, dinner for a number of ironwenkers that evening, and the quarts of ale were supplied by four di.ferent persons. The matter was brought before the justices the following morning, and under the advice of Mr.l White no proceedings were taken, as beer was suppiied and I not spirituous liquour ; but he was desired to bring the 1 report forward at the Brewster Sessiogs. He thought it was! fair to say that that was the only report lie had had against 1 Mrs. Kershaw during the year. She bad kept the house for ' 12 years, the license having been transferred to her on April 106, 1871.—Alderman Davies thought the Chief Constable had acted very properly in bringing the matter before the magistrates that day. In the " public " line more discretion had to be used than in auy other trade. and the Bench as far as possible wanted to make Warrington as good and as sober a town as they could srom their point of view. If persons I kept public-houses they must understand the full responsi- bility that attached to them—that was, that they must exercise due discretion, and take care that people under age were not saved, and in every other way conduct their houses respectably. Out of 87 licensed public-houses there were four who had been convicted of breaking the law.—The Bench thought the publicans in Warringeon as a body kept their houses well, and they wanted the publicans to preserve that respectability.—The license was granted.—Councillor Broadbent said that when Mrs. Kershaw was particularly engaged getting ready for a large party, or anything else, she should provide some thoroughly responsible person to take charge of the other part of her business. The whole of the licenses were renewed.

John Heavey Victoria Vaults, Mersey-street, made an application for the renewal of his license.—Mr. Hunt said that Mr. Heavey had been fined for permitting drunkenness on his premises. On Sunday, the 14th May, he and P.S. James found 17 n:en upstairs. Every man seemed perfectly sober and were "a; business." There was a man on guard at the top of the stairs who gave alarm when the police arrived, and they began to scuffle and turn things over. It had been equestion with him whether he should not object to the license being granted. After further observations it was decided to adjourn the granting of the license until the sth September. James Worrall, Bewsey Inn, ale,o applied for the renewal of his license, when Mr. Hunt said that he was fined in the costs on the 30th December last for allowiug gaming. He had had reports from people living in the neighbourhood that a deal of drunkenness was allowed to go on in the house, and when the people got drunk he tumbled them. into the street. The other day he received the letter which he held in his hand from a lady who gave her full name and address, and who stated that her husband went to the public-house, got drunk, and then came home and abused her. Some people knew that he was in possession of those facts, and he thought it was his duty to lay them before the licensing justices. (Hear, Lear.) The case was ad- journed to the sth September, as were the whole of the off- licenses.

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

The annual licensing session for the Petty Sessional Division of Runcorn, was held in the Court-room ore Mon- day. The magistrates on the Bench wire :—Mr. W. Banices, Mr. James Reynolds., Mr. S. B. Chadwick, Mr. Henry Reynolds.

The -following report was read :—" Runcorn Division, Cheshire Constabulary, Superintendent Office, 21st August, 1882. Gentlemen,—l have the honour to:submit my annual report with reference to the conduct of the licensed victuallers and beer retailers in this division during the past year. There are 45 licensed victuallers, 52 beersellers, and 7 others who sell cff the premises, total 104; which gives-an average of 184 of the population to each license. Five licensed victuallers have been proceeded against during the year; one of whom was convicted. Six beersellers have been proceeded against, and four convicted. Ninety-four persons have been convicted of drunkenness during the year, against us in previous year; decrease 21.—1 have the honour to

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, AUGUST 26, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, AUGUST 26, 1882.
be, gentlemen, your obedient servant, SAMUEL WILLIAMSON, superintendent. To • the magistrates assembled in petty session, Runcorn."

TneirsFEßs.—The Mariner's Hotel, Percival's-lane, from John Walker to William Tinsley; Waterman's Arms, Queen-street, from Samuel Johnson to Henry Urmson ; Albion Inn, Peel-street, from Catherine Roberts to John Wilson; Crown Vaults, Heath-road, from George Beech to Thomas Sefton.

APPLICATION Tole A WINE LICENSE.—Mr. Fletcher, of Northwich, appeared on behalf of George Heyes, landlord of the Bridge Inn, Ashridge-street, Runcorn, to make, he said, a modest application, and one he trusted the Bench would have no difficulty in acceding to. He thought the Bench ought to be congratulated upon the report which had just been presented by the Superintendent of Police, and last year it was good fortune to be able to congratulate them upon the report which was then presented. They might take it that sucl,a state of things as far as the , licensed victuallers were concerned was very satisfactory, I and he hoped that so much merit would not go unrewarded. His application was for a wine license to an existing beer- house. It was not an application which anyone could say Vikild in any way tend to increase the drunkenness of the Nicality, nor on any moral ground should it be opposed. Mr. Heyes had been a resident in Runcorn the whole of his life, and was a person of undoubted respectability. For ten years he had been a licensed victualler, and never during that period bad there been the shadow of a conviction cast upon him. Previously he was a grocer in the town, so that he was a man well known in the district, and he was sure , the police, who were the guardians of the public in this I matter, would say no man was better qualified than Mr. Heyes to hold a license of any description, whether for the sale of spirits or the sale of beer. The application was made under these circumstances. Mr. Heyes had good pre- mises, which were assessed at £35 a year, and he proposed, subject to their worst ips' approval, to add to them the house adjoining, which was rented at £lO. Behind the premises there was a large bowline. green, 2,500 yards in extent, and without saying anything disparaging about the other bowl- ing greens in Runcorn, Mr. Heyes might coegratulate him- self upon having the best. The persons who visited the house were, especially those using the bowling green, of a better class than those usually fiecoenting a beerhouse. Gentlemen came from a distance to the green, and the in- habitants of the town to a large extent also used it. These gentlemen wished for something other than beer; they asked for claret, which Mr. Heyes was not in a position to supply them. Light wines were also much in request. He (Mr. Fletcher) did not think their worshiPs would say it was wrong to grant the applicant authority to supply the less intoxicating beverage, when he already held authority to sell the heavier beverage—beer. Taking into consideration the fact that Mr. Heyes had conducted this place so well for a number of years, looking at the character of the house, the character of the guests, and the surround- ings of the neighbourhood, lie thought, at least he hoped , not, their worships would have no difficulty in acceding to the request which he sow made. During the past few veers a population of about 3,000 persons had arisen on D'uke's I Field, and there was not a publc-house for the sale of beer or spirits on the estate, a state of things existing on no other estate in Cheshire. Mr. Heyes on three occasions had applied for a spirit license, but their worships in their dis- cretion refused to grant the license, and, acquiescing in that decision, he now simply asked for a wine license. The house was situated near to the Bridge and a railway crossing and people passing on their way to Widnes called for refreshment. He hoped the Bench would extend to the applicant this privilege and give him a wine license. There was no opposition that morning, and he trusted that would weigh with their worships in considering the case.—Mr. , Heyes was called, and proved the serving of the notices and ' his advocate's statement.—The Bench adjourned to consider their decision, and after an absence of 15 minutes they returned. Mr. Bankes said : We have carefully considered your application and decided to refuse the license. All the licenses were renewed with the exception of those which wore held by persons whose names appeared on thel "black list," who were warned to appear before the Bench on the adjourned licensing day.
PRESCOT BREWSTER SESSIONS. - These sessions were held at Prescot on Thursday, the pre- siding magistrates being Mr. F. W. Earle, Col. Blackburne, M.P., and Mr. H. S. Hall.

Superintendent Barker presented the following report :—I have the honour to lay before you returns of the licensed persons in this petty sessional division. Licensed victuallers 118, beersellers for consumption on the premises 63, beer- sellers for consumption off the premises 25, other licenses 11 —222 Population 44,264, being one licensed house to about every 200 persons. Twenty-one licensed victuallers have been proceeded against during the year ended this date, of whom 17 were convicted, 2 paid costs, and 2 dis- missed. Five beersellers have also been proceeded against, 3 were convicted, 1 withdrawn, and 1 dismissed, 1 license endorsed. I think these figures show that many of the licensed houss within this division might be better con- ducted than they have been during the past year. The convictions for drunkenness have greatly increased. 'Pro- ceeded against this year 880, last year 546, being an increase of 534. This is caused to a considerable extent by people of the very lowest class, both male and female, drinking to all appear- ance, the greatest part of any money they can get hold of. There are three new applications under the Licensing Act— one being for beer, another for spirits and wine to be con- sumed off the premises, the other for an extension to an already licensed house.

The licenses were renewed, with a few exceptions, in which the applications were adjourned until the next licensing day. The first adjourned case Was that of John Horner, Bali lon, Ditton, who had been fined 101. and costs in June last for being drunk on his licensed premises. George Dingsdale, Red Lion, Ptenot, who had been fined 405.. and costs for having his house open during prohibited hours, applied for the renewal of his license.—Mr. J. 0. Swift said he was instructed by the owners, Messrs. Green- all and Co., to appear in this case, in which there were smile special circumstances that he thought would induce the Beech to renew the licens3 that day. It was true that Mr. Dingsdale was fined for supplying mon who went to his house one Sunday afternoon. His excuse was that the men represented themselves to be travellers.—Mr. Earle : I think we have already made a rule that all these cases in which there was any complaints will stand over.—Mr.- Swift : Very well.—Mr. Earle : It is adjourned to the next licensing day.

Isaac Sankey, Grosvenor Hotel, Widnes, applied for a renewal of his license. Superintendent Barker said Mr. Sankey, on the 22nd February last, was lined £lO and costs for having his house opened during prohibited hours, and he was also summoned for permitting drunkenness, but that case was dismissed.—Mr. Beasley, of Widnes, said he re- presented Mr. Sankey, and also Mr. Bolland, the trustee. The affairs of Mr. Sankey were in liquidation, and as their worships were aware, the interest of the tenant in the license vested by virtue of the petition in the trustee. Mr. Sankey, the present tenant, was only in the house temporarily, and imagined that the Bench, would, almost as a matter of course, renew the license in the name of the trustee.—The Clerk : Oh, no.—Mr. Beasley : Provision is tads for it by Act of Parliament.—The Clerk: As I gather, you are instructed by Mr. Sankey and not by the trustee.—Mr. Beasley: I was instructed by Mr. Gibson, the trustee's partner, last week.— Mr. Earle : The case is adjourned to the next licensing day.

The other defaulters were :—Charles Harrison, Barn's Head, Whines; John Clay, Commercial Inn, Widnes; John Webb, Kims's Arms, Widnes; Benjamin Holden, Albert Hotel, Widnes ; Thomas Littler, Main Top, Widnes ; Patrick O'Loughlin, Star Inn, Widnes; William Twist, Central Inn beerhouse, Widnes; John Gill, Manchester House, Widnes ; and John Clay, Widnes. husband, of Widnes, applied on behalf of Mr. Daniel Harrison-Lowry, for a license to sell off, at a shop in Travis- row, Whines. The notices had all been duly served, and pre- vious to a recent Act of Parliament, their worships had no dis- cretion, but this Act hed introduced discretion of which he had no doubt the: 'Bench know all about. He referred to the Act because it bad just been pissed, and it had certainly put a whip in the hands of the magistrates which he hoped they would not use on this occasion. Everything was done in this cese before the Act of Parliament came into force. His client had gone to some expense, and previous to almost the last few days persons who had done as Mr. Lowry had done could not be refused a license.—Mr. Lowry was then called to prove the service of the notices, and he stated the nearest public-house was 200 yards away from his shop. Mr. John Bennett, Widnes-road, Widnes, next applied for a wine and spirit license. 'Mr. Bennett said be held two grocers' licenses already, and his application was for a third. This was for an entirely new shop. He was going to give up one of-the shops in Lugsdale-rod, as the lease would expire in-February. The nearest public-house was between 100 to 200 yards off. Mr. McKenzie then made an application on behalf of Mr. Edward Rogers, Seal Arms, Huyton Quarry, for permission to erect new building on a piece of land adjoining the Seal Arne Hotel. To prove the service of the notices, he called a witness who stated that he served the notices on Mr. H. Makin. of Huyton.—The Clerk pointed out that Mr. Makin was not one of the overseers.—Mr. McKenzie said he was the assistant-overseer, and contended- that to all intents and purposes Mr. Makin was an overseer. He further remarked that it was a question whether the application required service of notices, as it was for an extension of license —The Clerk You either went the justices', authority or you don't.—Mr. McKenzie: I take it the magistrates will waive the objec- tion.—The Clerk: Oh, they cannot.—Mr. McKenzie: It has been a custom, your worships, for these notices to be served en the assistant overseer.—The Clerk: Can you prove the emetom ?—Mr. McKenzie: I cannot.—The Clerk: What is the good of putting that to the Bench if you can't prove it? Custom won't over-ride an Act of Parliament. He then quoted the Act which referred to "one of the overseers of the parish or township." "If," said the Clerk, "you can any decision which says the assistant overseer is an overseer, then the Bench will consider it. I do not know of anv."—Mr. McKenzie: If I were applying for a new license I should have served these notices upon the overseers, church doors, and so on. This is not an application for a new license, but au extension of license, and I doubt very muck whether any notice is necessary.—The Clerk: Will you define for the magistrates' information what an extension of license means? Because there is no such thing in the Licensing Act that I am aware of.—Mr. Earle: The Bench are quite satisfied, Mr. McKenzie, this notice has not been properly served on the overseer.—Mr. McKenzie: I shall have to apply at the adjourned sessions.' Mr. Husband' said on Wednesday, at Widnes, Andrew j Quinn, beerhouse-keeper, was summoned before the magis- trates for having sold liquor without a license. The cir-

eumstancei of the case were these :—Quinn applied to the Bench at Widnes, on the sth July, for a temporary transfer which was granted to him, and which said he was entitled to sell on his premises until the 15th August, that was the special sessions held at Prescot last week. On obtaining; the transfer Mr. Quinn commenced to sell on his new pre- mises, happy in the idea that he was going to carry on this public-house to his own advantage, and with the permission of the police. Notice was afterwards served upon him by the police to the effect that the general annual licensing meeting was to be held at Prescot, on Thursday, the 24th August. When his client saw that notice, he presumed that was the day he had to attend at Prescot like all other pub- licans, and he omitted to present himself there on the 15th instant. The result was a policeman went, on the 16th instant., and purchased a glass of beer, and defendant was summoned. On Wednesday the magistrates considered the case, and said it was a pure mistake. Mr. Quinn at once shut his house, and he ap- plied to the Bench to extend the license, for they had power, he contended, to grant a tempoiary transfer until the next special sessions.—After consideration the Chairman said the Bench had no power to grant the man Quinn a transfer, and he would have to wait until the 17th October. If he chose to forget the day for transferring licenses he must take the consequences. In regard to the application of Mr. Lowry, the Bench were unanimous in refusing it. As to Mr. Bennett's application, unfortunately the magistrates had not option. He had got two licences already, and they thought he might have done very well without a third. However, it was granted, but he hoped the law would be altered another year

POLICE INTELLIGENCE. .WARRINGTON POLICE COURT. SATURDAY —Be'ere Aldermen Burgess and Chandley. A DESERTER.—John Davies was brought up on remand charged on his own c ,nfession with having deserted from Her Majesty's 11th Regiment of Hussars, stationed at Gosport, whilst acting as an escort.—The ptisonsr was again remanded pmding the arrival of further information from 'Gosport. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmers), Major Cartwright, and Councillor Fairelough. TIPPLETIS.—The following were charged with being drunk and disorderly :—Patrick Fallon, Cis and costs; Martin Gal- lagher, 55 and costs; Joseph Winsoer, 5s and costs; Mary Owens, 5s and costs; Patrick Marty., 5s and costs; John Rohan, 55 and costs; Thomas Taylor, 5s and costs; Thomas McCormick, 5s and costs; WilliarrrThomason, 5s and costs. Jame; Ward, who appeared in court in an intoxicated state, was fined 20s and costs, or the alternative of one month's im- prisonment, for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart, in Bridge-street, on the 12th inst.

STONE THROWERS. —Patrick Burke (II) and William Foley (13) were charged with stone-thr,wing in Old-road, on the 16tb inst.—A lad nam,d Patrick Higgins, who was in the company of defendants,- said that they wPre in Old-road, near to tise Mission, when the two defendants got on a wall and com- menced to threw stones at the Mission door. One c.f the st3nes, abut half a pound in weight, wkich was produced, struck a young I,dy named Miss Nixon, a teacher at the Mission, as she was waiting for admittance. The blow was of such a violent nature that the stone penetrated her hat and cut her head.—lhe Rev. W. Mules observed that stones were constantly being thrown at the Mission-room, and be asked for a sufficient exitmple to be made of the lads to prevent the offence being repeated.—Ti-se Bench ordered Foley, the elder lad, to receive nine strokes of the birch, and Burke six strokes.
A SELF-ACCUSED PESERTER.—John Davies, who had been several times charged, on his own confession, with being a deserted from the 11th Regiment of Hussars, was again brought up and discharged.

SCILOOL ATTENDANCE OASES —At the instance of Mr. George Riley, school attendance in, pector, the following persons were summoned for neglecting to send their children to sch.ol, and fined as stated :—William Bichardsorl, labourer, 53, Erick- street, ss; Patrick Butler, Vernon's-yard, 5s ; P. Bagley, Kinder's-yard (9th apt.learanee), ; Lawrence Laff, Portland- street, 5s ; J. Pendlebury, Tilley-street, 5s ; 11. Danie's, Greenall-street, 5s ;T. Rathbone, Groenall-street. ; Thomas Butler, Kerfoot-street 53 ; Samuel Lea, Orchard-street. 2s 6d, BREACH OF TUE PEACE —Thos. Moran, labourer, Kinder's- yard, was charged with fighting in Ship-yard or. Sunday, and also 'with assaulting Patrick Kelly. Defendant was fighting with two men in Kinder's-yard, and when Kelly passed through the yard to his house defendant struck him violet,tly In the face and blackened his eyes —For the firzt offence defendant was b -und over to keep the peace for six months in two sureties of R 3 each, or in default to go to gaol one month ; and for the assault on Kelly he was fined 40s and c.A.),ts, with the alternative of one month's imprisonment.
TUESDAY.—nefore _Majr,r .Cartwright (ch-tirman), Alderman
Davie., and Councillors Mc:rinks and Broad6ent.

ECHOOL ATTENDANCE CASE —John Fallon was charged under a warrant with neglecting to send his two children to school, and was at the inslance of Mr. George hiley fined lOs iNTOXICANT —Jo.eph Barker. for being drunk in Irlau.-street on the previous day, was fined 5s and costs.

ABSENTEES. —Bartholomew Welsh, !Dennis Quinn, and Ber- narA Flannigan. were charged with absenting themselves from the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, now at Altcar.— They were remanded to await an escort from Aitear. A DESERTER.—John Ryan was charged wsth deserting from Her Majesty's 2011 Regiment of Foot stationed at Bury, on January Ist, I'±Bl. P.S. Spinks met the ptisoner in Butter- market-street that morning. He put some questions to him, when prisoner confessed that he was a itserter. He was com- mitted to Walton Gaol tO await an escort.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley and Councillor Fairelough. INEEIIITEL—Ifary Callagha ) Dolman's-lane, yrs; fined 5s and costs; and Jane Riley and Maria Shields. Pillinz's-conrt, were each fined 10s and costs, or, in default, 14 days. They chme the latter.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASE —John Cartledge was ordered to pay a fine of 10s, or go to prison for seven days, for neglecting to send his daughter to school as require I by the Elementary Education Act.—Mr. George Riley proved the case. ASSAULT—Jane Hennessey, 8, Cropper's-brow, was charged. under a warrant. with assaulting and beating Catherine Brannon, on Monday night Prosecutrix went Into a shop in Battermarket,treet. and had no sooner got inside when the prisoner clme running .in and seized her by the hair of the heal, at the same time throwing her to the floor A man. named George Davenport, who saw the affair, released the prisoner other hold of Mrs. itrannon's hair—Prisoner stated that the presecutrix hai on previous cuasions assaulted her.— Fined les and costs, or 14 days. REMAND CASE.—Thomas Fallon was charged under a war- rant with having neglected to maintain his two children, who have been chargeable to the Union since 12th Marcia last.—Mr. Hunt stated that the police had been In search of the p.isoner since March last, but could not find him. div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.
ALTRINCHAM.

BREWSTER SESSIOIIS.—The annual licensing session was held at Altrincharn on Monday Superintendent Leighton reported that there were in the division 58 licensed victual- lers, 51 beersellers, and 102 others holding out-door beer licenses, giving one house to each 191 of the population. During the year no licensed victualler had been proceeded against, although five beersellers had been sumtloned, four convicted, and two licenses endorsed. 324 persons had been convicted for drunkenness. The Chairman (Mr. R. H. Joynson) observed that there was an increase in the number of persons convicted for drunkenness. The whole of the increase in the number of licenses was in respect to off licenses, with respect to which, until recently, the magistrates had no discretionary power. They should not grant the renewal of the off licenses, that day, but would adjourn them until ihe 25th prox. The license of Thomas Boardman, 9f the Orange Tree, Market-place. Altrincham, was withdrawn, the lanellord having been fined for per- mitting drunkenness. An application made by Mr. Marma- duke Whitty, of the Sale Botanical Gardens, for the exten- sion of the hotel license to the ballroom, was declined, as was also the application to declare the Peel Causeway district a populous place, and so extend the hour of closing to 11 p.m.

THE WELSH WESLEYANS AT STIMISHAW CROSS. The Welsh Wesleyans, who worship in the old Independent Chapel, Stubshaw Cross, held their annual sermons on Sun- day and Monday last. On Sunday morning the preachers were the Rev. H. Hughes, of Birkenhead (lately returned from America), and Mr. J. Williams, of Earlestown ; the afternoon and evening preacher was the Rev. ll. Hughes. On Monday morning the pulpit was occupied by the Rey: 0. Lloyd navies of Liverpool, and in the afternoon by the Rev. H. Hughes. In the evening both the rev, gentlemen named preached short, though interesting sermons. The services on the whole were :very well attended, and wilh the exception of that on Sunday afternoon were conducted in the Welsh language. Collections were made in aid of the chapel fund. On Wednesday evening a fair number of per- sons assembled in the chapel to hear a lecture by the Rev. H. Hughes. The chair was occupicd by Mr. Russell Jones,of Earlestown. The lecture was given in the Welsh language, and its title was " Yr hyn a hoffais a'r hyn ni hoffais o'r pethau a Welais yr America." The address consisted of an eloquent and interesting description of a three months' tour in America, and was listened to with much attentton. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lec- turer

TEACHERS' ANNUAL FIC-NlC.—The annual pic-nic in connection with the Wigan and District Teachers' Associa- tion, took place on Saturday afternoon last, and a very en- joyable afternoon was spent. The association includes among its members teachers in the Billinge, Ashton. Aspill; Ince,-four CrAborne districts, and those in the Wigan dis- trict met at the Wigan station shortly after two o'clock. They were then conveyed in two conveyances, through Billings and Downall Green to Ashton. Here the local contingent joined them, and the whole party, numbering abeut 40, proceeded to Newton lake. • Some few hours were spent in a pleasant row on the lake, or in strolling about the neighbourhood, the weather being eminently favourable for the occasion. The return journey to Ashton was com- menced in due course, and tea was provided for the party at St. Thomas's school, Ashton, at seven o'clock. The tea was arranged for six o'clock, but owing to a slight accident to one of the horses, about an hour's delay was experienced. The tea was a most substantial one, and full justice was dene to the good things provided. The president afterwards briefly addressed those assembled, speaking of the very pleasant afternoon they had spent. The room was then cleared for dancing, and tte party. thoroughly enjoyed themselves uh to about nine 'o'clock, when the Wigan com- pany took to their waggonettes and repaired homewards via Billinge.- Two COLLIERY HANDS ON STRIKE GETTING MARRIED.— An occurrence of an unusual 'character took place at Ashton on Monday last, when two colliery hands, both of whom are out on strike, were united at the hymeneal alter, by the Rev. H. Siddall, of St. Thomas's Church. The young man follows the occupation of a collier, while his now, "better half" has worked as a "brow girl," but as before stated, le-ith are out on strike, a circumstance that has taken many persons by surprise. After the ceremony had been duly per- formed, the "happy couple," with a large circle of friends repaired to the Fleece Inn, kept by Mr. Thomas Prescott, and here the party thoroughly enjoyed themselves. For the occasion the genial host went to the expense of purchasing a handsome colour, which was gaily flying in the breeze, while others were also displayed by friends of the couple. Quite a "jolly day " was made of the affair, the rejoicings being kept up until late in tne evening. During the after- noon and evening the company was considerably augmented, and a visit was paid to Ashton Heath. Hero a -number of gipsies were encamped in their tents, and by arrangement an " illuminated " dance was indulged in. By means of torches, and quite a picturesque scene was presented, avd about 300 spectators and friends were present. Members Of the gipsy tribe also favoured them with a " gipsy dance," the proceedings being of a very enjoyable and pleasant character throughout.

RE-OPENING OF THE PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, STuRSHAW CROSS.—The special services in connection with the re-opening of the Stubshaw Cross Primitive Methodist Chapel, were commenced on Sunday last, when Mr. J. Moore, of Chester, preached an excellent sermon both afternoon and evening. Special selections were sung by the choir, and collections were made in aid of the alteration and enlargement fund. The building has be6n closed for a few months while undergoing alterations and enlargement, so as to find sitting accommodation . for an increased number of worshippers. Hitherto the building would only seat about 150 persons, but provision has now been made for GO or 70 beyond that number. The contract was originally let for £lBO, but " extra " expenditure has brought the cost up to nearly £2O). Though the alterations were not quite com- pleted on Sunday last they were advanced sufficiently td allow of the holding of service's therein. The collections during the day amounted to about £7. SHCCKING ACCIDENTS AT THE MAINS" COLLIERY: A MINER KILLED AND ANOTHER INJURED. About half- past four o'clock on Wednesday morning, two sad and shocking accidents occurred in the Mains Colliery, and resulted in fatal injuries being sustained by one miner, while another miner received severe injuries. The colliery in question belongs to the firm of Messrs. Cross, Tetley, and Co., of the Bamfurlong and Mains Col- lieries, who employ a large number of hands in connection therewith. At the time stated James Gerrant, 41 years of age, a day-wagetnan, residing at 31, Church-terrace, Gol- borne, was following his eccupAtion in the No. 2 Mains Colliery,and with two other men was engaged filling the tubs with coal dust, when some rooting fell in from above them, , and the lights were blown out. A man named Mansley, who was working near, at once sent for some lights,and on those being procured a shocking sight met their gaze. A large stone, estimated to weigh about two tons, had fallen from the roof and had alighted on Gerrant, who seas lying, crushed, beneath it.. Assistance was immediately obtained, and with some difficulty the stone was removed. Mr. Gerrant was lying on hsi right side, but never spoke after the occurrence. Ile sobbed and breathed several times, but expired in fifteen minutes after his release. He was at once put into a " tub,'2 and the body was ultimately taken to the pit bank. A cart was obtained, and the body of the deceased was shortly afterwards removed to his late home. A few hours pre- vious to the sad,occarrence reported above, another similar accident occurred in the same pit, and serious injuries were sustained by Charles Heyes, a miner residing at 6, Druid- street, Ashton Heath. . About half-past two o'clock that Morning Heyes was following his accustomed occupation, when a stone measuring about half a yard square, and weighing about half a cwt., fell" from the roof. It alighted on Heyes' head, and also struck his thigh. • A deep cut was made in his head, in addition to which his thigh was injured. He was conveyed to the pit bank, on his way . passing the man Gerrant, who was then working as hearty as ever. He afterwards managed to walk home, where he has since been attended by Dr. Hannah.

LEIGH. AGRICULTURAL SITOW AT LEIGII.--:-The second show of tke Leigh Agricultural Association since its discontinuance in 1871 was held on Wednesday. The weather was most un- favourable in the morning, and the marquee in which the luncheon was held was blown down, but was again erected, and there was no further mishap. The rain ceased about noon, and there was a good attendance, about 7,000 visiting the show, which was one of the b2st in the sOciety's annals. The president for the year was Colonel Al‘Corquodale, of Newton-le-Willows, High Sheriff of the county. There were 95,5 entries, being about the same as last year, though there

was a distinct improvement in the quality of the stock sod horses. The entries for cattle numbered 138, as against 20 last year; the homes being 108, 40 in excess of the previons show. The High Shariff (Colonel M'Corquodale), presided at the luncheon. The chairman gave "The army, navy, and rese,rve forces,'' to which the Hon. A. Egerton responded. In proposing "The Leigh Agricultural Association," .the chairman said the Legislature was contemplating a thange in the rand laws, and they looked to the good feeling that existed between landlord and tenant in the hope of a re- arrangement being effected by which there would be proper coropenSation for legitimate expenditure upon the land by the tenant. He hoped landlord and tenant would feel that their inNrests were identical. Captain Withington respon- ded. Mr. Hulton proposed "The town and trade of Leigh," Mr. Booth responding. The health of "The High Sheriff" was proposed by Mr. Jabez Johnson, Colonel Blaekburne,, M.P., giving the toast.

div.p: WIGAN.

_ THE CI-TAHOE AGAINST A WIGAN GENTLEMAN.—Thomas byes Robison, of Orrell Mount, gentleman, charged with shooting last week at two constables, with intent to murder, whilst they were attempting to apprehend him under a warrant from the High Court of Chancery, was on Monday again remanded by the Wigan county magistrate's. Mr. S'egar, who appeared for the prisoner, called a medical gentleman to prove that Robison was in a very precarious state of ill-health and not fit to appear. EXTRAORDINARY ACCIDENT ON THE RAILWAY NEAR WIGAN. —An extraordinary I.iccident happened on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway on Monday morning, a short distance from Ilindley station. In order to do away with a level crossing at this spot a large iron footbridge had been placed over the line, and the work was nearly completed. The contractors weie on Monday fixing rollers underneath the structure to allow for expansion and contraction, when, as one end of the bridge was being lowered on to the rollers, it is alleged that a sudden gust of wind caused it to cant, and the structure fell on to the railway, completely block- ing the whole of the lines. One workman, who was on the bridge at the time, was precipitated to the ground, and sus- tained a severe shaking. Breakdown gangs were quickly on the spot, but the task of removing the bridge, which is 1321 t. long, was both tedious and difficult. In six hours one line was cleared, but it was not until late that the traffic was resumed. Meanwhile trains were run up to the spot on one side, and the passengers had to change.into other trains waiting on the other side of the block. The express had only just passed when the accident happened. The structure weighs thirty tons, and it is most fortunate that no loss of life has to be recorded. WINSFORD.

LANDSLIP.-Juq behind the cocoa-house and contiguous property within the last few days has occurred a small landslip. On the appearance of this a few old persons began to remember that there was a brine shaft on the spot many years ago, and pans erected in.which salt was made. The slip has not been dangerous so far, and was soon filled up, but it indicates whereon° may expect another, and will need watching. _ _

On Monday last there was a trip to Behroir Castle from various stations between Manchester and Crewe. Winsford and district sent its contingent to the great Temperance gatherine; in one of the finest districts of England, especially from the elevation on which the Duke of Rut- land's castle stands. The view was magnificent, and the grounds attractive.

SCHOOL SERMONS.—The annual sermons on behalf of the Free Methodist Sunday-school, Station-road, Winsford, were preached on Sunday last, by the Rev. W. Steventon, of Liverpool, afternoon and evening. The school children and their teachers, headed by the Lew circuit minister, the Rev. Win. T. :Symons, and the preacher for the day missioned the streets round Wharton in the morning, so that the attend- ance at sermons was very good. Two earnest sernams and better collections than usual rewarded the efforts made. There was a public tea meeting on Monday afternoon and a meeting after, when Mr. Manning was called to the chair, and speeches were:made. by the Revs. W. Steventon, W. T. Symons, Mr. J. H. Massey, and Mr. Bennett. The result of the anniversary will be a substantial gain of several pounds to the Sundav-school funds.

ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. The Cemetery-road, Crewe, has been opened as a public highway. To the time of its acceptance by the HighwaV Board it has cost £174 145., towards which £154 14s. have been subscribed ; it is proposed tO appeal to the public to rake the ddiciencv.

A file broke cut the ether evening, in the greenhouse of Mr. Parrott, Nantwich, destroying a number of valuable plants he had purposed exhibiting at the forthcoming show. Some laths lying on the top of the flue are said to have caused the fire.

Partridges are very plentiful throughout Cheshire. A very successful breeding season has been experienced, and large conveys are met with. In consequence of the luxuriant growth of vegetation, ample cover abounds for the birds, which are unusually forward. JOY BELLS.—On Mond ty evening last, the bells of Fatn • don church rang a merry peal to celehrat: the return from their bridal tone, of E. W. Sweetenham, Esq , and his br:cl2, a danghter of the late Major Barnston, of Crewe Hill, who were married on the 9th inst., at Farndon church, amid great rejoicings in that village and the neighbourhood. At the annual dinner in connection with the Crewe Agri- cultural Society on Saturday, Captain Cotton who pre- sided, intimated, in proposing the health of the • county members, that Mr, W. F. Tollemache proposed retiring from the representation of West Cheshire at the next election. The hon. gentleman referred to, who was present and replied to the toast, said it had long been his intention to retire at the end of the present Parliament. PRESENTATION TO A POLICE INSPECTOR AT NANTWICIL —lnspector Atherton, late sergeant of the Nantwich Con- stahelary, was presented the other evening with a handsome marble drawing-room clock and a purse of 30 sovereigns, subscribed by the tradespeople and other residents of Nit- with, in recognition of his services and the esteem in which he was held during his eight years' connection with the Nantwich division of the constabulary force. The inspector was afterwards entertained at dinner at the George and Dragon, Pillory-street.

„ BOATING.—Last Saturday evening and Sunday morning there were again numerous visitors to Farndon from Chester, and among these were some from Liverpool and a few from Manchester. •Those who have any acquaintance will the river at Manchester will be surprised to hear that on the waters of the 'mei' there can be anything in the way of boating. As a duck cannot always have the pure spring and _must take advantage of such water as is within reach, the Manchester boatman is compelled, if he wants a ” row "at hand, to skim the inky Irwell: No doubt when he goes to the Dee for his occasional water trip he enjoys the change as much as he does a breathe at Blackpool after leaving Deansgate. Many on Saturday had an excellent spin in their skiffs from Chester, some spending the Sunday at Farndon and a few going across to Holt ; leaving Cheshire for Denbighshire, and England for Wales. Holt is an interesting little town, a contributory to the Wrexham dis- trict of boroughs, has an extensive ruin of a castle, once the property of a Stanley who fell a victim to Henry VIPs avarice, and it has a splendel church of the early Tudor era. CHESHIRE DAIRY FARMERS' ASSOCIATION.—A meeting of the members of this association was held on Saturday, at the Golden Lion Hotel, Chester, Mr. Henry Davies (Wervin) presiding. Lord Tollmache wrote thanking the association for electing him as one o; the vice-presidents. Mr. G. W. Latham, of Bradwall Hall, in his letter, said—"! hope to be at your meeting, and would like to see the programme of the committee for your show. So far as I have been able to gather their intentions from writers in the public press, the plan seems to me to be quite inadequate to the occasion. Prizes for ton and half-ton lots of cheese can only be com- peted for by those who can bring their cheese by carts, and no one in these parts will send any quantity by rail. Nor do I find any proposal for instruction in the art of making cheese other than Cheshire cheese. I hope at the Nantwich meeting to bear a statement of what is proposed to be done. I feel certain, if the committee show that they are prepared to do efficient work, means will not be wanting to support them, but a mere proposal to give prizes and hold a show will not be accepted as sufficient." The secretary presented a list of donations and subscriptions towards the funds of the association, amounting to nearly £l2O, among the donors being the Duke of Westminster, the Marquis of Cholmonde- ley, Viscount Combermere, Lord Delamere, Lord 'Poi I emache, Earl Grosvenor, Sir Philip Egerton, the Hon. W. F. Tolle- mache, M.P Colonel Humberston, Lieut.-Colonel France- Hav)inrst, daptain Tomkinson, Captain Cotton, Captain Massey. Mr. Wilbraham Tollemache, Mr. H. J. Tollemache, M.P., Mr. John Churton, &c., &c. The secretary also announced that he had received £29 15s. since the last meeting. EXTRAORDINARY HOAX UPON THE CHESHIRE POLICE: A SINGULAR STORY.—The county police of Chester have just, been made the victims of an extraordinary hoax. A short time ago, a girl 16 years of age went at midnight to the C:ty Police Office, and complained of having been indecently assaulted and nearly murdered by two men. She described herself as the daughter of a boatman, and said that on the night in question she was going to commence an engagement she had secured as servant, at Eceleston, a village ~about two miles and a half from Chester. Her father rowed her up the river to a point known as Heron Bridge, about hell-a-mile from the village, and there landed her, with her clothes tied in a bundle. She informed the police that in crossing a field, between the river and the road, she was set upon by two rough-looking men, indecently assaulted, and deprived of her bundle. Finding that the place where the girl said the affair had taken place was beyond their district, the city officials had transferred the matter to the county authorities, who took it up with vigour. The girl gave a detailed description of the appearance of the men, and an assiduous search was made of the surrounding district, the result being that several men were arrested. Two of them were respectable blacksmiths, whose appearance corresponded to the particulars supplied. The girl failed to identify any of those arrested, but still insisted on the truth of her story. The police, however, became rather dubious after their fruitless efforts and asked the girl to show them the place where she alleged the struggle took place. She pointed out several places in an indefinite manner, but no marks of a struggle were found. After giving the police further trouble, she confessed her story was nothing but a hoax. Having become acqUainted with some young women of loose character, she was strongly tempted to join them. Her companions persuaded her not to go to the place at Fceleston, and acting on their advice she threw her bundle in the river after getting on shore, and returned to town. The same night she got drunk, and got drawn into a brawl and severely abuvd. Repenting of her conduct, she con- cocted the above story and went to the police, being anxious to return to her pareitts. The consequences have been shown. After baying been severely reprimanded, she was sent bow.
