div.head: FRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS,
div.p: FRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS,

Tll3 usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thursday, at the Workhouse, Whiston, when there were present—Messrs. Marsh (chairman), Hall, Gilbody, New- some, Jackson, Buckley, Dobell, Hulme, Birchall, Tyrer, ILeatherbarrow, Tuson, Birch, Kenwright, Paris, Griffith, W. B.Longton, and the Revs. T. Chambers and Finegan, and lir. B. H. Hartley (clerk.) THE WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT. • Mr. HAR i.Hv read the report of the Master of the Work- house, which stated that during the past week there had Peen 484 inmates' as against 445 in the preceding week, and 425 the corresp mding week of last year. There had been •4 deaths during the fortnight. The report also stated that the porter had a friend staying with him, which he (Mr. Martley) thought could nci be objeeted to, as there would be no extra rations needed.—Mr. DonELL : Is it a lady friend? (Laughter.)—Mr. HARTLEY : The Master does not say that.

div.head: PIYUENT OF ASSISTANT-OYEBSBERS BY POUNDAGE.
div.p: PIYUENT OF ASSISTANT-OYEBSBERS BY POUNDAGE.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board directing the Guardians to pay the assistant-everseers the undermentioned rates of poundage, on the amounts respectively collected by them, viz. :—Mr. Jas. Houghton, Bo:d district, 5d.: Mr. Jno. Goff, Widnes district, sd. ; Mr. Henry Liakic. Prescot district, 6d. ; Mr. John Kitchen, Sutton district, SL-d. ; Mr. Henry Twist, Windla district, 7d.; Mr. John -R. Wood, Wootton district, VA.: Mr. David Swallow, Rainford district, ; Mr. John G. Dunn, Eccleston district, Bd.; Mr. Edmund Hinge, Whiston district, sd. The Local G-overnmeut Board also requested that the Guardians should ascertain whether the security of any of the existing assistant overseers would be affected by this change in the Lunde of remuneration. The Clark was directed to inform the Local Government board that the security would not be affected by the • Change.

div.head: LUNATICS IX THE WORIEHOUSE.
div.p: THE LUNATICS IX THE WORIEHOUSE.

A. communication was read from the Local Government Hoard calling the attention of the Guardians to an accom- panying copy of a report which the Board had received from the Commissioners of Lunacy of a visit made to the Workhouse on the 11th ult. by Mr. Philips, one of the visiting commissioners. This report stated that the pe&lons classed as of unsound Blind in the Workhouse had been moved into another block which afforded them better accommodation and provided for proper separation of the sexes. The males were now 30 in number, and the females 42. He found no cause of complaint as to the arrangements of the ward, but hoped the Guardians would enliven them by a few cheap framed pictures. He also called attention to the advisability of having more attendants, and of giving these inmates more exercise.—Theso communications were referred to the Visiting Committee.

div.head: RESIGNATION' OF A MEDICAL OFFICER.
div.p: RESIGNATION' OF A MEDICAL OFFICER.

il_ letter was read from Dr. W. J. I attersall, medical and vaccination officer for the Woolton and Hale districts, tendering his resignation on account of ill-health.—Mr. HARTLEY said Dr. Tattersall had called upon him on the previous day, and said he was going to leave the district, and, indeed, the country. He (Mr. Hartley) told him it would be desirable to resign at once, SO that the Guardians might have another niadical officer appointed to commence his duties with the new half year, that was the en aof September. It was for the Guardians to say whether they would advertise or not. It was only a small appointment.—The CHAIRMAN What is the salary ?—Mr. HARTLEY : £lO for Hale, and £3O for Woolton. Dr. Chisholm had for some time done a good eat of the work, and perhaps some gentleman w.uld give Aotice that he be appointed.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said ho would give a notice of motion that Dr. Chisholm be ap- pointed.—Mr. HARTLEY said it would save the coat of advertising and it was still perfectly competent fer any OtlaOr gentleman to make application. DEMANDING AN APOLOGY.

A letter WAS read from Mr. T. J. Brown, on of the over- goers of the township of Parr, stating that he had seen in a newspaper that Mr. Hall had charged the overseers of Parr with owing £6OO to the Union. He beved to inform Mr. Hall that the overseers of Parr did not owe anything at the time that statement was made. An apology from Mr. Hall through the papers would oblige. (Laughter.) —Mr. JACICSO/4 Said the simplest manner to get out of the _

difficulty would be fer Mr. Hall to say be v'ias wrong and get the papers to publish it. There was a call made on the township of Parr on April oth, 1882. fer £Bl6. Of that there had been paid on April 18th, £272; on May 30th, £272; and on July 4th, £274 to the Union. The call which was made on the 27th July, and due on the 21st August, was paid on the 19b. Now he (Mr. Jackson) bad given Mr. Hall a moment to spare to consider his position ae to whether he was justified in getting up in that assembly and saying that there were certain arrears whereas Parr and Sutton did not owe one farthing. (Hear, hear.)— The CHAIRMAN said it might be Mr. Jackson's kindness which led him to take the part of the township, but he should like to ask him if be was in point of fact a representative of Mr. Brown, of the over- seers or of anybody connected with the matter.—Mr. JACKSON: No, sir, I am not —The CHAIRMAN: No, there- fore I say.—Mr. JACKSON, interrupting, said although he FAS not authorised by the overseers to represent them there, yet he Lad a list of their call, and why Mr. Hall should . . . . _

Bay that township had paid nothing since June, whereas they had paid on July 4th £272, he could not say. If Mr. Hall did not think proper to withdraw that statement, he would charge him with assuming a position that no one had given him authority to do. Mr. Hall assumed there a position he had no right to do. They had a paid Clerk who was able to do hie own work with respect to the business and affairs of the Board, but Mr. Hall was clerk, he was chairman, in fact he was the whole Board. (Laughter.) If they all stopped at home Mr. Hall was in a position to manage all the business that there was to do ; it would le better even if they did not come therm at all—it was

simply a waste of time. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Jackson) only wished the chairman would do his duty—(hear, hear, and laughter)—and call Mr. Hall to order as every Guar- diaia ought to be called to order. But he let Mr. Hall say what he liked, and never interfered with him. (Hear, hear, and laughter.)—Mr. HALL said he was muc% obliged to Mr. Jackson for the compliment he had paid him in saying that he was the whole Board, but with rega,d to his other r emarks he did not intend to reply to them at all—they were r ooted in extremes. (Mr. JAmesow : No, no.) He (Mr. Illall)-mig•ht say that he hid had the matter pointed out to • film, and explained the matter to Mr. Brown himself, but whether the mistake was owing to the returns laid on the table or not he could not Say. He would ask Mr. Hartley whether or not Parr hail been written to about iita arrears. Mr. HARTLEY said it had ,not As it was not in arrears.—Mr. HALL said he might have Mentioned that Parr was in arrears, if he had it was a mis- take. He did not think, however, that after his explana- tion to Mr. Brown that there was any necessity for that Letter, and he did not see why he should make an apology after that explanation.—Mr. HARTLEY said that if there tad been any clerical error it had not arisen in his office. At the last meeting he had said that the township of Parr was not in arrears, neither was Rainford, nor Sutton, nor Much Woolton ; all the other townships in the Union were in arrears, but these four had paid all the requirements of the Guardians.—Mr. DOBELL : Were these four referred to as being in arrears P—Mr. HARTLEY said they were not in the sheet.—Mr. DOBELL : But in committee.—Mr. HART- LEY said he sin:ply followed his usual course in preparing the returns. That report had been picked up and read, but te had no knowledge that Parr or Sutton was celled out.— Mr. HALL: It was agreed that they be written to.—The CHAIRMAN: I know it was.—Mr. JACKSON said, with regard to the statement which Mr. Hall had made to them, that if he (Mr. Jackson) had made any wrong remarks, he only begged Mr. Hall's pardon. He was not so stiff-necked but that when he had dene wrong he could make acknowledg- ment for it. But Mr. Hall had distinctly told him that morning that he had never mentioned Parr, and he (Mr. Jackson) would leave it to the Guardians to say whether he Lad or had not. He would not charge Mr. Hell as Mr. Hall had charged him, but he would charge him with being un- truthful. (Cries of "No, no.") He would; Mr. Hall had told him that morning that he never mentioned Parr,—Mr. CALL: I said I might have macie a mistake; I did not say I tad not done so.—The CHAIRMAN said at the very time the statement was made he had been rather afraid that Mr. Hall was making a mistake. But there was another town- ship to which he had before impressed them a letter ought to be written, and that was Eccleston. He hid named it re- ! peatedly that day fortnight, but they had let it drop, he could not say why. It was in arrears to a very big figure— £2,7oo.—Mr. HALL said what he complained of was that after he had axplained the matter to Mr. Brown, that letter Lad been written.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said he wished ta pronose that an end be put to the discussion; they had had quite enough of it. They were all liable to make mis- takes, and he proposed that they proceed to bnsiness.—Mr. HARTLEY then submitted an account of arrears, from which the Chairman read the following: Bold, £228; Cronton, £340; Ditton, £092; Eceleston, £2,747; Hale, £820; Halewood. £1,050; Huyton-with-Roby, £2,333; and Wid- nes, £6707 ; although, the Chairman added, the latter township had been sticking to work lately and paid a large amount.—Mr. NEWSOME said he believed they meant to beep it up.—The CHAIRMAN: There is not another figure equal to it—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS: May I ask, sir, as time is getting on, it this business is on the agenda of busi- rcess re —Mr. HALT-, referring to Huyton, said the overseers -there had already collected over £2,000, and refused to pay it over to the Union because Widnes was so much in arrears. He did net think it fair that other townships should pay their calls while Huyton kept that £2 000. The Board should thtehmeY could _tr. not let the yetoanctidoinc,tabteecatuose certainly take e sHome having again remo2strated that they ought to proceed to the business of the raeeting, Mr. HARTLEY read a letter from the r T ...uvton overseers stat- ing that they did not think it right or legal that they I should pay their call while other townships remained in arrears. Mr. Hartley said he had written in answer to that letter to the effect that because other townships were in arrears it was no excuse for the Huyton overseers refusing ta meet the demands of the Guardians.--Mr. PALL moved that action be taken against them.—For some maments no one offered to second this proposal, but ultimately Mr. Jackson seconded it.—Mr. DAVIS said other townships had got money in hand but were not honest enough to acknow- ledge it.—Mr. SWIFT: Why take action against Huyton, and not against other townships P—Mr. Penn moved as an amendment that no action be taken against Huyton unless It was also taken against other townships. Mr. HALL laid he was willing to withdraw his motion, -id second Mr. Paris's proposal. The CHAIR-

MAlt : You move, Mr. Paris, that action be taken against the whole of the townships in arrears.—Mr. Peso : imove Huyton shall be singled out.—Mr. CHAMBERS did not think there was any necessity for an amendment, as ha did not believe•that one Guardian would up his hand in favour of Mr. Hall's motion.—lt was agreed, on the suggestion of the Clerk, that the natter should be left over till next meet- ing, when a new estimate would be hid before the Board.

ANNUAL lIILECTION OF GUAUDIANS. An order was read from the Local Governmeut Board directing that a poll be taken with a view to ascertaining the opinion of the owners and ratepayers of the Prescot Union upon the question of a triennial election of Gusrdians.--It was agreed that the Clerk should be remunerated for his trouble in connection with this poll at the same rate as an ordinary election of Guardians.—The Rev. FATHER FINEGAN hoped that proper care would be taken to let every person entitled to vote have a paper, as he knew from his own ex- perience that bad not always be done at Widnes.—The CLERK explained that he was regulated by the rate books, and he was afraid those of Widnes were not a credit to that place, but he would promise that every care should be taken.
This concluded the business of public interest.

div.head: CHURCH BUILDING AT WIDNES.
div.p: CHURCH BUILDING AT WIDNES.

It will be difficult for the majority of the present denizens of Widnes, surrounded as they are with the ceaseless activity of its industries, to imagine the time, 50 years when the centre of the chemical trade was a quiet, peaceful, agricultural village; when upon the now grey and un- inviting soil of the old marsh waved the golden grain; when orchards, rich with fruit, flourished where now exist barren and ugly wastes; when trees put forth their foliage on the banks of the river ; and when, in place of nauseous and irritating smells, the perfume of the blossom and the rose filled the air. Truly Arcadian compared with it present aspect. The inhabitants in those days, it is safe to presume, were • a plodding, contented people, gifted, perhaps, with a little recxlessness and desire for change, but pursuing the even tenor of their way uninterruptedly. And the labour of six days per- formed, the farmers and villagers, accompanied, it may be, with their wives, would repair to at least one service on the seventh, to hear the parson preach at the old Parish Church, for country folks generally attend the church. Whines was then included in the parish of Farnworth, but before the stage coach and the spring waggon, as a means of travelling, was superseded by the locomotive, a walk of two miles to church was not much thought of. Now, we are afraid, the distance of the church from the home has a little influence on a man's religion, or on his attendance at worship, and the nearest place has the benefit of his presence because it saves him a five minutes' walk. But Widnes, as we have said, was only a small place, and the ancient Parish Church of Farnworth afforded sufficient ac- commodation for the church - going portion of ' its 1,800 or 2,000 inhabitants. The population of the whole parish did not probably exceed 4,000, but it was scattered over a wide area. The district of which the pretty village of Farnworth was the centre, included, besides Wid- nes, Crouton, Bold, Ditton, and Sankey. The work entailed in attending to the spiritual needs era community so scattered must have been considerable, and the intellect of the clergyman, who undertook its oversight, would require to be conj•ined with a strong constitution and a healthy physical frame. Changes took place. Sankey acquired a , church of its own, and subsequently Ditton also. But events were occurring which were to transform the whole district, physically and socially, the obscure village was to become in a remarkably short space of time, a ,thriving and important town. Chemical works were established at Widnes, and with their establishment came an increase of population and an increase of wealth. ) More church ac,commxiation was required, and Farnworth parish had to again undergo partition, when in 18513 the ' present Widnes Parish Church was erected. The trade of the place extended; wages were high; profits enormous; all was prosperity. The manner in which the village developed was almost phenomenal. In 20 years the popula- tion had increased fouriold, and the church accommodation , years before that period had become greatly inadequate. It was not, however, until 1874 that an organised effort was made to remedy this. Donations amounting to £6,000 were promised, and it was recommended in public meeting that two churches should be erected, one at Halton View and one at Anderson's Corner. The recommendation was adopted, and the constructioa of the Church of St. Ambrose was commenced. But,the foun- dation laid, the plan for the superstructure was altered to give more accommodation, the cost of the erection being proportionately increased. The edifice is now erected and open. For the site of the church at Anderson's corner there had been 1,000 yards promised by the owner of the Leigh estate, while the committee in charge ef the scheme had guaranteed £3,000. When the Rev. J. Wright-Williams ' took the oversight of the parish, he pushed forward the extension, and about twelve montns ago, Mrs. Leigh made the promised gift of 1,000 yards of land into an acre, but not until a week or two age was it transferred to the Ecclesiastical Commissioners. The Vicar, in a state- ment published a few days ago, says it has been decided to proceed with the erection at once to the extent of the £3,000 promised; and Mr. H. Shelmerdine, of Liverpool, the architect, is engaged upon the necessary specifications. The total cost of the church is estimated at between £7,000 and £B,OOO. The sum promised, therefore, will only suffice -to build the nave and aisles, and to complete the edifice a large amount will have to be raised. True, the trade of the town is by no means flourishing, but it would be in the highest degree unwise to build only part of the church. "A thing half done is better not done at all," is a common but a true maxim, and we feel convinced that the church people of Widnes, by a determined and combined effort, will be.enabled to carry out the work in its entirety. The com- mittee entrusted with the execution of the scheme is com- posed of the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar of Widnes; the Rev. G. Bond, vicar of Farnworth; Messrs. I'. Sutton Tin2tnis, H. W. Deacon, John Brock, H. Brunner, G. Pilkington, J. Matthews, T. Balmer, L. Kilcross, G. Roger- son, J. T. Allen, Jas. Hunt, and Majlr Cros3.

div.head: FATAL BOATING ACCIDENT ON THE MERSEY. INQUEST AT WIDNES.
div.p: FATAL BOATING ACCIDENT ON THE MERSEY. INQUEST AT WIDNES.

A boating accident by which a labourer named Charles Hendra, living at 5. Viaduct-street, Widnes, lost his life, took place on the Mersey, opposite Runcorn Pier, on Sun- day evening. The facts of the occurrence appear to be these. About three o'clock the deceased, who had been a sailor for over 20 years, and a man named Battersby, en- gaged a small boat at the West Bank promenade, and rowed to Weston Point, where they arrived without mishap. The police report stated the deceased was drunk, but his companion, when examined by the coroner, said he believed he was sober when he left Widnes, but admitted that they each had a pint of beer at Wester. Point, and had a bottle of rum in the boat. The conduct of the deceased, however, was somewhat boisterous, and on the return journey would "have his own way." When near Runcorn Pier he, in some way which remains unexplained, fell out of the boat, but with the aid of his companion, regained his seat, with merely a wetting. Shortly afterwards leaning over the boat to seize a piece of rope he again fell into the river, almost upsetting the boat, and so strong was the tide running at the time that he was 30 yards away from the boat when he rose to :the surface. No help could be afforded him, and ha perished. His body was recovered on Monday morning, and was badly marked about the face and neck, probably caused whilst lying in the river. The body was conveyed to the home of the deceased at Widnes.

Mr. T. W. Barker, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body at the Bridge Inn, Widnes, on Wednesday. Elizabeth Hendra, the widow of the deceased, said her late husband had been a sailor for 24 years, and 10 years in the Royal Navy Reserve, but was not fond of the sea. He did not like sailing small boats, and she never knew him to cross the river in one before this occurrence. He was, how- ever, well acquainted with their management. On Sunday he had some beer for his dinner, but was sober when he left home. Henry Battersby, foreman and engineman, in the employ of the Widnes Metal Company, said he met the deceased, whom he knew very well, about three o'clock on Sunday afternoon, and he (witness) offered to pay for the hire of a boat if the deceased would go for a- sail. The deceased assented, and, in a boat they hired from a man named Hulse, they started for Weston Point, where they arrived in safety. The tide was flowing at the time. At the village they had each a pint of beer. He believed the deceased was sober when they left Widnes. On the return journey, and when the boat was opposite Duke's Dock, Runcorn, the deceased went overboard, but with the help of the witness, he safely regained the boat, and went on rowing as he had done pre- viously. Whilst this episode was occurring the boat had drifted a considerabledistance down the river; but for a second time they got opposit9 Duke's Dock, and he (witness) ex- pressed a desire to go no further. Deceased, however, stated his determination to go on, but he nevertheless leaned over the bow of the boat to secure a piece of rope to tie the boat up, when he over-balanced himself and fell into the water. Witness tried to help him to get in the boat but could not, and he shouted for help • but althoup,h there was someone at the pier head they c aid do nothing, the current was so strong, and the deceased was whirled away. He (witness) did not even touch him, but saw him when he rose to the surface 30 yards distant from the boat.

P.S. Robinson, who was present, stated in reply to the coroner, that he had stated in the po:ice report that deceased was very drank, because he understood so from Battersby, who also told him they had a bottle of rum in the boat. Battersby was then put through a cross-examination by the coroner, who felt called upon to caution him to tell the whole truth, in consequence of the manner in which he answered the questions. He admitted they had a pop bottle filled with rum at Weston, and from which the deceased had a drink before entering the boat. He denied telling the police that deceased was drunk, but said he told them deceased had some drink.

P.S. Robinson : Didn't you say he would have his own way with the boat? Yes. The Foreman: There is no doubt about that. Witness said he could not say deceased was quite sober, but be was capable of managing the boat. A Juror: How far from Duke's Dock wefo you when the accident occurred? About three yards. Do you think he could have knocked against the wall? Re is very hardly marked.—No ; he fell on the other side. In reply to other questions, witness said if ho had attempted to go to the side of the boat to• aid deceased, it

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 26, lBB2.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 26, lBB2.

would have capsized. In falling the deceased caught hold of the rowlocks of the boat. Thomas Ogden, of Church-street, Widnes, said he had , known deceased for seven years. He was not a "drinking man," although he took a drink sometimes. He (witness) foul* the body near Weston Point, between nine and half- past on Monday morning. He put it in a boat, and conveyed it to Widnes. Deceased was quite capable of managing the boat. Wm. Ham said he lived at Westbn Point, and on the day in question, about three o'clock, he saw the deceased in a beat. He appeared te be able to manage the boat. I Battersby was in the stern, steering. The boat went % along shore on the Cheshire side, and he told them to be careful, as it was an ebb tide. The deceased might have had drink for anything he knew. The Coroner said this was the whole of the evidence, and having summed up, the jury returned a verdict of " Acci- I dental death."

div.head: PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, ROCK SAVAGE.
div.p: PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, ROCK SAVAGE.

OPENING SERVICES. The new chapel and school built by the Primitive Metho- dist connexion, at Rock Savage, a description of which has previously appeared in The Examiner, were opened on Mon- day afternoon. There was a good congregation at the open- ing ceremony, which consisted simply of a sermon preached by Mr. John Jones, of Chester, from Phillipians I. 21 v., 1 "For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.' Afterwards la large number of persons sat down to tea, over which the following ladies presided :—Mesdames Basnett, Coventry t and Hoxworth, and Miss Hoxworth. After tea a pubic meet- ing was held in the chapel. Mr. Joseph Stokes presided, and there were present—the Revs. J. Pickwell and D. Scho- I field, Messrs. M. Stringfellow, W. F. Robinson, H. Rowland, 1, W. Booth, J. Stubbs, Samuel Stubbs, James Sayles, W. Row- land, &c.—Mr. T. SCRINGFELOW read a report which i -sketched the progress of the Movement for the erection of a 1 new chapel, and observed that they had found many friends ' who had helped them in their work. Nowhere, with one exception, had their appeals been refused, and they were 1 grateful for the help given them. There had been a little opposition certainly, but they had surmounted the obstacles and taken fresh courage. and now, as they contemplated ! their success, they were filled with pride and wonder. Mr. ; Stringfellow, in the name of the trustees, ,tendered thanks to all who had assisted them. The following work had been !given them gratis :—Mr. J. Stokes, carting bricks, £3; Mr. Baker, carting bricks, £4; Mr. Jos. Ashley, carting, £5; Mr. 1 Wm. Stanway, carting, 65.; Mr. Isaac Broadhurst, carting, : 35.; Mr. Win. Hoxworth, painting, glazing, and varnishing ' interior, £2 Ios. ; •Mr. John and Charles Johnson, dressing memorial stones, £1; Mr. John Wilson, preparing plans, £1; Messrs. Stubbs and Son, putting roof on, 155.; Mr. J. D. Jones, plastering, £l. Mr. Stringfellow further stated that Mr. Jos. Williams had preselited them with a clock value ; £3, and the Runcorn Good Templars had also presented them with a bible cushion and stand. Other work had been given free of cost, and to all who had treated them so very liberally they returned their sincerest thanks. (Ap- plause.)—The CHAIRMAN congratulated the meeting upon the very satisfactory report and said he thought it was ex- ceedingly satisfactory that they had only about £25 .or £3O to clear off. It was only a short time ago that they were thinking of the chapel. Now it was erected, . and he hoped prosperity would attend it. (Applause.)— Mr. HENRY itowLasm said he was very thankful they had , at last succeeded in erecting a chapel and school at Rock Savage. Only a few years ago he never thought they would have a place like that in which they might meet for the worship of the Almighty. Their success had far exceeded his anticipations. It was true that he and Mr. Stringfellow had a few years ago planned the aff sir in their minds, but the mere thought was not sufficient. The prac- tical effort was needed, and when opportunity offered, the effcrt was made, and that day, as the result, they were met ; to celebrate the opening of a new chapel, of which Rock ;Savage was proud. He was surprised at the many friends they had now. At one time he had an idea that no one felt any respect for Rock Savage, but in arriving at their present position- they had met with many friends, who had not been , !slow to assist them. He expressed his conviction that they , would soon be able to say that they were out of debt and on the path of prosperity. (Applause.)—The Rev. J. PICSWELL, who was received with applause, said they had built a very beautiful and suitable chapel, and he trusted it would be made the birthplace of many souls. He exclaimed with the apostle "We preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord." He trusted their hopes of success were well founded. They were grateful for their material success, but they ; wanted the spiritual success of the Lord. They were anxious 1 for the welfare of the young in their midst, and with earnest land prayerful effort he believed they were sure to succeed. (Applause.) The Rev. D. Schofield and Mr. W. F. Robin- son also addressed the meeting. The ptoceeds of the day amounted to £5 25. lid.

div.head: LICENSING PROSECUTIONS AT WIDNES.
div.p: LICENSING PROSECUTIONS AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. W. N. Heald and Mr. John Brock, Wm. Twist, landlord of the Central Inn. Farnworth, was summoned for keeping his house open daring prohibited hours; and Geo. H. Yates, Chas. H. Yates (one of whom is a veterinary surgeon), and Peter Morriss, a boy were summoned for being on the premises.—P.C. Almond stated that at five minutes to ten on the night of Sunday the 13th inst., he was in Derby-street, in company with P.C. Douse. The door of the Central, kept by the defendant Twist, was then closed. He saw a light shining inside and went under the window. From this position he heard the sound of voices inside, and be waited there until a quarter past ten. At that time he went to the back entrance of the house, leaving P.C. Douse to guard the front entrance. The door at the back was closed and he knocked, and some female asked. "Who is there P" The officer replied, "A policeman. Open the door." The door was then opened by the landlady, who, in reply to his inefairy, told him the landlord was in the parlour, with two other gentlemen. He went into the parlour, where were all the defendants, and on the table two glasses three parts full of beer, and a bottle of ginger beer near Morris.. He told the landlord he should report him for , supplying liquor during prohibited hours, when he admitted he had filled the other defendants beer. Afterwards the landlord and he (witness) went to admit P.C. Douse, and on returning to the parlour the beer was not in the glasses. Be asked where the beer had gone, and Yates said they had hid no beer. On hearing this statement, the landlord said "I filled them the beer but they did not pay for it." To corroborate this assertion, he fetched a puppy dog from the kitchen, which he said they had just brought from Yates's house, and be had given them the beer. George Yates then said, "We have not been here a ' jiff ; we left Smith's beerhouse at 10 o'clock."—P.C. Douse corroborated.—For the defence Mr. Husband stated that during the afternoon of the day in question two persons called at Twist's house, and represented themselves as travellers. He was in consequence obliged to admit them. Whilst there one of them took in his hands a puppy greyhound dog which the landlord was rearing for Captain Hornby. He dropped it and broke its leg. He sent to Mr. Yates, veterinary sur- geen, and at half-past nine at night the boy Morris fetched it. About twelve minutes past ten the defendants brought the dog, and the landlord asked them in and gave them a glass of beer.—The defendant Twist and Mrs. Twist, who stated when she admitted the defendants, about twelve minutes past twelve, she did not see anybody under the window.- The beer was not paid for.—George H. Yates said he was a veterinary surgeon and related the circumatances of the case. He emphatically stated the beer was given him by the landlord, and he asserted he told the officers he had had a glass of been—Other evidence was given. and P.C. Almond was re-called. He stated tbat no person could go in or come out of the housa without him seeing them be- tween five minutes to ten to a quarter-past.—After a little consideration the Bench fined Ttrist and 17s. costs, and the:other defendants 5.5. and costs each. Andrew Quinn as charged with selling liquor without a license on the 16th Augnst.—Mr. Superintendent Barker said the defendant, on the sth July, obtained permission to sell beer at a beerhouse known by the sign of the Unicorn Vaults. This permission would cease on the 15th August,l when he ought to have applied for the license to be trans- ferred to him, for if he sold beyond that day without so doing he would be breaking the law. On the transfer day the defendant's name was called several times in the court, and also in the streets but he did not appear. The following day P.C. Almond, in plain clothes, went to the house, when he saw the defendant serving persons with beer, and also bad a glass himself. In the evening P.S. Strickland visited the house, and informed defendant as he was selling liquor without license he should report him. The sergeant said the defendant seemed very much surprised—Mr. Husband, who appeared for the defendant, showed the Bench that it was entirely a mistake, and not with any wilful intention to break the law, that the defendant had not applied for the transfer.—The Bench took this view of the case, which was dismissed.—Mr. Husband asked the Bench to extend the present license, or grant a new one.—The Chairman said the Bench could not de so; it was a question whether the de- fendant was fit to hold a license, when he coold not under- stand so simple a matter as that of applying for a transfer. It was a very stupid mistake the defendant bad made.

div.head: SUPPOSED RUSE OF THE ENEMY:
div.p: A SUPPOSED RUSE OF THE ENEMY:

A telegram from Alexandria at 11-15 a.m. yesterday, says :—The enemy were seen yesterday evening removing tents from their position at Katt. Dower. This morning a number of tents, variously estimated at from 500 to 1,000, were being pitched in front of the enemy's position, but this is believed to be only a ruse to mask the withdrawal of Arabi. It is now confirmed that the enemy are making entrench- ments a few miles east of Cairo.

div.head: MILITARY CONVENTION.
div.p: THE MILITARY CONVENTION.

The military orders originally issued not to allow the dis- embarkation of Turkish troops without the previous signa- ture of the Araglo-Turkish military convention, and the issue of the Sultan's proclamation upholding the Khedive's authority and proclaiming Arabi a rebel, still remain an- cancelled.

div.head: ARABI SOLD.
div.p: ARABI SOLD.

A Port Said telegram of Th arsday'a date says :—Mr. Clark, superintendent of the Egyptian telegraphs, succeeded on Sunday in pta7ing a very clever trick upon Arabi. He managed to work the wire to Zagazig in such a manner that the enemy sent down three trains to Ismailia, all of which fell into oac hands, and are proving a really invaluable present. A VISIT OF INSPECTION.

Telegraphing from Ismailia at six o'clock yesterday morning, the Central News correspondent gays : Six more fugitives were taken last evening, all c 'trying rifles. Sir G. WolselLy went again yesterday to Serapeum on a visit of inspection. He returned last night, having found all in good order. The railway from the wharf here to Nefiche is making good progress.

Earl Granville arrived at Canton House Terrace last evening from Walmer Castle. Colonel E. C. -wdon, R. E.. has been appointed President of the Royal Engineer Commi.tee at the War Office. Cetwayo drove out yesterday morning with Mr. Shepston, and visited Mr. Whitley's huge series of shops in West- bourne Grove.
The Erie Railway elevator at Buffalo has been burn,d. Four men perished. The loss is estimated at 250,000 dollars.
Mr. Joynes, of Eton College, who was recently arrested with Mr. Henry George, was again arrested near Limerick on Thursday while watching an eviction. He was speedily released.

Mr. Gladstone, who returned to London yesterday after- noon from Lore} Virolerton's seat in Dorset, was shortly afterwards waited upon by Mr. Childers and Lord North- bro3k, who remained for some time in consultation. A telegram from Warsaw says that frightful outrages have again been committed upon the Jews at Sulwalkee, in Russian Poland, including the usual catalogue of violation, murder, and destruction of property by fire. The officials are charged with looking on unconcernedly while these barbarities were in progress. The body of a man of about 50 years of age was found floating in the river Ribble, at Ribchester, on Thursday afternoon. It is supposed to be that of a tramp who .was seen to take shelter from the rain at the bridge, and it is assumed that he there slipped into the river. A resolution was passed at a meeting of the Balloon society last night, congratulating Mr. Leigh Smith on his escape from the Arctic Regions, and expressing satisfaction at the fact that the Balloon Society was the first to urge upon the Government the necessity for the relief expedi- tion.

The Queen has officially approved the appointments of Lieutenant Col. Webber, RE., as Assistant and Quarter Master General on the Head Quarter Staff in Egypt; Col. E. E. Growan, to command a reserve depot in the Mediter- ranean ; and Commander Sir Baldwin Walker has been appointed to the Northumberland, vice-Commander Kane. The latter officer was slightly wounded last Sunday at Ismailia.

A subscription list was, some time since, opened at Oldham towards the foundation and endowment of a college of music. OR Thursday night the Corporation General Purposes Committee, on the motion of the Mayor, resolved to grant the use of the Town Hall for a high class- concert in aid of the movement. The Mayor stated, that such concerts were being held in 60 of the largest towns of the kingdom. At Birmingham, yesterday, Joseph Osborne, carpenter, nearly 60 years of age, was remanded upon a charge of dangerously assaulting his wife, who is not expected to recover. The injured woman, whose depositions have been taken, states that during a quarrel a fortnight since she threw a jug at her husband's feet to frighten him. He returned it at her held with such violence as to inflict a , most serious wound.

div.head: FEVER EPIDEMIC AT ACCRINGTON.
div.p: THE FEVER EPIDEMIC AT ACCRINGTON.

There have been five deaths registered from scarlet fever during the week at Accrington. The Corporation have had an analysis of the water made by Mr. Barnes, analytical. chemist, Acz.brington, who states that it po:sesses no delete- rious properties to which might be attributed any serious epidemic diseases.

div.head: CATHOLIC CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATEON.
div.p: THE CATHOLIC CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATEON.

The Marquis of Bute has signified his approval of the new Catholic Conservative Association in a practical way by- a handsome subscription to its funds. Mr. Bellingham, M.P., is connected with it. The Irish policy of the association. ia described as no separation from England, but an Irish Paz-, 'lament subject to the Imperial Parliament. Communica, tions are going on urging the establishment of branches. in Lancashire. At Oldhana the local branch of the Lnncl League has been industriously at work in registration, and has sent in a number of claims.

div.head: LENIENT PUNISHMENT FOR WIFE ASFAULTS.
div.p: LENIENT PUNISHMENT FOR WIFE ASFAULTS.

_ At Accrington yesterday morning, William Ledgwick, labourer, was charged with brutally assaultiag his wife. Prisoner, before going to his work last Tuesday, struak his wife on the head and thigh with his bait. At igeakfast time, heoatoe gthe could not provide a bezzrbag„, he grtlek her
on the face; and at noon, because she objected to his pledg- ing the family Bible, he kicked her. Prisoner was fined 20s. and costs; in default one month.

DEATH OF MR. HUTCHINSON, LATE M.P. FOR HALIFAX. Yesterday morning, at a few minutes after 12, Mr. J. D. Hutchinson, late borough member for Halifax, and who had just accepted the Chiltern Hundreds, died in London. He was 60 years of age last month, and was elected as member for Halifax in February, 1877, and continued to hold that position until the last few weeks. He had also held the office of President of the Press Association and of the Provincial Newspaper Society, a handsome testimonial hav- ing been presented to him by the latter society for intro- cinch-fig and conducting through the House of Commons the Newspaper Libel Bill. MYSTERIOUS AFFA/R AT LEICESTER. -•

The police yesterday morning made a step in elucidating the mysterious finding of a blood-stained hammer on the canal bank at Leicester. It has been identified as the pro- perty of a man named Gurney, who is new in the custody of the police. Gurney, who has been an inmate of a lunatic asylum, has been drinking lately, and, in a very excited condition, left home early on Thursday morning. The coal hammer was missed with Gurney in the morning, and was identified by his wife as their property. Gurney's clothes were saturated with blood, and they were taken away for a minute examination. There is great excitement in the dis- trict. The canal was being carefully dragged yesterday morning at the place where the pool of blood and the traces of a struggle were found. Gurney is an exceedingly power- ful man, and is being carefully watched. EMIGRATION OF IRISH HARVEST-MEN. _

The harvest in Cheshire will be seriously delayed by the absence of Irish labourers. For years past farmers have usually been assisted over each harvest by Irish harvest- men. This year, however, scarcely any Irish labourers bare arrived. The few labourers in Cheshire state that the quality of the harvest in Ireland and the great increase of emigration will almost ,put a stop to the annual visits of Irish harvestmen.

div.head: SHOCKING CRUELTY TO A FAMILY.
div.p: SHOCKING CRUELTY TO A FAMILY.

At Accrington, yesterday, Patrick Weanney, labourer, was committed for two months, with hard labour, for neg- lecting to maintain his wife and four young children. Pri- soner deserted them in May. When at home he was earning 245. per week, but only gave his wife about 43. and drank the rest. He often attempted to kill her. The family were found almost starved to death, and were even eating their clothes.
A REVOLTING FUNERAL PROCESSION IN
DUBLIN.

_ Yesterday morning, a revolting scene mu witnessed in Dublin. A funeral procession passing through the principal streets was made up of jaunting cars following the hearse. On these were a number of people many of whom were in a complete state of intoxication. Two women were so violent that they were held by their friends, and another lay fast asleep. They had evidently just left the wake to attend the funeral.
MR. GIADSTONE AND THE COUNTY FRANCHISE.

Replying to a resolution passed tr.r the Buckingham Liberal Association, asking the Government to introduce early an extension of the county franchise, Mr. Gladstone said that her Majesty's Government confidently hope the present Parliament will deal with the question.

THE QUESTION OF "OFF" LICENSES. Yesterday morning, at the Burnley Borough Licensing Sessions, memorials against the granting of additional off licenses to grocers' shops, &c., were presented by the British Temperance League, the Blue Ribbon Union, and others. One petition contained upwards of ,6,000 names. The bench said they would endeavour to give a full consideration to the prayer of the different petitions. There was much ex- citement in court.

div.head: ROBBERY OF £15,000.
div.p: ROBBERY OF £15,000.

The Press Association understands that on Tuesday a serious robbery was committed under remarsable circum- stances. Mr. Savitch, an Odessa merchant, came to London recently to receive upwards of £15,000, left by his brother. Not knowing the English language, be engaged as interpre- ter John Novitzky, a Russian. On Tuesday Mr. Savitch re:eived this money from, the Bank of England, afterwards accompanying Novitzky to his lodgings where, as Savitch was about leaving after supper, Novitzky seized Savitch by the thnat, nearly strangling him, and then &camped, with a hag of money, getting clear away. A rewatd of £IOO is offered for the arrest of Novitzky, whose description is given. MR. GRAY'S IMPRISONMENT.

The Lord-Lieutenant received at Dublin Castle yesterday afternoon the Lord Mayor and members of the Dublin Cor- poration, who presented a memoria which spoke of the arbi- trary and excessive sentence passed, on Mr. Gray, M P., and asked that a searching inquiry be instituted on oath into the charges made as to the empanelling of jurors and the alleged misconduct of the jury in the trial of the condemned man Hynes. Lady Florence Dixie, writing to. Mr. Gray, expresses deep abhorrence of the arbitrary and unfair sentence passed upon him, and applauds him for Making public a case of extreme gravity and disgraceful scandal. She is desirous that criminals should be brought to Justice, but a jury's finding should not be from men barely recovered from a night's- orgie. A pamphlet containing an account of the whole proceedings will at once be forwarded to all the Ministers.

A rirkw EXPLOSIVE.—A consular report from Sweden, just issued by the Foreign Office, gives a description of a new explosive called sebastine, which, it is said, has corn- peted ntost favourably with dynamite. S,bastine appears ta be an explosive based upon nitro-glycerine, but safer to hanile than the ordinary dynamite, while more powerful in effect and cheaper to purchase... The greater safety of seb as- tine depends on two circumstances—first, that the explosive oil is more completely absorbed and bound by a specially prepared kind of charcoal and other ingredients ; and secondly, that in ordinary cases it requires no percussion cap to explode. As to use in mining, it is reported that the new sebastine is exploded simply by the fuse, providing thp bore hole is properly secured by a stronger wadding as in an ordinary charge of blasting powder. According to otli- cial statements, there has not been one single instance of accident happening when using the hew sebastine. The Swedish Government having ordered trials of sebastine against dynamite, it is said to have been proved that sob at- tine was far superior in effect and about equal in forca to Eaglish gun-cotton when used in torpedoes. The Consul at Gothenburg adds :—" As an explosive of great power, and offering superior security, particularly for mining and similar purposes, I would raommend the new sebastine, or, more properly. its improved form, yirite, to the notice of her Majesty's Government."

TO BE SOLD BY PUBLIC AUCTION, in Two Lots, by MESSRS. HUGH C. CLARKE & SON, At their AUCVION MART, ROSEMA.Rv-sr , BELFAST. On FRIDAY, the 29th day of SEPTEMBER, 1882, At Twelve o'clock ncon. LOT I.—That Valuab`e Mine, called ard known as the MAIDENMOUNT SALT MINE, being the Salt, Salt Rock, and Springs of Brine lying under and within the limits of a parcel of land containing lea.. 3r. 37p. statute measure, or thereabouts, known as the Maldenmount Salt Mine, situate in the Middle Division of the county of the town of Carrickfergus and county of Antrim, held -under lease dated the Ist day of March, 1872, for 31 years from the Ist November. 18fA, and by endorsement on said lease, dated the 3rd day of May. 1872, for the further term of 10 years, computed from the expiration of the said lease. LOT 2.—The AIAIDEIsi MOUNT SALT WORKS, situate at Wilson's Quay, Carr'ckfcrgus, held under lease dated Bth May, 1872, for 26 years from Ist November, 1859. Private proposals for purchase of either or both lots will be received by the solicitor having carriage of the sale up to the 20th day of September. 1882, and, if approved of, will oe sub- mitted to the Judge evithout further notice. Dated this 3rd day of August, 1882. JOHN MARrLEY. for Examiner. • DESCRIPTIVE PARTICULARS. Lot I.—The Maidenmount Salt Mine. This Mine is situate within a short distance of Carrickfergus, and has been working for about 10 years. There are Iwo shatts, adjoining each other, for the purpose of working the Hine ; the depth of each shalt is about 90J feet, and the workings extend over a large area, the rock running north. There are about 40 men and 18 horses in constant work. The annual output of rock is about 15,000 tons ; about one-third of this goes to the Carrickfergus Works (Lot 2 described below) for manufacture. The working plant consists of one horizontal engine, 30 H-P,, winding belts and pulleys; one grinding 'mill and engine. 10 ti-P.. grinding 50 to 60 tons per day; weigh- bridge, trucks, buckets, and the usual quarrying tools. The Shafts are 4 feet square, timbered with pine, and guides for ropes. The Buildings on the premises constst of an Engine House, the foundation of which is of stone and brick, the structure wood, and a felt roof, rock loft being a wooden shed.; offices, powder store, engine driver or caretaker's house (wood) and a small stable. Lot 2.—Carrickfergus S tit Works. These Works are situate In the Town. adjoining the Harbour; they consist of the usual boiling and melting pans, small engine 8 H-P., pumping gear, Ice. • rto. 'The premises being all in Mr. Dalvray's possession, immediate possession can be obtained. The sale of Lot 2 is subject to the Landlord's approval. The terms upon which tite Landlord's consent tea sale has been given are. t' e approval by him of the Purchaser, and that the premises shall be used solely for the purposes of the busi- ne's heretofore carried on therein. The deed of Conveyance will not pass to the Purchaser any trade fixtures on the premises, but such trade 'fixtures may be taken by the Purchaser, at a valuation ta be agreed upon between him and the Official and Trade Assignees of the Court of Bankruptcy in the matter of Marriott Robert Dalway. an 'Arranging Debtor, who are willing to sell the same. Lot I. These premises, including the machinery, trade fixtures. Ac. (which will not, however, pass to the Purchaser) -as a going concern, has been recently valued by Mr. Edward Allworthy, valuator, at £6,250. Lot 2 has been also recently valued by same gentleman at 4760. PARTICULARS APPLICABLE TO BOTH LOTS. , The demand for Salt Rock and Salt has increased of late , years. The Commissiovers of the town of Carrickfergus have , lately borrowed 214.000 Ibm the Board of Works. for the pur- ' pose of making a new Pier and Harbour at that town. , These works are expected to provide a depth of 18 feet of water at high tide, and of 10 feet at low water thus affording aecommodation for vessels of large tonnage. The Works are under contract to be finished on Ist May, 1883. A Bill is being promoted in the present -Session of Rutile- •anent for the purpose of connecting the above-mentioned new Pier -and Harbour with the Belast and Northern Counties Railway. It Is expected that the above scheme will largely Increase the coal carrying trade to Carrickfergus, and from thence to inland Districts, and thereby the export of Salt from • that port, vessels dischirgiug emit being likely to reload with Salt or Salt Rock. The Salt export is expected also to be largely Increased dire,Aly the improved Harbour accommodation, •enabling Teasels of a larger tonnage than heretofore (which , previously took In ballast at Belfast) to take in ballast or cargo of Sett Rock (ir Salt at the Carrickfergus Harbour. For Rentals, Maps, and further particulars apply at the Registrar's Office of tie said Land Judges, Chancery Disisi n, Inns quay, Dublin. OMAR o. LATEST NEWS. THE WAR IN EGYPT. SHARP ENGAGEMENT WITH THE ENEMY. GALLANT CONDUCT OF BRITISH TROOPS. The Central News Agency has received the following from the War Office :—Telegram from Sir Garnet Wolseley, to the Secretary of State for War, dated Ismailia, August 24; Port Said, 25th August noon ; received August 25, 5-30 p.m. The water in the Fresh Water Canal has been falling for the last three days, and although I had Serapeum nine miles south of this, if I felt it necessary to push for- ward and occupy that part of the canal which I had been warned was the point on it where we could be most seriously damaged, about seven miles west of Ismailia, I advanced this morning before daybreak with the Household Cavalry, two guns, Horse Artillery, with about 30 Mounted Infantry, and about 1,000 Infantry of York and Lancaster, and Royal Marines. After some skirmishing, took possession of the dam the enemy had constructed across the Canal between the villages of Mayfair and Mahala. During the operations two squad- rons of the Household Artillery charged the enemy's broken infantry very gallantly. I soon found the enemy were being lafiely reinforced from Tel-el-Kebir, in rear. I could see trains arrive. I did not think it could be in consonance with the traditions of the Queen's army that we should retire before any number of Egyptian troops, so I decided upon holding my ground until the evening, when I knew the reinforcements I had sent for would reach me. All day long I have had an Egyptian force of 10,000 men with ten guns in my front and my right flank. The precision of their artillery fire was very good, but fortunately they fired common shell ,pearly all day, and when they did fire shrapnel their fuses were badly cut. The enemy had their cavalry regiments in line, and our horses having been so recently on board ship, were not in condition to gallop much. Our two horse artillery guns were over-matched all day, but we were served with pluck and ability by Lieutenant Hickman and his men, the Royal Marine Artillery helping when our men were very tired. Oar casualties have been few. Will send you names to-morrow. Captain Hallam Parr and Lord lidelgand were wounded, the former through the leg and the latter through the hand. One or two other officers were slightly wounded. The Mounted Infantry, under Captain Farr, was handled admirably, and distinguished itself; and all the troops engaged did well. To-morrow I shall attack the enemy's position at Halenka, and hope to take possession ol:the dam they constructed there this morning. A further telegram from Sir G. Wolseley to the Secretary of State for War. dated Ismailia, 25th August, 2 a.m., Port Said, 25th August, 12 5 p.m., received 25th August, says;— "In my telegram of last night I omitted to mention that I' had, with men in the engagement yesterday, two gattlirgs worked by a detachment of seamen from the fleet, who per- formed the duty admirably."
